knowledge_statements.title: Penalized-Probability Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the bounded-position dual representation of lower-semicontinuous convex monetary risk measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\), let \(\rho:L^\infty(P)\to\mathbb R\) be a convex monetary risk measure with the Fatou property. Then there exists a penalty function \(\alpha:\mathcal Q\to[0,\infty]\), where \(\mathcal Q=\{Q:Q\ll P\}\), such that \[\rho(X)=\sup_{Q\in\mathcal Q}\bigl(E_Q[-X]-\alpha(Q)\bigr),\qquad X\in L^\infty(P).\] Conversely, the displayed supremum defines a convex, monotone, cash-additive functional whenever it is proper and \(\alpha\) is not identically infinite; its lower-semicontinuity depends on the chosen dual topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fatou-continuous convex monetary risk measure is the supremum of expected losses under alternative probabilities minus probability-specific penalties.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho:L^\infty(P)\to\mathbb R\) is convex, monotone, and cash additive

notation.meaning: Probability measures absolutely continuous with respect to P
Penalty assigned to each alternative probability measure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality role fits the container, but a nonnegative penalty is not justified without an appropriate normalization convention; general monetary risk measures can require penalties with negative values. The Fatou-property and converse topology claims also lack a source and locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Penalty Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the smallest penalty producing the convex dual representation on bounded positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper convex monetary risk measure \(\rho:L^\infty(P)\to(-\infty,\infty]\), define \[\alpha_{\min}(Q)=\sup_{X\in L^\infty(P)}\bigl(E_Q[-X]-\rho(X)\bigr),\qquad Q\ll P.\] Equivalently, for the acceptance set \(A_\rho=\{X:\rho(X)\le0\}\), \(\alpha_{\min}(Q)=\sup_{X\in A_\rho}E_Q[-X]\). Whenever \(\rho\) admits a penalized-probability representation, \[\rho(X)=\sup_{Q\ll P}\bigl(E_Q[-X]-\alpha_{\min}(Q)\bigr),\] and every other representing penalty \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\alpha(Q)\ge\alpha_{\min}(Q)\) for all \(Q\ll P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal penalty is the convex conjugate of the risk measure and is pointwise no larger than any other representing penalty.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho\) is a proper convex monetary risk measure on \(L^\infty(P)\)

notation.meaning: Minimal dual penalty of the risk measure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conjugate formula, acceptance-set formula, and pointwise minimality claim are standard and fit the container, but none has an inspectable citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Envelope Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specializes convex duality to coherent risk measures whose penalties are indicator functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho:L^\infty(P)\to\mathbb R\) be a coherent monetary risk measure with the Fatou property. Then there exists a nonempty convex set \(\mathcal U\) of probability measures absolutely continuous with respect to \(P\) such that \[\rho(X)=\sup_{Q\in\mathcal U}E_Q[-X].\] Equivalently, writing \(Z=dQ/dP\), the density envelope satisfies \(Z\ge0\), \(E_P[Z]=1\), and \(\rho(X)=\sup_{Z\in\mathcal Z}E_P[-XZ]\). The minimal penalty is \(0\) on the maximal representing envelope and \(+\infty\) outside it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coherent Fatou-continuous risk measure is the worst expected loss over a convex envelope of absolutely continuous probability measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(X)=\sup_{Q\in\mathcal U}E_Q[-X]\) for a nonempty convex risk envelope \(\mathcal U\).

notation.meaning: Risk envelope of alternative probability measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coherent risk-envelope representation is plausible and appropriately classified as duality, but the Fatou representation and the asserted maximal envelope require an authoritative source specifying the relevant closure topology.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Expectation Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interprets coherent risk as robust expected loss over a specified ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonempty set \(\mathcal U\) of probability measures on \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\), all absolutely continuous with respect to a reference measure \(P\), define \(\rho_{\mathcal U}:L^\infty(P)\to\mathbb R\) by \[\rho_{\mathcal U}(X)=\sup_{Q\in\mathcal U}E_Q[-X].\] Then \(\rho_{\mathcal U}\) is monotone, cash additive, positively homogeneous, and subadditive. Thus it assigns to a financial position the largest expected loss among the models in \(\mathcal U\); if the supremum is attained at \(Q^\star\), then \(Q^\star\) is a worst-case model for \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set defines a coherent risk measure, with any maximizing probability serving as a worst-case model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_{\mathcal U}(X)=\sup_{Q\in\mathcal U}E_Q[-X]\) is coherent, and an attaining \(Q^\star\) is worst-case for \(X\).

notation.meaning: A probability model attaining the supremum

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The worst-case expectation interpretation and coherence properties are mathematically standard and match the container, but the record supplies no citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Quantile-Integral Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a law-invariant risk functional as a weighted integral of loss quantiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\in L^1(P)\) be a loss and define its lower quantile by \(q_L(u)=\inf\{x\in\mathbb R:P(L\le x)\ge u\}\) for \(u\in(0,1)\). If \(\phi:(0,1)\to[0,\infty)\) is measurable, nondecreasing, and satisfies \(\int_0^1\phi(u)\,du=1\), then \[\rho_\phi(L)=\int_0^1 q_L(u)\phi(u)\,du\] whenever the integral is finite. The value depends only on the distribution of \(L\), is monotone and cash additive in the loss convention, and is a spectral coherent risk measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrating loss quantiles against a normalized nondecreasing weight produces a law-invariant coherent risk measure whenever the integral is finite.
assumptions_latex: \(L\in L^1(P)\) and the displayed weighted integral is finite
\(\phi\ge0\) is measurable, nondecreasing, and integrates to one
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_\phi(L)=\int_0^1q_L(u)\phi(u)\,du\) is a law-invariant coherent loss risk measure.

notation.meaning: Lower quantile function of the loss L

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quantile formula uses a consistent loss convention, but the precise linear or extended-valued domain on which coherence is asserted is not specified. An authoritative source is needed for the integrability regime and spectral-risk conclusion.

children.title: Spectral Representations
children.top_down_role: Quantile-weighted representation structure indexed by spectral weighting profiles.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the normalized increasing-spectrum representation for risk measured on losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A spectral risk measure on an integrable loss \(L\) has the form \[\rho_\phi(L)=\int_0^1 q_L(u)\phi(u)\,du,\] where the spectrum \(\phi\) is nonnegative, nondecreasing, and normalized by \(\int_0^1\phi(u)\,du=1\). Nonnegativity gives monotonicity, normalization gives cash additivity \(\rho_\phi(L+c)=\rho_\phi(L)+c\), and monotonicity of \(\phi\) assigns no less weight to worse loss quantiles. On every domain where the integral is finite, \(\rho_\phi\) is law invariant, positively homogeneous, and subadditive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectral risk measure averages loss quantiles using normalized weights that increase toward worse outcomes, yielding a law-invariant coherent risk measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_\phi(L)=\int_0^1q_L(u)\phi(u)\,du\) is coherent and law invariant on its finite domain.

notation.meaning: Quantile of loss L at probability level u
Spectral weight at probability level u

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spectral formula and weight conditions fit the container, but “every domain where the integral is finite” does not identify a stable function-space domain for the coherence claim. No supporting citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Distortion Representations
children.top_down_role: Representation structure induced by transformed probability levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Distortion Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a concave probability distortion to define a coherent Choquet integral of losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be an integrable real loss and let \(g:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) be nondecreasing with \(g(0)=0\) and \(g(1)=1\). Its distortion risk functional is the Choquet integral \[\rho_g(L)=\int_0^\infty g(P(L>t))\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0\bigl(g(P(L>t))-1\bigr)\,dt,\] whenever both improper integrals are finite. The functional is law invariant, monotone, cash additive, and positively homogeneous. If \(g\) is concave, then \(\rho_g\) is also subadditive and hence coherent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distorting loss-tail probabilities and integrating them gives a law-invariant risk functional; concavity of the distortion makes it coherent.
assumptions_latex: The displayed Choquet integrals are finite
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_g\) is a distortion risk functional, and concave \(g\) makes \(\rho_g\) coherent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Choquet tail formula and concavity-based coherence claim are plausible under the stated loss convention, but the sign, tail, finiteness, and subadditivity conventions require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Spectrum–Distortion Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Translation between spectral weights and probability distortions.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectrum–Distortion Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the differentiable concave-distortion formula equivalent to an increasing spectral weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) be concave and absolutely continuous with \(g(0)=0\) and \(g(1)=1\). Define \(\phi(u)=g'(1-u)\) for almost every \(u\in(0,1)\). Then \(\phi\ge0\), \(\phi\) is nondecreasing almost everywhere, and \(\int_0^1\phi(u)\,du=1\). For every loss \(L\) for which the integrals are finite, the distortion and spectral forms coincide: \[\rho_g(L)=\int_0^1q_L(u)\phi(u)\,du.\] Conversely, an integrable normalized nondecreasing spectrum \(\phi\) generates the concave distortion \(g(s)=\int_0^s\phi(1-v)\,dv\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolutely continuous concave distortion corresponds to a normalized increasing spectrum through reflected differentiation, and the two risk formulas agree.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is concave, absolutely continuous, and satisfies \(g(0)=0\), \(g(1)=1\)

notation.meaning: Lower quantile function of loss L

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reflected derivative formulas are consistent with the stated loss-tail convention, but the equivalence depends critically on quantile and distortion conventions. No authoritative source or locator supports the exact correspondence.

children.title: Representation Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regularity regimes controlling when spectral and distortion forms coincide.

assumptions_latex: \(X\in L^1\) is interpreted as a loss, and \(q_X(u)=\inf\{x:F_X(x)\ge u\}\).
The distortion induces a probability measure \(\nu_g\) on \((0,1)\) such that \(\rho_g(X)=\int_0^1 q_X(u)\,\nu_g(du)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_g\) has an ordinary spectral representation exactly when \(\nu_g\ll du\).

notation.meaning: quantile-weight measure induced by the distortion

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equivalence follows from absolute continuity of the induced quantile-weight measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the loss-quantile convention; endpoint atoms correspond to singular or essential-supremum components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated convention, a distortion representation \(ho_g(X)=\int_0^1 q_X(u)\,
u_g(du)\) is representable as \(ho_g(X)=\int_0^1 q_X(u)\phi(u)\,du\) for every admissible \(X\) if and only if \(
u_g\) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, with \(\phi=d
u_g/du\) almost everywhere. Singular mass in \(
u_g\), including endpoint mass, cannot be represented by an ordinary integrable spectral density, although it remains representable by a generalized spectral measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distortion and ordinary spectral formulas coincide exactly when the distortion's quantile-weight measure has a density; singular or endpoint mass marks the boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Equivalence Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the claimed iff boundary. Its validity depends on the distortion convention, endpoint treatment, admissible loss class, and whether quantile functions separate the relevant measures.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a probability measure on \([0,1]\), with the integral interpreted in the extended-real sense when \(\mu(\{1\})>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_\mu(X)=\int_{[0,1]}\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(X)\,\mu(d\alpha)\) is a law-invariant coherent risk functional.

notation.meaning: mixing probability measure over confidence levels

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: positive mixtures preserve coherence and law invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the endpoint convention \(\operatorname{AVaR}_1(X)=\operatorname{ess\,sup}X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(X)=(1-\alpha)^{-1}\int_\alpha^1 q_X(u)\,du\) for \(0\le\alpha<1\), and \(\operatorname{AVaR}_1(X)=\operatorname{ess\,sup}X\). The \(\mu\)-mixture is \[M_\mu(X)=\int_{[0,1]}\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(X)\,\mu(d\alpha).\] It is monotone, cash additive, positively homogeneous, subadditive, and law invariant on its effective domain. For suitable sets \(\mathcal M\) of mixing measures, Kusuoka-type functionals take the form \(\rho(X)=\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal M}M_\mu(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability-weighted mixture of Average Value-at-Risk levels is coherent and law invariant; suprema of such mixtures form Kusuoka representations.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixtures of Average Value-at-Risk

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mixture formula is standard, but an authoritative locator is required for the extended-real treatment of mass at alpha=1 and the stated effective-domain coherence claim.

children.title: Atomless-Space Regime
children.top_down_role: Kusuoka-type representation structure on probability spaces without atoms.

assumptions_latex: \(\rho:L^\infty\to\mathbb R\) is coherent, law invariant, and has the Fatou property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a nonempty set \(\mathcal M\subset\mathcal P([0,1])\) such that \(\rho(X)=\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal M}\int_{[0,1]}\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(X)\,\mu(d\alpha)\).

notation.meaning: probability measures on the confidence-level interval

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical atomless Kusuoka representation for Fatou-continuous coherent law-invariant risk measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical bounded-loss, atomless-space form of the Kusuoka theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(X\in L^\infty\), there exists a nonempty convex set \(\mathcal M\) of probability measures on \([0,1]\) for which \[\rho(X)=\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal M}\int_{[0,1]}\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(X)\,\mu(d\alpha).\] The set may be chosen so that the displayed supremum represents \(\rho\) simultaneously for all \(X\). Atomlessness supplies random variables with arbitrary distributions and permits law invariance to be expressed through the full quantile function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an atomless probability space, every coherent law-invariant risk measure with the Fatou property is a supremum of mixtures of Average Value-at-Risk.
knowledge_statements.title: Atomless-Space Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a substantive Kusuoka representation theorem. No source verifies the precise Fatou-property hypotheses, atomless-space assumptions, or simultaneous representing set.

children.title: Finite-Space Regime
children.top_down_role: Discrete representation structure on probability spaces with finite support.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is identified with a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Law invariance acts only on vectors having the same weighted empirical distribution \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\delta_{x_i}\).

notation.meaning: weighted empirical law of a loss vector

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-space law invariance is equality on weighted empirical distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the finite probability-space predicate from atomless Kusuoka conclusions.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Finite state space p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\), define their weighted empirical laws by \(P_x=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\delta_{x_i}\) and \(P_y=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\delta_{y_i}\). A functional \(\rho:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is law invariant on this finite space precisely when \[P_x=P_y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \rho(x)=\rho(y).\] If the probabilities are unequal, arbitrary coordinate permutations need not preserve \(P_x\); thus permutation invariance and law invariance coincide only for probability-preserving permutations, including all permutations in the uniform case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite probability space, law invariance means equality on loss vectors with identical weighted empirical distributions, not unrestricted permutation invariance when probabilities differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Space Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.1 Finite state space p. 58

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited locator is a finite-state Markov-chain section and the local file exposes only its table-of-contents entry; it does not inspectably support finite-space law invariance. Moreover, with unequal atom weights, equality of weighted empirical laws need not be characterized merely by probability-preserving coordinate permutations.

children.title: Finite-Space Representation Gap
children.top_down_role: Differences between atomless representation results and their finite-space counterparts.

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) has finitely many atoms.
\(\rho\) is coherent and law invariant on the resulting finite-dimensional loss space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The atomless Kusuoka theorem cannot be transferred solely from finite-space law invariance without an extension or an independent finite-space representation theorem.

notation.meaning: set of distributions realizable on the finite space
set of all bounded probability laws

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a finite space realizes only a restricted class of laws, so atomless extension arguments require extra hypotheses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the transfer gap, not nonexistence of every discrete AVaR representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite probability space realizes only a proper subset \(\mathcal D_\Omega\subsetneq\mathcal D_\infty\) of bounded laws. Consequently, law invariance of \(\rho\) constrains it only on \(\mathcal D_\Omega\), whereas the atomless Kusuoka argument compares arbitrary bounded laws and quantiles. Therefore the implication from coherence, law invariance, and the Fatou property to an atomless Kusuoka representation is not justified on a finite space unless \(\rho\) admits a suitable law-invariant extension to an atomless space or separate finite-space hypotheses establish the representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite spaces realize too few distributions for the atomless Kusuoka theorem to transfer automatically; an extension or a separate discrete representation result is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Space Representation Gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction from the atomless theorem is plausible, but the asserted representation-transfer gap requires a finite-space theorem, extension result, or explicit counterexample with a precise locator.

assumptions_latex: \(\rho:L^\infty\to\mathbb R\) is coherent, law invariant, Fatou continuous, and comonotone additive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists one probability measure \(\mu\) on \([0,1]\) such that \(\rho(X)=\int_{[0,1]}\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(X)\,\mu(d\alpha)\) for every \(X\in L^\infty\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: comonotone additivity specializes a coherent law-invariant functional to a single distortion or spectral measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomless bounded-loss specialization using the loss convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Comonotone additivity means \(\rho(X+Y)=\rho(X)+\rho(Y)\) whenever \(X=f(Z)\) and \(Y=g(Z)\) for some random variable \(Z\) and nondecreasing functions \(f,g\). Under the stated hypotheses, the supremum over Kusuoka mixtures specializes to a single mixture: there is a probability measure \(\mu\) on \([0,1]\) satisfying \[\rho(X)=\int_{[0,1]}\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(X)\,\mu(d\alpha)\] for every \(X\in L^\infty\). Equivalently, \(\rho\) is a coherent distortion risk functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Comonotone additivity reduces an atomless Kusuoka supremum to one Average Value-at-Risk mixture, equivalently a coherent distortion risk measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Comonotone Specialization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction from a Kusuoka supremum to a single AVaR mixture is a nontrivial theorem whose exact continuity and comonotone-additivity hypotheses require authoritative support.

children.title: Threshold Liftings
children.top_down_role: Lifted formulations organized around an auxiliary loss threshold.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical threshold representation of Average Value-at-Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss-oriented scalar threshold lifting for \(0\le\alpha<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Average Value-at-Risk admits the scalar threshold lifting \[\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(X)=\inf_{t\in\mathbb R}\left[t+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]\right].\] The lifted objective is convex in \(t\). Its minimizers are precisely the thresholds satisfying \(\mathbb P(X<t)\le\alpha\le\mathbb P(X\le t)\); hence every \(\alpha\)-quantile is an optimal threshold, with an interval of minimizers possible when the distribution has an atom or a gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average Value-at-Risk equals a one-dimensional minimization over a threshold; optimal thresholds are alpha-quantiles of the loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Liftings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The AVaR threshold formula and quantile condition need a cited theorem. The added statement that an interval of minimizers may result from an atom is imprecise: atoms can yield a unique minimizer; nontrivial intervals arise when the quantile set itself is an interval, typically from a distributional gap at the relevant level.

children.title: Excess-Loss Liftings
children.top_down_role: Lifted formulations organized around loss exceeding a reference level.

assumptions_latex: The auxiliary variable \(Y\in L^1\) is constrained almost surely.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: positive part is the pointwise least nonnegative majorant of the threshold excess
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional lifting of the positive-part term appearing in threshold risk formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed threshold \(t\), the excess-loss term has the exact lifting \[\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]=\inf_{Y\in L^1}\left\{\mathbb E[Y]:Y\ge X-t,\ Y\ge0\ \text{almost surely}\right\}.\] The infimum is attained by \(Y=(X-t)_+\). Consequently, any objective containing a positive coefficient multiplying \(\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]\) may replace that term by an auxiliary excess variable and the two almost-sure inequalities without changing its optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-part expectation is exactly the minimum expected auxiliary excess subject to majorizing both the threshold exceedance and zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Excess-Loss Liftings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-part lifting is mathematically standard and the representation kind fits, but no inspectable citation supports the functional-space and attainment conditions.

children.title: Threshold–Excess Coupling
children.top_down_role: Structural interaction between threshold selection and excess-loss terms.

assumptions_latex: \(t\in\mathbb R\) and \(Y\in L^1\) satisfy \(Y\ge X-t\) and \(Y\ge0\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifting is exact at \(Y=(X-t)_+\), and joint minimization yields \(\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(X)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: monotonicity of expectation makes the least feasible excess variable exact
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact coupling certificate for the threshold and excess variables in the AVaR lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every feasible pair \((t,Y)\) satisfies \[t+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[Y]\ge t+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]\ge\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(X).\] Equality in the first inequality is certified by \(Y=(X-t)_+\), and equality throughout holds when \(t\) is an \(\alpha\)-quantile of \(X\). Thus \[\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(X)=\inf_{t,Y}\left\{t+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[Y]:Y\ge X-t,\ Y\ge0\ \text{a.s.}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A threshold and excess variable certify AVaR exactly when the excess is the positive exceedance and the threshold is an alpha-quantile.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold–Excess Coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the exact threshold–excess coupling, but the equality and quantile-attainment characterization has no cited source.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real-valued loss for which the displayed expectation is well defined.
\(\ell:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_\ell(X)=\inf_{m\in\mathbb R}\{m+\mathbb E[\ell(X-m)]\}\) defines the optimized certainty equivalent in the loss convention.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard loss-oriented infimal definition of optimized certainty equivalents
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the loss convention; utility-oriented texts may state the sign-reversed supremal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The optimized certainty equivalent generated by \(\ell\) is \[\rho_\ell(X)=\inf_{m\in\mathbb R}\left\{m+\mathbb E[\ell(X-m)]\right\}.\] It is cash additive because \(\rho_\ell(X+c)=\rho_\ell(X)+c\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R\), and it is convex and monotone on its effective domain. If normalization is required, one additionally imposes \(\inf_{z\in\mathbb R}\{\ell(z)-z\}=0\), which gives \(\rho_\ell(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimized certainty equivalent minimizes cash plus expected transformed residual loss; convexity and monotonicity of the loss function yield a convex monetary risk functional.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimized Certainty Equivalents

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: OCE sign and normalization conventions vary. A source is required, and the stated assumptions do not by themselves exclude an identically minus-infinity infimum, so conditions ensuring a proper risk functional must be specified.

children.title: Epigraphical Liftings
children.top_down_role: Extended formulations based on epigraph geometry for risk-related functions.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(Z\) is a random vector for which at least one feasible majorant has finite expectation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pointwise epigraph majorization is exact under a minimizing expectation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise epigraph lifting followed by expectation minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The expectation of a convex integrand has the epigraphical lifting \[\mathbb E[f(Z)]=\inf_{Y}\left\{\mathbb E[Y]:(Z,Y)\in\operatorname{epi}f\ \text{almost surely}\right\}.\] Equivalently, feasibility requires \(Y\ge f(Z)\) almost surely. Every feasible \(Y\) provides an upper bound on \(\mathbb E[f(Z)]\), and equality is attained by \(Y=f(Z)\) whenever this random variable is measurable and integrable. The lifting is therefore exact under the stated integrability condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected convex cost equals the minimum expected epigraph variable constrained to dominate the cost pointwise almost surely.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Liftings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The epigraphical identity is standard, but the assumption of one finite feasible majorant does not alone ensure that the extended-real expectation of f(Z) is well defined. Measurability and negative-part or integrability conditions require a source and precise formulation.

children.title: Perspective Liftings
children.top_down_role: Extended formulations based on perspective transformations and scaled variables.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed perspective \(f^\pi\) is convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively homogeneous on \(\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: closed perspective of the convex function

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard closed-perspective construction in convex analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex perspective, including its zero-scale recession boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed perspective of \(f\) is the extended-real function \[f^\pi(z,\tau)=\begin{cases}\tau f(z/\tau),&\tau>0,\\ f^\infty(z),&\tau=0,\\ +\infty,&\tau<0.\end{cases}\] Its epigraph is the closure of \(\{(z,\tau,r):\tau>0,\ r\ge\tau f(z/\tau)\}\). The function \(f^\pi\) is proper, closed, convex, and positively homogeneous. Hence constraints involving a scaled convex cost can be lifted by introducing \(\tau\ge0\) and imposing \(r\ge f^\pi(z,\tau)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective lifts a scaled convex cost, using the recession function at zero scale to preserve closedness and convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Perspective Liftings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed-perspective definition and its convexity, closedness, homogeneity, and epigraph-closure properties are substantive convex-analysis claims with no cited authoritative locator.

children.title: Closed-Perspective Boundary
children.top_down_role: Closure and zero-scaling regimes affecting perspective-based formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Perspective Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex perspective at the zero scaling coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Its closed perspective is
\[
\operatorname{persp}f(x,t)=
\begin{cases}
tf(x/t),&t>0,\\
f^{\infty}(x),&t=0,\\
+\infty,&t<0,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(f^{\infty}\) is the recession function of \(f\). Consequently, the boundary value at zero scale is exactly \(\operatorname{persp}f(x,0)=f^{\infty}(x)\), rather than an arbitrary extension of the positive-scale formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective extends the positive-scale perspective to zero scale using the recession function and assigns infinity to negative scales.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard closed-perspective representation from convex analysis
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and content kind fit the boundary leaf, but no inspectable source supports the closed-perspective convention or its recession-function boundary value.

children.title: Canonical Risk-Measure Families
children.top_down_role: Named static risk and deviation families organized without duplicating their representation theory.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Shapiro, Dentcheva, and Ruszczynski, Lectures on Stochastic Programming
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Sections 6.2–6.3: semideviations, quantile deviations, Average Value-at-Risk, and examples
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Shapiro, Dentcheva, and Ruszczynski, Lectures on Stochastic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Value-at-Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-quantile definition under the loss convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real-valued loss and let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). The Value-at-Risk of \(X\) at confidence level \(\alpha\) is the lower \(\alpha\)-quantile
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)=q_X(\alpha):=\inf\{x\in\mathbb{R}:\mathbb{P}(X\le x)\ge\alpha\}.
\]
Thus \(\mathbb{P}(X\le \operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X))\ge\alpha\); no continuity or uniqueness of the quantile is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Value-at-Risk is the smallest loss threshold whose cumulative probability is at least the selected confidence level.

notation.meaning: Lower quantile of X at level alpha.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard lower-quantile definition under the loss convention
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-quantile loss convention is mathematically precise and fits a definition leaf, but the record has no citation or locator.

children.title: Average Value-at-Risk
children.top_down_role: Tail-average risk measure under the average-value-at-risk convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Average Value-at-Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-tail quantile-average convention for integrable losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\in L^1\) be a loss, let \(q_X(u)=\inf\{x:\mathbb{P}(X\le x)\ge u\}\), and let \(\alpha\in[0,1)\). Average Value-at-Risk is
\[
\operatorname{AVaR}_{\alpha}(X)=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\int_{\alpha}^{1}q_X(u)\,du.
\]
This quantile-integral definition remains valid when the distribution of \(X\) has atoms and averages precisely the upper \(1-\alpha\) fraction of the quantile function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average Value-at-Risk averages the loss quantiles from the confidence level through the upper endpoint.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard quantile-integral definition of Average Value-at-Risk
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quantile-integral definition is standard and correctly handles atoms, but no inspectable source supports the stated AVaR convention.

children.title: Conditional Value-at-Risk
children.top_down_role: Tail-conditional risk measure under the conditional-value-at-risk convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Value-at-Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar–Uryasev loss-side representation, valid with atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\in L^1\) and \(\alpha\in[0,1)\), define Conditional Value-at-Risk by
\[
\operatorname{CVaR}_{\alpha}(X)=\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{t+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb{E}[(X-t)_+]\right\}.
\]
The infimum is attained, every minimizing \(t\) is an \(\alpha\)-quantile of \(X\), and the optimal value equals \((1-\alpha)^{-1}\int_{\alpha}^{1}q_X(u)\,du\). This formulation handles probability mass at the quantile without conditioning ambiguities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional Value-at-Risk is the minimum of a threshold plus a scaled expected excess loss; it equals the upper quantile average.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variational representation fits this leaf, but the CVaR naming convention and the assertions about minimizers and equivalence require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Expected Shortfall
children.top_down_role: Tail-loss risk measure under the expected-shortfall convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Expected Shortfall
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-robust upper-tail definition for losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\in L^1\), let \(q_X\) be its lower quantile function, and let \(\alpha\in[0,1)\). Expected Shortfall at confidence level \(\alpha\) is
\[
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\int_{\alpha}^{1}q_X(u)\,du.
\]
For a continuous distribution this equals \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid X\ge q_X(\alpha)]\) whenever the conditioning event has probability \(1-\alpha\); with atoms, the quantile integral is the governing definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected Shortfall is the mean of upper-tail quantiles; the quantile formula remains well-defined when the loss distribution has atoms.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard quantile-integral definition of Expected Shortfall
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quantile-average definition is precise and the conditional-tail qualification is appropriately restricted, but the record lacks an inspectable citation.

children.title: Naming Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Distributional and convention-dependent regimes governing equivalence among the three names.

knowledge_statements.title: Naming Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence and non-equivalence of common tail-risk names.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(X\in L^1\) and \(\alpha\in[0,1)\), the quantile-average definitions satisfy
\[
\operatorname{AVaR}_{\alpha}(X)=\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}(X)=\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{t+\frac{\mathbb{E}[(X-t)_+]}{1-\alpha}\right\}.
\]
Thus CVaR is equivalent to AVaR and Expected Shortfall when CVaR denotes this variational value. The informal expression \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid X\ge\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(X)]\) is equivalent under suitable continuity, but can differ when an atom occurs at the quantile.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AVaR, Expected Shortfall, and variational CVaR coincide; naive conditional-tail means may differ when probability mass lies at Value-at-Risk.

notation.meaning: Lower alpha-quantile under the loss convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Tail-Risk Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-excess extension of first-order tail risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(p\in[1,\infty)\), \(\alpha\in[0,1)\), and a loss \(X\in L^p\). The order-\(p\) higher-order tail-risk functional is
\[
\rho_{\alpha,p}(X)=\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{t+(1-\alpha)^{-1/p}\lVert(X-t)_+\rVert_p\right\}.
\]
At \(p=1\), this reduces to the standard variational representation of Average Value-at-Risk. For \(p>1\), larger excesses receive superlinear weight through the \(L^p\)-norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-order tail-risk measure replaces mean excess above a threshold by a scaled power norm; order one recovers Average Value-at-Risk.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is internally coherent and recovers AVaR at p=1, but “higher-order tail-risk measure” is not uniquely standardized; an authoritative source is needed to establish that this is the intended family for the leaf.

children.title: Range Value-at-Risk
children.top_down_role: Tail-risk aggregation over a selected range of probability levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Range Value-at-Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantile-band convention with confidence-level endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\in L^1\) and let \(0\le\alpha<\beta<1\). Under the quantile-band convention, Range Value-at-Risk is
\[
\operatorname{RVaR}_{\alpha,\beta}(X)=\frac{1}{\beta-\alpha}\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}q_X(u)\,du,
\]
where \(q_X\) is the lower quantile function of the loss. It averages losses over the quantile-level range from \(\alpha\) to \(\beta\), including atoms through generalized quantiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Range Value-at-Risk averages the loss quantile function over a specified interval of confidence levels.

notation.meaning: Range Value-at-Risk on quantile levels alpha through beta.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard quantile-band convention for Range Value-at-Risk

children.title: Interval Value-at-Risk
children.top_down_role: Value-at-risk aggregation restricted to a specified probability interval.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Value-at-Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Average quantile over an explicitly oriented level interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\in L^1\) and \(0\le a<b<1\). Under the confidence-level convention, Interval Value-at-Risk is
\[
\operatorname{IVaR}_{[a,b]}(X)=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b q_X(u)\,du,
\]
where \(q_X(u)=\inf\{x\in\mathbb{R}:\mathbb{P}(X\le x)\ge u\}\). The interval endpoints index cumulative quantile levels, not upper-tail probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval Value-at-Risk is the average loss quantile across a stated interval of cumulative probability levels.

children.title: Range–Interval Convention Mapping
children.top_down_role: Naming, endpoint, and normalization conventions linking range and interval variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Range–Interval Convention Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter mapping between cumulative-level range and interval conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose both range and interval measures average the lower quantile function of \(X\in L^1\). For \(0\le\alpha<\beta<1\), identifying the interval endpoints by \(a=\alpha\) and \(b=\beta\) gives
\[
\operatorname{RVaR}_{\alpha,\beta}(X)=\operatorname{IVaR}_{[\alpha,\beta]}(X)
=\frac{(1-\alpha)\operatorname{AVaR}_{\alpha}(X)-(1-\beta)\operatorname{AVaR}_{\beta}(X)}{\beta-\alpha}.
\]
If endpoints are instead reported as upper-tail probabilities, the cumulative levels are obtained by the reversal \(u=1-p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Range and interval Value-at-Risk coincide when their cumulative-level endpoints match; upper-tail endpoint notation requires complementing and reversing the endpoints.
assumptions_latex: Both names use quantile averages rather than conditional-event means.

notation.meaning: Average Value-at-Risk at cumulative level u.
Upper-tail probability, related to cumulative level by u=1-p.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Risk Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantile-weighted coherent risk functional for losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\in L^1\). A spectral risk measure has the form
\[
\rho_{\phi}(X)=\int_0^1 q_X(u)\phi(u)\,du,
\]
where the measurable spectrum \(\phi:[0,1]\to[0,\infty)\) is nondecreasing and satisfies \(\int_0^1\phi(u)\,du=1\), with integrability sufficient for the displayed integral to be finite. Nonnegativity, normalization, and monotonicity of \(\phi\) encode increasing weight on worse loss quantiles and yield a law-invariant coherent risk measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectral risk measure is a normalized weighted average of loss quantiles whose weights do not decrease toward worse outcomes.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in L^1\) and the weighted quantile integral is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_{\phi}(X)=\int_0^1q_X(u)\phi(u)\,du\) is a law-invariant coherent risk functional.

notation.meaning: Risk spectrum assigning weights to quantile levels.
Spectral risk measure induced by phi.

knowledge_statements.title: Distortion Risk Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Choquet-integral definition under the loss and survival conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real-valued loss and let \(g:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) be nondecreasing with \(g(0)=0\) and \(g(1)=1\). When the integrals are finite, the distortion risk measure is
\[
\rho_g(X)=\int_0^{\infty}g(\mathbb{P}(X>t))\,dt-\int_{-\infty}^{0}\bigl[1-g(\mathbb{P}(X>t))\bigr]dt.
\]
It is the Choquet integral of \(X\) under the distorted probability capacity. If \(g\) is concave, \(\rho_g\) is coherent under this loss convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distortion risk measure applies a monotone distortion to loss survival probabilities before integrating; concave distortions produce coherent risk measures.
assumptions_latex: The two displayed improper integrals are finite.

notation.meaning: Distortion risk measure induced by g.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Effective-CDF representation of a worst-case expected cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For the stated cost function F and a family of nonnegative-demand distributions with uniformly bounded means.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathfrak M\) be a set of cumulative distribution functions satisfying \(H(z)=0\) for every \(H\in\mathfrak M\) and \(z<0\), and suppose \(\sup_{H\in\mathfrak M}\mathbb E_H[D]<+\infty\). Define \(f(x):=\sup_{H\in\mathfrak M}\mathbb E_H[F(x,D)]\) and \(\eta:=b/(b+h)\). Then there exists a cumulative distribution function \(\bar H\), depending on \(\mathfrak M\) and \(\eta\), such that \(\bar H(z)=0\) for \(z<0\) and
\[
f(x)=b\sup_{H\in\mathfrak M}\mathbb E_H[D]+(c-b)x+(b+h)\int_{-\infty}^{x}\bar H(z)\,dz.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a family of demand distributions supported on the nonnegative reals and having uniformly bounded means, the worst-case expected cost can be represented using a single effective cdf, determined by the distribution family and b/(b+h), plus affine and mean terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\,\bar H\text{ a cdf depending on }(\mathfrak M,\eta):\ \bar H(z)=0\ \forall z<0,\quad f(x)=b\sup_{H\in\mathfrak M}\mathbb E_H[D]+(c-b)x+(b+h)\int_{-\infty}^{x}\bar H(z)\,dz.\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss-oriented continuous mixtures of Average Value-at-Risk levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0\leq\alpha<1\), define \[\operatorname{AVaR}_{\alpha}(X):=\inf_{t\in\mathbb R}\left\{t+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]\right\}.\] The weighted Average Value-at-Risk generated by \(\mu\) is \[\operatorname{WAVaR}_{\mu}(X):=\int_{[0,1)}\operatorname{AVaR}_{\alpha}(X)\,\mu(d\alpha).\] The integrability condition on \(\mu\) ensures finiteness for every \(X\in L^1\). A finite discrete \(\mu\) yields a convex combination of AVaR levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted Average Value-at-Risk is a probability-weighted mixture of Average Value-at-Risk across confidence levels, with an integrability condition ensuring finite values for integrable losses.

children.title: Absolute Deviations
children.top_down_role: Dispersion measures based on absolute departures from a reference level.

notation.meaning: Mean absolute deviation about the expectation
Positive part of a real number

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Centered absolute deviation for an integrable random outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mean absolute deviation of \(X\) about its expectation is \[D_1(X):=\mathbb E\bigl[|X-\mathbb E[X]|\bigr].\] Equivalently, \[D_1(X)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])_+]+\mathbb E[(\mathbb E[X]-X)_+]=2\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])_+],\] where the last equality follows from the centering identity \(\mathbb E[X-\mathbb E[X]]=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean absolute deviation is the expected absolute distance from the mean; it equals twice either centered one-sided first semideviation.
knowledge_statements.title: Absolute Deviations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The centered mean absolute-deviation identity is standard and internally consistent, but the record has no citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Upper Semideviations
children.top_down_role: One-sided dispersion measures restricted to upper departures from a reference level.

notation.meaning: Order-p upper semideviation about the mean

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss-oriented upper semideviation centered at the expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The upper semideviation of order \(p\) is \[S_p^+(X):=\left(\mathbb E\left[(X-\mathbb E[X])_+^p\right]\right)^{1/p}=\|(X-\mathbb E[X])_+\|_p.\] It measures only realizations exceeding the mean. For \(p=1\), \(S_1^+(X)=\tfrac12\mathbb E[|X-\mathbb E[X]|]\). For any \(c\in\mathbb R\), it is translation invariant as a deviation: \(S_p^+(X+c)=S_p^+(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper semideviation is the L-p size of outcomes above their mean; it ignores lower outcomes and is unchanged by deterministic shifts.
knowledge_statements.title: Upper Semideviations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The upper-semideviation definition and stated properties are mathematically consistent, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Reference-Level Regimes
children.top_down_role: Mean-based, target-based, and optimized reference choices for deviation measurement.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{p,r}^+(X)=\|(X-r)_+\|_p\), with \(r\) fixed, endogenous, or distribution-dependent according to the regime.

notation.meaning: Order-p upper deviation above reference r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by how the one-sided deviation reference is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the one-sided deviation \[D_{p,r}^+(X):=\left(\mathbb E[(X-r)_+^p]\right)^{1/p},\] the reference-level regime is: fixed-target when \(r\) is prescribed independently of \(X\); endogenous when \(r\) is a decision variable optimized jointly with other variables; or distribution-dependent when \(r=T(X)\) for a specified location functional \(T\), such as \(T(X)=\mathbb E[X]\) or an \(\alpha\)-quantile. The regime must be fixed before comparing or optimizing deviations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-sided deviation may use a prescribed target, an optimized reference, or a distribution-dependent location such as the mean or a quantile.
knowledge_statements.title: Reference-Level Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is well-defined, but the three-way classification of reference-level regimes requires an authoritative source because the terminology is not canonical enough to validate from standard-field rationale alone.

assumptions_latex: \(p>0\), \(Y\) is a real-valued payoff, and \(\mathbb E[(\tau-Y)_+^p]<\infty\).

notation.meaning: Lower partial moment of order p about target tau

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Payoff-oriented lower partial moments relative to a fixed target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower partial moment of order \(p\) about \(\tau\) is \[\operatorname{LPM}_{p,\tau}(Y):=\mathbb E[(\tau-Y)_+^p]=\int_{(-\infty,\tau)}(\tau-y)^p\,P_Y(dy).\] It measures only payoff shortfalls below \(\tau\). For \(p=0\), when defined by the separate convention \(u_+^0=\mathbf 1_{\{u>0\}}\), it reduces to \(\mathbb P(Y<\tau)\); for \(p=1\), it is expected shortfall below the target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower partial moment averages a power of payoff shortfall below a fixed target, ignoring outcomes at or above that target.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower Partial-Moment Measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-order lower partial moment is standard, but the separate order-zero convention and terminology require a cited source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_\alpha(X)=\inf_{m\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E[\alpha(X-m)_++(1-\alpha)(m-X)_+]\), and every minimizer is an \(\alpha\)-quantile.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantile-centered deviation represented through asymmetric absolute loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the level-\(\alpha\) quantile deviation by \[Q_\alpha(X):=\inf_{m\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E[\ell_\alpha(X-m)],\qquad \ell_\alpha(u):=\alpha u_++(1-\alpha)(-u)_+.\] A number \(m\) attains the infimum if and only if \[\mathbb P(X<m)\leq\alpha\leq\mathbb P(X\leq m),\] so the optimizing reference is an \(\alpha\)-quantile. The infimum is finite for every integrable \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quantile deviation is minimum expected asymmetric absolute loss; its optimal reference points are exactly the selected-level quantiles.
knowledge_statements.title: Quantile-Deviation Measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The check-loss representation and quantile optimality condition are mathematically consistent, but the name and normalization of the quantile-deviation functional need authoritative support.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a loss and \(\mathbb E[e^{\theta X}]<\infty\).

notation.meaning: Entropic risk measure with risk-aversion parameter theta

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss convention with positive exponential risk aversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The entropic risk measure with parameter \(\theta\) is \[\rho_\theta(X):=\frac{1}{\theta}\log\mathbb E[e^{\theta X}].\] Its effective domain consists of losses having a finite exponential moment at \(\theta\). It is monotone, convex, and cash additive: for every constant \(c\in\mathbb R\), \(\rho_\theta(X+c)=\rho_\theta(X)+c\). Generally it is not positively homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entropic risk is the log exponential moment divided by risk aversion; it is convex, monotone, cash additive, and generally not homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.title: Entropic Risk Measure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The loss-oriented entropic-risk definition and listed properties are standard and consistent, but no citation with an inspectable locator is provided.

assumptions_latex: \(\ell:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, nondecreasing, and not constant.
\(c\) lies in the range permitting a finite feasible capital level.

notation.meaning: Loss function measuring residual loss after capital

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cash-additive loss-based shortfall risk under an expected-loss acceptance criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The shortfall risk measure induced by \(\ell\) and threshold \(c\) is \[\rho_{\ell,c}(X):=\inf\left\{m\in\mathbb R:\mathbb E[\ell(X-m)]\leq c\right\}.\] Thus \(\rho_{\ell,c}(X)\) is the least deterministic capital subtracted from the loss that makes expected residual loss acceptable. Whenever finite, it is monotone and cash additive. If \(\ell\) is convex, then \(\rho_{\ell,c}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shortfall risk is the least capital that reduces expected transformed residual loss below an acceptable threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Shortfall Risk Measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shortfall-risk formula uses a recognized convention, but the domain of X and the admissibility condition on c are not stated precisely enough to validate finiteness and the asserted properties without a source.

assumptions_latex: \(\phi:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, nondecreasing, and satisfies \(\phi(0)=0\) and \(1\in\partial\phi(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss-oriented optimized certainty equivalent with normalized convex loss function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The optimized certainty-equivalent risk measure generated by \(\phi\) is \[\rho_\phi(X):=\inf_{m\in\mathbb R}\left\{m+\mathbb E[\phi(X-m)]\right\},\] with value \(+\infty\) when the objective is never finite. The scalar \(m\) is optimized jointly with the expected transformed residual loss. Under the stated normalization, \(\rho_\phi(0)=0\); the functional is monotone, convex, and cash additive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimized certainty equivalent minimizes capital plus expected convex loss of the residual, producing a normalized convex cash-additive risk measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimized Certainty-Equivalent Measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optimized certainty-equivalent formula and normalization are mathematically plausible, but the random-variable domain and expectation convention for extended-valued phi are not specified and no authoritative citation is supplied.

notation.meaning: Exponential moment of X at theta

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raw and logarithmically normalized exponential-moment criteria for losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exponential-moment criterion at sensitivity \(\theta\) is \[M_X(\theta):=\mathbb E[e^{\theta X}].\] Its cash-additive logarithmic normalization is \[R_\theta(X):=\frac{1}{\theta}\log M_X(\theta).\] Because the logarithm is strictly increasing, minimizing \(M_{X(x)}(\theta)\) over a common feasible set is equivalent to minimizing \(R_\theta(X(x))\). The raw criterion satisfies \(M_{X+c}(\theta)=e^{\theta c}M_X(\theta)\), whereas \(R_\theta(X+c)=R_\theta(X)+c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponential-moment risk uses an expected exponential loss; taking its scaled logarithm preserves minimizers and makes the criterion cash additive.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Moment Risk Measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The raw exponential moment, logarithmic normalization, and optimization equivalence are correct under the stated common theta and feasible set, but the intended family scope lacks authoritative support.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pure risk-minimization model has the form \[v^*:=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\rho(L(x,\xi)).\] A decision \(x^*\in\mathcal X\) is optimal when \(\rho(L(x^*,\xi))=v^*\). No distinct expected-value reward or cost is assigned an independent weight; any sensitivity to location, dispersion, or tails is encoded entirely by \(\rho\). If \(\mathcal X\) is convex, \(L(\cdot,\xi)\) is convex almost surely, and \(\rho\) is convex and monotone, then the objective is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pure risk minimization chooses a feasible decision solely by minimizing one risk functional of its random loss.

If \(\mathcal X\) is convex and both mappings \(x\mapsto\mathbb E[L(x,\xi)]\) and \(x\mapsto D(L(x,\xi))\) are convex, then the scalarized objective is convex for every \(\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mean-risk model minimizes expected loss plus a nonnegative weighted deviation penalty; the weight controls aversion to dispersion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mean–Risk Scalarization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static scalarization of expected outcome and dispersion for a minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an uncertain outcome Z_x=F(x,\omega) and a dispersion functional \mathbb D, mean–risk analysis considers the criteria \mathbb E[Z_x] and \mathbb D[Z_x]. For c\ge 0, the scalarized minimization model is \[\min_{x\in X}\left\{\mathbb E[Z_x]+c\mathbb D[Z_x]\right\}.\] Varying c provides a parametric means of generating mean–risk tradeoffs. If \mathbb D[Z]=\operatorname{Var}(Z), then Z must be square-integrable, and variance penalizes deviations above and below the mean symmetrically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean–risk analysis combines expected outcome and dispersion through a nonnegative risk-price parameter. Varying that parameter explores mean–risk tradeoffs. Variance requires square-integrable outcomes and treats favorable and unfavorable deviations symmetrically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X}\left\{\mathbb E[Z_x]+c\mathbb D[Z_x]\right\}\text{ is the scalarized mean–risk minimization model.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, variational representation, quantile minimizers, and mean–risk uses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Z\in\mathcal L_1(\Omega,\mathcal F,P), let H_Z(z)=\Pr(Z\le z), and fix \alpha\in(0,1). With H_Z^{-1}(\alpha)=\inf\{t:H_Z(t)\ge\alpha\}, define \[\mathfrak q_\alpha[Z]=\mathbb E\left[\max\left\{(1-\alpha)(H_Z^{-1}(\alpha)-Z),\alpha(Z-H_Z^{-1}(\alpha))\right\}\right].\] This functional is finite and has the representation \[\mathfrak q_\alpha[Z]=\min_{t\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E\left[\max\left\{(1-\alpha)(t-Z),\alpha(Z-t)\right\}\right].\] Every t satisfying \(\Pr(Z<t)\le\alpha\le\Pr(Z\le t)\) is a minimizer. For c\ge0, it yields the models \[\min_{x\in X}\{\mathbb E[Z_x]+c\mathfrak q_{1-\alpha}[Z_x]\},\qquad \max_{x\in X}\{\mathbb E[Z_x]-c\mathfrak q_\alpha[Z_x]\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted mean deviation from an alpha-quantile is a finite asymmetric deviation measure for integrable outcomes. It equals the minimum of an asymmetric absolute-loss objective, and every alpha-quantile minimizes that objective. The measure can penalize upper loss deviations in minimization or lower reward deviations in maximization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and Lower Central Semideviations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided central dispersion measures and their direction-specific mean–risk models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix p\in[1,\infty) and let Z\in\mathcal L_p(\Omega,\mathcal F,P). The upper and lower central semideviations are \[\sigma_p^+[Z]=\left(\mathbb E[(Z-\mathbb E[Z])_+^p]\right)^{1/p},\qquad \sigma_p^-[Z]=\left(\mathbb E[(\mathbb E[Z]-Z)_+^p]\right)^{1/p}.\] Both are finite on \mathcal L_p. For c\ge0, cost minimization may use \[\min_{x\in X}\left\{\mathbb E[Z_x]+c\sigma_p^+[Z_x]\right\},\] which penalizes costs above their mean, whereas reward maximization may use \[\max_{x\in X}\left\{\mathbb E[Z_x]-c\sigma_p^-[Z_x]\right\},\] which penalizes rewards below their mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper and lower central semideviations measure departures above and below the mean. They are finite for random variables with finite pth moments. Upper semideviation is used to penalize excessive costs, while lower semideviation penalizes deficient rewards.

knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Constrained Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical stochastic program with explicit upper bounds on one or more loss-risk functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a feasible set, let \(L_0(x,\xi),L_1(x,\xi),\ldots,L_m(x,\xi)\) be integrable random losses, and let \(\rho_j\) be real-valued risk functionals. A risk-constrained model is
\[\min_{x\in X}\ \mathbb{E}[L_0(x,\xi)]\quad\text{subject to}\quad \rho_j(L_j(x,\xi))\le b_j,\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.\]
Its feasible set is \(X_R=\{x\in X:\rho_j(L_j(x,\xi))\le b_j\text{ for every }j\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A risk-constrained model minimizes a nominal objective while requiring every specified loss-risk measure to remain below its prescribed budget.
assumptions_latex: \(L_j(x,\xi)\) belongs to the domain of \(\rho_j\) for every relevant \(x\) and \(j\).

notation.meaning: random loss associated with criterion j

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Risk Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued formulation for simultaneously comparing several risk measures or loss components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(m\ge2\), define the risk vector \(R:X\to\mathbb{R}^m\) by
\[R(x)=\bigl(\rho_1(L_1(x,\xi)),\ldots,\rho_m(L_m(x,\xi))\bigr).\]
A feasible point \(x^\star\in X\) is risk-efficient if no \(x\in X\) satisfies \(R_j(x)\le R_j(x^\star)\) for all \(j\) with strict inequality for at least one \(j\). For weights \(w\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\), a standard scalarization minimizes \(\sum_{j=1}^m w_jR_j(x)\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple-risk optimization compares a vector of risk criteria; efficiency forbids simultaneous improvement of all criteria, and nonnegative weights provide a scalarized model.
assumptions_latex: \(L_j(x,\xi)\) lies in the domain of \(\rho_j\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) is risk-efficient exactly when no feasible risk vector dominates \(R(x^\star)\) componentwise.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: AVaR Variational Form and Conservative Chance-Constraint Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static Average Value-at-Risk for integrable losses, including its threshold representation, properties, and safe-approximation role.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \alpha\in(0,1) and Z\in\mathcal L_1(\Omega,\mathcal F,P). Average Value-at-Risk is \[\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(Z)=\inf_{t\in\mathbb R}\left\{t+\alpha^{-1}\mathbb E[(Z-t)_+]\right\}.\] The threshold objective is convex, and its minimum is attained between the left and right \((1-\alpha)\)-quantiles; in particular, \(\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(Z)\) is a minimizer. Consequently, \(\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(Z)\ge\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(Z)\), and \[\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(Z+\tau)=\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(Z)+\tau\qquad(\tau\in\mathbb R).\] Thus \[\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(Z_x)\le\tau\;\Longrightarrow\;\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(Z_x)\le\tau\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\Pr(Z_x\le\tau)\ge1-\alpha.\] Hence the AVaR constraint is a conservative inner approximation of the corresponding chance constraint. AVaR is convex and monotone; therefore, if x\mapsto G(x,\xi) is convex for almost every \xi, then x\mapsto\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(G(x,\xi)) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AVaR is the minimum over thresholds of the threshold plus scaled expected excess loss. A VaR quantile minimizes this convex problem, so AVaR dominates VaR and an AVaR bound safely implies the corresponding chance constraint. AVaR is translation equivariant, convex, monotone, and preserves convexity of an almost-surely convex random loss.
assumptions_latex: x\mapsto G(x,\xi)\text{ is convex for a.e. }\xi\text{ for the composition claim}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrated-Quantile and Mean-Deviation Representations of AVaR
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent static AVaR formulas, with continuity required for the conditional-tail representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Z\in\mathcal L_1(\Omega,\mathcal F,P), let H be its cdf, and let \alpha\in(0,1). Then \[\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(Z)=\frac1\alpha\int_{1-\alpha}^{1}\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\tau}(Z)\,d\tau=\mathbb E[Z]+\frac1\alpha\mathfrak q_{1-\alpha}[Z].\] If H is continuous at \(\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(Z)\), then \[\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(Z)=\frac1\alpha\int_{\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(Z)}^{\infty}z\,dH(z)=\mathbb E\left[Z\mid Z\ge\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(Z)\right].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every integrable outcome, AVaR equals an average of upper quantiles and also the mean plus a scaled weighted deviation from a quantile. If the distribution function is continuous at VaR, AVaR additionally equals the upper-tail integral and the conditional mean beyond VaR.
assumptions_latex: H\text{ is continuous at }\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(Z)\text{ for the tail-integral and conditional-expectation identities}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(Z)=\alpha^{-1}\int_{1-\alpha}^{1}\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\tau}(Z)\,d\tau=\mathbb E[Z]+\alpha^{-1}\mathfrak q_{1-\alpha}[Z],\quad H\text{ continuous at VaR}\Rightarrow\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(Z)=\mathbb E[Z\mid Z\ge\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(Z)].

knowledge_statements.title: Rockafellar–Uryasev Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-tail average value-at-risk representation for an integrable loss under the loss-quantile convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z\) be an integrable real-valued loss and let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Define \((u)_+=\max\{u,0\}\). Then upper-tail average value-at-risk satisfies
\[\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(Z)=\min_{\eta\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\eta+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb{E}[(Z-\eta)_+]\right\}.\]
The minimum is attained, and its minimizers are precisely the \(\alpha\)-quantiles \(\eta\) satisfying \(\mathbb{P}(Z<\eta)\le\alpha\le\mathbb{P}(Z\le\eta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average value-at-risk equals the minimum of a threshold plus a scaled expected excess loss; minimizing thresholds are alpha-quantiles.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and quantile characterization are standard and mathematically plausible, but no source or locator is supplied for the stated AVaR convention and complete minimizer characterization.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Scenario Linear Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear epigraph lifting of finite-scenario average value-at-risk for affine scenario losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let scenarios \(i=1,\ldots,N\) have probabilities \(p_i\ge 0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^N p_i=1\), and affine losses \(\ell_i(x)\). For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), the constraint \(\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(\ell(x))\le t\) is equivalent to the existence of \(\eta\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(s_i\ge0\) such that
\[s_i\ge \ell_i(x)-\eta\quad(i=1,\ldots,N),\qquad \eta+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^N p_i s_i\le t.\]
Thus an AVaR objective or constraint admits a linear-programming representation whenever the remaining model is linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-scenario AVaR becomes linear by introducing a threshold and one nonnegative excess variable per scenario.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(\ell(x))\le t\) is equivalent to the displayed finite linear system.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Optimization Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiability of the Rockafellar–Uryasev objective away from probability mass at the active threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be open, let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and define
\[F(x,\eta)=\eta+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb{E}[(L(x,\xi)-\eta)_+].\]
Fix \((x,\eta)\in X\times\mathbb{R}\). Suppose \(L(\cdot,\xi)\) is continuously differentiable almost surely, \(L(y,\xi)\) is integrable for \(y\) near \(x\), and there are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) and an integrable random variable \(M\) such that \(\sup_{y\in U}\|\nabla_xL(y,\xi)\|\le M(\xi)\) almost surely. If \(\mathbb{P}(L(x,\xi)=\eta)=0\), then \(F\) is differentiable at \((x,\eta)\), with
\[\nabla_xF(x,\eta)=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_{\{L(x,\xi)>\eta\}}\nabla_xL(x,\xi)],\qquad \partial_\eta F(x,\eta)=1-\frac{\mathbb{P}(L(x,\xi)>\eta)}{1-\alpha}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the loss has no probability mass at the active threshold and differentiation may be interchanged with expectation, the AVaR auxiliary objective is differentiable and its decision gradient averages loss gradients over tail outcomes.
assumptions_latex: \(L(\cdot,\xi)\) is continuously differentiable almost surely and locally integrable.
The local loss gradients are dominated by an integrable random variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is differentiable at \((x,\eta)\) with the displayed derivatives.

notation.meaning: integrable local bound for the loss gradient

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Optimization Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient interface for convex loss models when scenarios can lie exactly at the AVaR threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(L(\cdot,\xi)\) is finite and convex almost surely and \(F(x,\eta)=\eta+(1-\alpha)^{-1}\mathbb{E}[(L(x,\xi)-\eta)_+]\). Choose measurable \(g(\xi)\in\partial_xL(x,\xi)\) and \(\theta(\xi)\) with \(\theta=0\) when \(L<\eta\), \(\theta=1\) when \(L>\eta\), and \(\theta\in[0,1]\) when \(L=\eta\). Under integrable boundedness permitting subdifferential interchange,
\[\left(\frac{\mathbb{E}[\theta g]}{1-\alpha},\ 1-\frac{\mathbb{E}[\theta]}{1-\alpha}\right)\in\partial F(x,\eta).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At threshold atoms, AVaR is handled by convex subgradients using fractional weights for outcomes exactly equal to the threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(L(\cdot,\xi)\) is finite and convex almost surely.
The selected subgradients are integrably bounded.
Expectation and convex subdifferentiation may be interchanged.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothing Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Softplus smoothing of the AVaR hinge with a uniform approximation bound and convergence of exact minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), let \(K\) be a nonempty compact feasible set for \((x,\eta)\), and, for \(\mu>0\), define \(h_\mu(u)=\mu\log(1+e^{u/\mu})\) and
\[F_\mu(x,\eta)=\eta+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb{E}[h_\mu(L(x,\xi)-\eta)].\]
Let
\[F(x,\eta)=\eta+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb{E}[(L(x,\xi)-\eta)_+].\]
Assume these expectations are finite on \(K\) and \(F\) is lower semicontinuous on \(K\). Since \(0\le h_\mu(u)-(u)_+\le\mu\log 2\) for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[0\le F_\mu(x,\eta)-F(x,\eta)\le\frac{\mu\log 2}{1-\alpha}\qquad((x,\eta)\in K).\]
Hence \(F_\mu\to F\) uniformly on \(K\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\). If each \(F_\mu\) attains its minimum on \(K\), every cluster point of exact minimizers of \(F_\mu\) minimizes \(F\) on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Softplus uniformly approximates the AVaR hinge with error at most the smoothing parameter times log two divided by the tail probability. On a compact feasible set with a lower-semicontinuous limiting objective, cluster points of exact smoothed minimizers solve the unsmoothed problem.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty compact feasible set for \((x,\eta)\).
The expectations defining \(F\) and \(F_\mu\) are finite on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{(x,\eta)\in K}|F_\mu(x,\eta)-F(x,\eta)|\le\mu\log(2)/(1-\alpha)\), and every cluster point of exact minimizers of \(F_\mu\) minimizes \(F\) on \(K\).

notation.meaning: softplus smoothing of the positive-part function

knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Envelope Adversaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of a coherent risk measure as worst-case expectation over admissible probability distortions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\rho:L^p(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)\to\mathbb{R}\) be a finite, lower-semicontinuous coherent risk measure with the loss convention. Then there exists a nonempty closed convex risk envelope \(\mathcal{Q}\subseteq L^q\) such that every \(Q\in\mathcal{Q}\) satisfies \(Q\ge0\) almost surely and \(\mathbb{E}_P[Q]=1\), and
\[\rho(Z)=\sup_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathbb{E}_P[QZ].\]
Thus risk optimization permits an adversary to select an admissible density \(Q\) that emphasizes costly outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coherent loss-risk measure is the worst expected loss under probability densities drawn from its convex risk envelope.
assumptions_latex: \(1\le p<\infty\) and \(q\) is the Hölder conjugate of \(p\).
\(\rho\) is finite, coherent, and lower semicontinuous on \(L^p\).

notation.meaning: density relative to the reference probability P

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is an appropriate duality statement for risk-envelope adversaries, but no source fixes the precise Lp topology, dual space, closure notion, and hypotheses supporting the representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Adjusted Probability Weights
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario risk-envelope weights for average value-at-risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For scenario losses \(z_i\in\mathbb{R}\), reference probabilities \(p_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_i p_i=1\), and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\),
\[\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(z)=\max_{q\in\mathbb{R}^N}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^N q_i z_i: \sum_{i=1}^Nq_i=1,\ 0\le q_i\le\frac{p_i}{1-\alpha}\right\}.\]
The maximizing \(q_i\) are risk-adjusted probabilities: they preserve total mass while shifting as much admissible weight as possible toward the largest losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-scenario AVaR maximizes expected loss over probability weights capped by each reference probability divided by the tail probability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-support reduction for a moment problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States equality of the worst-case expectation over the full moment ambiguity set and its subclass supported on at most q+1 points; it does not assert attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Risk Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saddle formulation separating a primal decision from a finite-scenario risk-envelope adversary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, let each \(\ell_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous and convex, and let \(\mathcal{Q}\subseteq\{q\ge0:\sum_iq_i=1\}\) be nonempty, compact, and convex. Then
\[\min_{x\in X}\rho(\ell(x))=\min_{x\in X}\max_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\sum_{i=1}^Nq_i\ell_i(x)=\max_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\min_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^Nq_i\ell_i(x).\]
The inner primal problem is an ordinary weighted scenario problem, while the dual problem selects the risk-adjusted weights.
