knowledge_statements.statement_title: Von Mises directional derivative and empirical plug-in linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The displayed plug-in relations are formal first-order approximations, not an asserted central limit theorem or asymptotic guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a law-invariant risk measure be represented by a statistical functional \(\mathfrak F(P)\), and let \(\theta^*=\mathfrak F(P)\) and \(\widehat\theta_N=\mathfrak F(P_N)\), where \(P_N\) is the empirical measure. For a probability measure \(Q\) on the same measurable space as \(P\), if the limit exists, the directional derivative along the mixture direction \(Q-P\) is
\[
\mathfrak F'(P,Q-P):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\mathfrak F(P+t(Q-P))-\mathfrak F(P)}{t}.
\]
If \(\mathfrak F'(P,\cdot)\) is linear on the admissible directions, then \(\mathfrak F\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(P\). Formally, its first-order empirical plug-in linearization is
\[
\mathfrak F(P_N)-\mathfrak F(P)\approx\mathfrak F'(P,P_N-P),
\qquad
\sqrt N(\widehat\theta_N-\theta^*)\approx\mathfrak F'\!\left(P,\sqrt N(P_N-P)\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A law-invariant risk measure may be treated as a functional of its probability law and estimated by applying that functional to the empirical law. Its Von Mises directional derivative is the one-sided derivative along mixtures with another probability law. Linearity in the admissible direction yields Gâteaux differentiability. Evaluation at the empirical-law perturbation gives a formal first-order approximation for large-sample analysis, but the extract itself does not establish an asymptotic distribution or error bound.
assumptions_latex: \mathfrak F(P)\text{ is well defined as a functional of the law }P
P\text{ and }Q\text{ are probability measures on the same measurable space}
P+t(Q-P)\text{ lies in the domain of }\mathfrak F\text{ for }t\in[0,1]
\mathfrak F'(P,Q-P)\text{ exists for the direction under consideration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathfrak F'(P,\cdot)\text{ linear on admissible directions}\Rightarrow\mathfrak F\text{ is Gâteaux differentiable at }P;\quad \sqrt N(\widehat\theta_N-\theta^*)\approx\mathfrak F'\!\left(P,\sqrt N(P_N-P)\right)\text{ formally}.

knowledge_statements.title: Plug-In Risk Estimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical-distribution substitution for estimating a law-invariant risk functional from loss observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) be real-valued loss observations and let
\[\widehat P_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{Z_i}\]
be their empirical distribution. Let \(\rho\) be a law-invariant risk functional, and denote by \(\mathcal{R}(P)\) its induced value on a loss distribution \(P\). The plug-in estimator is
\[\widehat\rho_n=\mathcal{R}(\widehat P_n).\]
For average value-at-risk at level \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), this becomes
\[\widehat{\operatorname{AVaR}}_{\alpha,n}=\min_{\eta\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\eta+\frac{1}{n(1-\alpha)}\sum_{i=1}^n(Z_i-\eta)_+\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A plug-in estimator evaluates the distributional form of a law-invariant risk functional at the empirical loss distribution; empirical AVaR replaces the population expectation by the sample average.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho\) is law invariant and its induced distributional functional \(\mathcal{R}\) is defined at \(\widehat P_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\rho_n=\mathcal{R}(\widehat P_n)\), with the displayed finite-sample formula for AVaR.

notation.meaning: distributional functional induced by the law-invariant risk functional

children.title: Risk-Estimator Consistency
children.top_down_role: Large-sample regimes supporting convergence of estimated risk values or optimizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Estimator Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong consistency of empirical average value-at-risk for an integrable independent loss sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z_1,Z_2,\ldots\) be independent and identically distributed copies of an integrable real-valued loss \(Z\), and fix \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Define
\[\widehat A_n=\min_{\eta\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\eta+\frac{1}{n(1-\alpha)}\sum_{i=1}^n(Z_i-\eta)_+\right\}.\]
Then
\[\widehat A_n\longrightarrow\operatorname{AVaR}_\alpha(Z)\qquad\text{almost surely as }n\to\infty.\]
Thus the empirical plug-in estimator consistently estimates population average value-at-risk without requiring continuity of the loss distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For iid integrable losses and a fixed tail level, empirical AVaR converges almost surely to population AVaR, even when the distribution has atoms.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_1,Z_2,\ldots\) are independent and identically distributed as \(Z\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-consistency theorem is standard and fits the exact container, but no authoritative theorem locator supports the almost-sure convergence claim under only integrability and without distributional continuity.

children.title: Risk-Estimator Asymptotic Distributions
children.top_down_role: Limiting fluctuation behavior for estimated risk quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Estimator Asymptotic Distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical central limit theorem for an empirical value-at-risk estimator at a regular quantile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L_1,\ldots,L_n\) be independent copies of a real loss \(L\), with distribution function \(F\). Fix \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define \(q_\alpha=F^{-1}(\alpha)\), and let \(\widehat q_{\alpha,n}=F_n^{-1}(\alpha)\). If \(F\) is differentiable near \(q_\alpha\), with continuous density \(f\) satisfying \(f(q_\alpha)>0\), then
\[
\sqrt n\bigl(\widehat q_{\alpha,n}-q_\alpha\bigr)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ N\!\left(0,\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{f(q_\alpha)^2}\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular empirical loss quantile is asymptotically normal, with variance increasing as the density at the target quantile decreases.

notation.meaning: Population value-at-risk, defined as the lower alpha-quantile of loss.
Empirical distribution function of the sampled losses.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem and theorem content kind fit the leaf, but no citation supports the precise quantile convention, hypotheses, and variance formula.

children.title: Tail-Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Distributional tail conditions governing estimator stability and limiting behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Regularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity conditions separating root-n quantile inference from expected-shortfall inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a loss \(L\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), the root-\(n\) regular regime for empirical value-at-risk requires that \(q_\alpha=F^{-1}(\alpha)\) be unique and that \(F\) admit a continuous density \(f\) with \(0<f(q_\alpha)<\infty\). For empirical expected shortfall, additionally require
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[(L-q_\alpha)_+^2\right]<\infty.
\]
The first conditions permit local linearization of the quantile; the moment condition makes the tail-average influence function square-integrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive density at the target quantile supports root-sample-size VaR inference; expected-shortfall normality additionally requires a finite second tail moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0<f(q_\alpha)<\infty\ \text{and}\ \mathbb E[(L-q_\alpha)_+^2]<\infty\ \text{define the regular joint VaR--ES regime}

notation.meaning: Positive part, max of u and zero.
Lower alpha-quantile of the loss distribution.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits, but the claim that these conditions are required is stronger than the usual statement of a sufficient regular regime. A source must establish the intended VaR–ES estimator and exact necessity or sufficiency formulation.

children.title: Asymptotic Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth, heavy-tailed, or nonunique regimes where standard asymptotic behavior changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of root-n quantile asymptotics when the distribution is flat to higher order at the target quantile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) and an integer \(k>1\). Suppose that, in a neighborhood of its unique \(\alpha\)-quantile \(q\), a distribution satisfies
\[
F(q+h)=\alpha+c\,\operatorname{sgn}(h)|h|^k+o(|h|^k),\qquad c>0.
\]
Then its empirical quantile \(\widehat q_{\alpha,n}\) generally has scale \(n^{-1/(2k)}\), not \(n^{-1/2}\). Consequently \(\sqrt n(\widehat q_{\alpha,n}-q)\) is not tight, and the regular Gaussian quantile limit fails because \(f(q)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the distribution crosses the target probability only at higher order, the empirical quantile converges more slowly and its usual root-sample-size Gaussian limit fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat q_{\alpha,n}-q=O_p(n^{-1/(2k)})\ \text{and the regular root-}n\text{ Gaussian limit fails}

notation.meaning: Local order at which the distribution crosses alpha.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the asserted rate and non-tightness require a source treating this higher-order quantile-crossing regime and the chosen empirical-quantile convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sample Risk Confidence Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-free confidence bracket for value-at-risk obtained from the empirical distribution and the DKW inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L_1,\ldots,L_n\) be i.i.d. with distribution function \(F\), empirical distribution \(F_n\), and quantiles \(q_u=F^{-1}(u)\), \(\widehat q_u=F_n^{-1}(u)\). For \(\delta\in(0,1)\), set \(\varepsilon_n=\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}\). If \(\varepsilon_n<\min\{\alpha,1-\alpha\}\), then
\[
\mathbb P\!\left(q_{\alpha-\varepsilon_n}\le \widehat q_\alpha\le q_{\alpha+\varepsilon_n}\right)\ge 1-\delta.
\]
Thus the two population quantiles certify a finite-sample, distribution-free confidence bracket for empirical value-at-risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The DKW inequality places empirical VaR between nearby population quantiles with confidence at least one minus delta.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.1 Variational inequalities and confidence bounds p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.1 Variational inequalities and confidence bounds p. 21

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate is mathematically plausible, but the cited locator does not clearly support the exact DKW-derived quantile bracket. A directly inspectable DKW or quantile-confidence source is required.

children.title: Value-at-Risk Nonconvexity
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex objective or feasible-set behavior induced by Value-at-Risk.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-at-Risk Nonconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-loss construction showing that value-at-risk is not a convex functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha\in(1/2,1)\), choose \(p\) with \((1-\alpha)/2<p\le1-\alpha\), and let \(A_1,A_2\) be disjoint events of probability \(p\). For \(M>0\), set \(L_i=M\mathbf 1_{A_i}\). Then \(\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L_1)=\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L_2)=0\), whereas
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha\!\left(\frac{L_1+L_2}{2}\right)=\frac M2>0
=\frac{\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L_1)+\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L_2)}2.
\]
Hence value-at-risk violates convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two individually acceptable rare-event losses can have an unacceptable average, so value-at-risk is not convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is internally consistent and fits the leaf, but it has no cited evidence for the VaR convention or construction.

children.title: Value-at-Risk Diversification Failure
children.top_down_role: Portfolio aggregation regimes where diversification does not reduce measured risk.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-at-Risk Diversification Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjoint rare losses demonstrate that aggregation can increase value-at-risk despite zero stand-alone value-at-risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha\in(1/2,1)\), let \((1-\alpha)/2<p\le1-\alpha\), and take disjoint events \(A_1,A_2\) with \(\mathbb P(A_i)=p\). For \(L_i=M\mathbf 1_{A_i}\), each position satisfies \(\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L_i)=0\). Because \(\mathbb P(A_1\cup A_2)=2p>1-\alpha\), however,
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L_1+L_2)=M>0.
\]
Thus combining positions exposes losses on a sufficiently frequent union of rare events and produces no value-at-risk diversification benefit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregating disjoint rare losses can produce positive VaR even though every stand-alone loss has zero VaR.

notation.meaning: Loss of the i-th stand-alone position.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample fits the diversification-failure leaf and its calculations are consistent, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Subadditivity Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Distributional and dependence settings associated with failed aggregation guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Subadditivity Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A rare-event regime in which value-at-risk violates subadditivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Suppose nonnegative losses \(L_1,L_2\) vanish outside disjoint events \(A_1,A_2\), take a common value \(M>0\) on those events, and satisfy
\[
\mathbb P(A_i)\le1-\alpha<\mathbb P(A_1)+\mathbb P(A_2).
\]
Then \(\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L_i)=0\) for each component, while \(\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L_1+L_2)=M\). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L_1+L_2)>
\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L_1)+\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L_2),
\]
so subadditivity fails whenever individually hidden tail events become visible after aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: VaR is non-subadditive when separate rare losses lie below the tail-probability threshold but their disjoint union exceeds it.

notation.meaning: Rare loss event for component i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated rare-event regime correctly targets subadditivity failure, but the exact result and VaR convention lack cited support.

children.title: Optimization Consequences
children.top_down_role: Structural effects of Value-at-Risk pathologies on tractability and solution stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-at-risk nonconvexity can make an affine-loss risk-feasible set nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Use losses \(L_1,L_2\) from the disjoint-event construction, and define the affine portfolio loss \(L(x)=x_1L_1+x_2L_2\) on \(X=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^2:x_1+x_2=1\}\). For the constraint \(\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L(x))\le0\), both endpoints \(e_1=(1,0)\) and \(e_2=(0,1)\) are feasible. Their midpoint is infeasible because
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha\!\left(L\!\left(\frac{e_1+e_2}{2}\right)\right)=\frac M2>0.
\]
Hence even affine portfolio losses may yield a nonconvex value-at-risk feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VaR constraint can create a nonconvex feasible set even when portfolio loss depends affinely on the decision.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the optimization-consequences leaf and the construction supports nonconvex feasibility, but it has no source.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Estimation Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity boundaries for empirical value-at-risk and expected-shortfall estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a unique \(\alpha\)-quantile \(q_\alpha\) with density \(f(q_\alpha)>0\), the asymptotic variance of empirical value-at-risk is \(\alpha(1-\alpha)/f(q_\alpha)^2\). Thus a family with \(f(q_\alpha)\downarrow0\) has unbounded root-\(n\) variance. For empirical expected shortfall, the corresponding Gaussian regime requires \(\mathbb E[(L-q_\alpha)_+^2]<\infty\); when this moment is infinite, the usual finite-variance central limit approximation is unavailable. Low quantile density and infinite tail variance are therefore distinct instability boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: VaR estimation destabilizes as quantile density vanishes, while expected-shortfall estimation loses its usual Gaussian approximation under infinite tail variance.
assumptions_latex: f(q_\alpha)>0\ \text{when the VaR variance formula is invoked}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(q_\alpha)\downarrow0\ \Rightarrow\ \operatorname{avar}(\widehat q_\alpha)\uparrow\infty;\quad \mathbb E[(L-q_\alpha)_+^2]=\infty\ \Rightarrow\ \text{no usual finite-variance ES CLT}

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two instability boundaries are plausible and fit the leaf, but the VaR variance formula and the precise ES central-limit boundary require authoritative support.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tail Integrability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto losses separate finite value-at-risk from finite expected shortfall.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) have Pareto tail \(\mathbb P(L>t)=t^{-\beta}\) for \(t\ge1\), with \(\beta>0\). For every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\),
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L)=(1-\alpha)^{-1/\beta}<\infty.
\]
Expected shortfall satisfies
\[
\operatorname{ES}_\alpha(L)=\frac{\beta}{\beta-1}\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L)<\infty
\quad\text{if and only if}\quad \beta>1,
\]
and is infinite for \(0<\beta\le1\). Thus quantile risk remains finite beyond the integrability boundary at which tail-mean risk ceases to be finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pareto VaR is finite for every positive tail index, but expected shortfall is finite exactly when the tail index exceeds one.

notation.meaning: Expected shortfall at confidence level alpha.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto formulas and failure-boundary kind fit the leaf, but the risk-measure definitions and integrability formulas have no cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Measure Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A small tail-probability error reverses the decision selected by a value-at-risk model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider actions \(a,b\). Action \(a\) has constant loss \(L_a=1\); action \(b\) has loss \(L_b=50\mathbf1_A\). At level \(\alpha=0.995\), suppose an assumed model \(Q\) assigns \(Q(A)=0.004\), while the true model \(P\) assigns \(P(A)=0.006\). Then
\[
\operatorname{VaR}^{Q}_{0.995}(L_b)=0<1=
\operatorname{VaR}^{Q}_{0.995}(L_a),
\]
but
\[
\operatorname{VaR}^{P}_{0.995}(L_b)=50>1=
\operatorname{VaR}^{P}_{0.995}(L_a).
\]
Thus optimization under the misspecified model selects \(b\), although \(a\) is optimal under the true risk measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slight error in rare-event probability can reverse VaR rankings and make the model-selected action truly inferior.

notation.meaning: Losses generated by the two actions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is arithmetically consistent and fits the leaf, but no evidence or explicit standard-field rationale supports it.

knowledge_statements.title: Individual Chance Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate probabilistic feasibility requirements imposed on each scalar constraint event.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\) be positive, let \(X\) be a decision set, let \(\xi\) be a random element taking values in \(\Xi\), and let \(g_i:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be measurable in \(\xi\) for every \(x\in X\). Given violation tolerances \(\varepsilon_i\in[0,1]\), individual chance constraints require
\[
\mathbb P\bigl(g_i(x,\xi)\le0\bigr)\ge1-\varepsilon_i,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
Each probability bound is enforced separately; it does not by itself impose a joint guarantee of the form \(\mathbb P(g_i(x,\xi)\le0\ \text{for every }i)\ge1-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive number m of scalar random constraints, individual chance constraints bound each constraint's violation probability separately and do not automatically provide a joint reliability guarantee.
assumptions_latex: g_i(x,\cdot)\ \text{is measurable for every }x\in X\text{ and }i=1,\ldots,m

notation.meaning: Positive number of scalar chance constraints.
Random data or uncertainty taking values in Xi.
The i-th scalar random constraint function.
Allowed violation probability for constraint i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic Representation of a Scalar Gaussian Chance Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantile representation of the feasible set for one probabilistic constraint with zero right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(m_1=1\), \(h_1=0\), and \(\mathbf A_{1\cdot}\) has mean \(\bar A_{1\cdot}\) and covariance matrix \(C_1\). Then, with \(\Phi\) denoting the standard normal distribution function, \[K_1(\alpha)=\left\{x:\bar A_{1\cdot}x-\Phi^{-1}(\alpha)\sqrt{x^TC_1x}\geq 0\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For one probabilistic constraint with zero right-hand side, the feasible set equals the points whose mean linear response exceeds the standard-normal quantile times the covariance-induced standard deviation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite families of scalar constraints sharing one joint reliability requirement.

source_refs.locator: 1.6 Properties of Probabilistic Constraints p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given measurable constraint functions \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\), a joint chance constraint at reliability \(1-\varepsilon\) requires all component inequalities to hold simultaneously with probability at least \(1-\varepsilon\). Thus the feasible set is
\[
F_{\mathrm{joint}}=\left\{x\in X:\mathbb{P}\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{\xi:g_i(x,\xi)\le 0\}\right)\ge 1-\varepsilon\right\}.
\]
Unlike separate individual chance constraints, this condition directly controls the probability of their union of violation events.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision is feasible when every random inequality holds simultaneously with the prescribed probability, thereby controlling the probability that any component constraint fails.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Violation-Probability Form and Joint Max Reformulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an ordinary chance constraint and represents a joint chance constraint by a scalar maximum without asserting preservation of component structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X\subset\mathbb R^n$ be closed, $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, and let $\xi$ have distribution $P$ supported on $\Xi\subset\mathbb R^d$. For a Carathéodory function $C:\mathbb R^n\times\Xi\to\mathbb R$, define $p(x):=\Pr\{C(x,\xi)>0\}$. Then $p(x)\leq\alpha$ is equivalent to $\Pr\{C(x,\xi)\leq0\}\geq1-\alpha$. Moreover, $\Pr\{C_i(x,\xi)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,q\}\geq1-\alpha$ is represented by $C(x,\xi):=\max_{1\leq i\leq q}C_i(x,\xi)$, although this replacement may destroy useful structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chance constraint bounds the probability of violation by alpha. A joint chance constraint can be written as one scalar chance constraint using the maximum component violation, but that representation may lose useful structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of Joint Gaussian Chance Constraints with Common Covariance Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient convexity condition for an ordinary joint chance constraint with jointly normal random coefficients and right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mathbf A_{1\cdot},\ldots,\mathbf A_{n_1\cdot},\mathbf h\) are jointly normally distributed, and there exist a matrix \(C\) and constants \(r_{ij}\) and \(s_i\) such that \(\operatorname E[(\mathbf A_{i\cdot}-\operatorname E\mathbf A_{i\cdot})(\mathbf A_{j\cdot}-\operatorname E\mathbf A_{j\cdot})^T]=r_{ij}C\) for all \(i,j=1,\ldots,n_1\), and \(\operatorname E[(\mathbf A_{i\cdot}-\operatorname E\mathbf A_{i\cdot})(\mathbf h-\operatorname E\mathbf h)]=s_iC\) for all \(i=1,\ldots,n_1\). Then \(K_1(\alpha)\) is convex for every \(\alpha\geq\tfrac12\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A joint Gaussian chance-constraint feasible set is convex at probability levels at least one half when the row-to-row and row-to-right-hand-side covariances share the stated common matrix structure.

\operatorname E[(\mathbf A_{i\cdot}-\operatorname E\mathbf A_{i\cdot})(\mathbf A_{j\cdot}-\operatorname E\mathbf A_{j\cdot})^T]=r_{ij}C\quad\forall i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n_1\}
\operatorname E[(\mathbf A_{i\cdot}-\operatorname E\mathbf A_{i\cdot})(\mathbf h-\operatorname E\mathbf h)]=s_iC\quad\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,n_1\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint and individual probabilistic constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes simultaneous probability control from componentwise probability control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For random constraints \(g_j(x,Z)\le0\), \(j\in\mathcal J\), a joint probabilistic constraint is \[\Pr\{g_j(x,Z)\le0\ \forall j\in\mathcal J\}\ge p.\] Individual probabilistic constraints have the form \[\Pr\{g_j(x,Z)\le0\}\ge p_j\quad\forall j\in\mathcal J,\qquad p_j\in[0,1].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A joint probabilistic constraint places one probability threshold on simultaneous satisfaction of all indexed inequalities. Individual probabilistic constraints place a separate threshold on each inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint chance-constrained optimization model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulates simultaneous random inequalities whose joint satisfaction probability must meet a prescribed level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(g_j:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^s\to\mathbb R\) for \(j\in\mathcal J\), \(Z\) be an \(s\)-dimensional random vector with distribution \(P_Z\), and \(p\) be a prescribed modeling parameter. The model is \[\min_{x\in X}c(x)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \Pr\{g_j(x,Z)\le0\ \forall j\in\mathcal J\}\ge p.\] If \(A(x)=\{g_j(x,Z)\le0\ \forall j\in\mathcal J\}\), then \(\Pr\{A(x)\}=\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{A(x)}]\). The objective may also have the form \(c(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,Z)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model minimizes an objective over a nonempty decision set while requiring all indexed random inequalities to hold simultaneously with probability at least p. knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A probabilistic constraint is separable in blocks when its satisfaction event has the form \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m E_i(x_i)\), with each \(E_i(x_i)\) depending only on \((x_i,\xi_i)\), and the uncertainty blocks are independent. Then
\[
\mathbb{P}\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m E_i(x_i)\right)=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathbb{P}(E_i(x_i)),
\]
so the requirement \(\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_iE_i(x_i))\ge1-\varepsilon\) is equivalent to \(\prod_i p_i(x_i)\ge1-\varepsilon\), where \(p_i(x_i)=\mathbb{P}(E_i(x_i))\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector inequalities are componentwise. The symbols \(\mathbb Z_p\), \(F\), and the index set \(\mathcal E\) retain their established source-context meanings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }\mathcal A\text{ be the set of possible values of an integer random vector }Z.\ \text{If }F_Z\text{ is }\alpha\text{-concave on }\mathcal A+\mathbb Z_+^m\text{ for some }\alpha\in[-\infty,\infty],\text{ then for every }p\in(0,1),\quad \mathbb Z_p=\left\{y\in\mathbb R^m:\exists z\in\mathbb Z^m,\ \exists(\lambda_j)_{j\in\mathcal E},\ y\ge z\ge\sum_{j\in\mathcal E}\lambda_jv^j,\ \sum_{j\in\mathcal E}\lambda_j=1,\ \lambda_j\ge0\right\},\text{ where }v^j,\ j\in\mathcal E,\text{ are the p-efficient points of }F.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the distribution function of an integer random vector is alpha-concave on its support plus the nonnegative integer orthant, then its probability set consists exactly of vectors that dominate an integer vector which dominates a convex combination of the p-efficient points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: p-Efficient Points of a Distribution Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise-minimal probability-level points used in separable probabilistic constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in(0,1)\) and let \(F\) be a distribution function on \(\mathbb R^m\). A point \(v\in\mathbb R^m\) is called \(p\)-efficient if \(F(v)\ge p\) and there is no \(z\le v\), \(z\ne v\), such that \(F(z)\ge p\). Thus the \(p\)-efficient points are the minimal elements of the level set \(\mathcal Z_p\) under the coordinatewise order generated by \(\mathbb R_+^m\). For a scalar random variable \(Z\), the unique \(p\)-efficient point is the smallest \(v\) satisfying \(F_Z(v)\ge p\), namely \(F_Z^{-1}(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A p-efficient point is a coordinatewise minimal point where a multivariate distribution function reaches at least p. In one dimension, the unique p-efficient point is the lower p-quantile.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is a distribution function on }\mathbb R^m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\text{ is }p\text{-efficient}\iff F(v)\ge p\ \text{and}\ \nexists z\le v,\ z\ne v:\ F(z)\ge p;\qquad m=1\Rightarrow v=F_Z^{-1}(p)\text{ uniquely}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alpha-Concavity of Independent Product Distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of distribution-function concavity under independent block composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z=(Z^1,\ldots,Z^L)\) with \(Z^l\in\mathbb{R}^{s_l}\), \(\sum_{l=1}^L s_l=s\), and suppose the blocks \(Z^1,\ldots,Z^L\) are independent. Assume each marginal distribution function \(F_{Z^l}:\mathbb{R}^{s_l}\to[0,1]\) is \(\alpha_l\)-concave on \(\mathcal A_l\subset\mathbb{Z}^{s_l}\). Then: (i) if \(\sum_{l=1}^L\alpha_l^{-1}>0\), the joint distribution function \(F_Z\) is \(\alpha\)-concave on \(\mathcal A=\mathcal A_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal A_L\), where \(\alpha=(\sum_{l=1}^L\alpha_l^{-1})^{-1}\); and (ii) if \(\alpha_l=0\) for every \(l\), then \(F_Z\) is log-concave on \(\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent random blocks, alpha-concavity of the marginal distribution functions transfers to their joint distribution function with the reciprocal-sum parameter. If every marginal is log-concave, the joint distribution function is log-concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\sum_{l=1}^L\alpha_l^{-1}>0\Rightarrow F_Z\text{ is }\left(\sum_{l=1}^L\alpha_l^{-1}\right)^{-1}\text{-concave on }\prod_{l=1}^L\mathcal A_l\right],\quad\left[\forall l,\ \alpha_l=0\Rightarrow F_Z\text{ is log-concave on }\prod_{l=1}^L\mathcal A_l\right]

knowledge_statements.title: Nonseparable Probabilistic Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint satisfaction probabilities that do not decompose into block-local component reliabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in X\) and let \(E_i(x)\) be measurable component-satisfaction events. A probabilistic constraint is nonseparable with respect to the designated blocks when its joint satisfaction probability
\[
p(x)=\mathbb{P}\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m E_i(x)\right)
\]
cannot be represented as \(\prod_{i=1}^m p_i(x_i)\) using block-local component reliabilities \(p_i\). Shared random factors, statistically dependent component events, or events depending jointly on several decision blocks can cause such nonseparability, although shared randomness alone does not imply it. The chance requirement is \(p(x)\ge 1-\varepsilon\) and must be evaluated from the joint law or enforced using a valid joint bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probabilistic constraint is nonseparable when its joint satisfaction probability cannot be factored into reliabilities depending only on the designated component blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in X\) is partitioned into designated decision blocks.
For each \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \(E_i(x)\) is a measurable satisfaction event.
The permitted joint violation probability satisfies \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonseparability means that no designated block-local functions \(p_i\) give \(\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{i=1}^mE_i(x))=\prod_{i=1}^m p_i(x_i)\) on \(X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Floating Body of a Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a measure on Euclidean space at a positive probability level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A measure \(P\) on \(\mathbb{R}^s\) has a floating body at level \(p>0\) if there exists a convex body \(C_p\subset\mathbb{R}^s\) such that, for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^s\), \[P\!\left(\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^s:z^{\mathsf T}x\ge s_{C_p}(z)\right\}\right)=1-p,\] where \(s_{C_p}\) is the support function of \(C_p\). Such a set \(C_p\) is called the floating body of \(P\) at level \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measure has a floating body at level p>0 when a convex body exists whose support value in every direction cuts off a halfspace having probability 1-p.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alpha-Concavity of a Distribution Function on a Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the componentwise order on \(\mathbb{R}^s\) and the generalized mean \(m_\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subset\mathbb{R}^s\) and \(\alpha\in[-\infty,\infty]\). A distribution function \(F\) is \(\alpha\)-concave on \(\mathcal A\) if, for every \(z,x,y\in\mathcal A\) and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\) satisfying \(z\ge \lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\) componentwise, \[F(z)\ge m_\alpha\bigl(F(x),F(y),\lambda\bigr).\] When \(\mathcal A=\mathbb{R}^s\), this agrees with the usual definition of \(\alpha\)-concavity of a distribution function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distribution function is alpha-concave on A when its value at every point lying componentwise above a convex combination is at least the corresponding alpha-mean of the endpoint values. On all of Euclidean space this is the usual definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Probability-Maximization Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization of satisfaction probability rather than enforcement of a fixed reliability threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A probability-maximization model chooses a deterministic decision to maximize the probability of a measurable satisfaction event. Define
\[
p(x)=\mathbb{P}(E(x)),\qquad p^\star=\sup_{x\in X}p(x).
\]
For constraint functions \(g_i\), a canonical event is \(E(x)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{\xi:g_i(x,\xi)\le 0\}\). If the supremum is attained, the solution set is \(\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in X}p(x)\). A chance constraint at reliability \(1-\varepsilon\) is feasible exactly when there exists \(x\in X\) with \(p(x)\ge 1-\varepsilon\); when the supremum is attained, this is equivalent to \(p^\star\ge 1-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model maximizes satisfaction probability. A reliability threshold is feasible when some decision reaches it; comparison with the optimal supremum is equivalent when that supremum is attained.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty deterministic decision set.
The probability law \(\mathbb{P}\) of \(\xi\) is fixed, and \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in X}p(x)\ne\varnothing\), each \(x^\star\) in that set attains \(p^\star\), and threshold feasibility is equivalent to \(p^\star\ge1-\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Random Right-Hand-Side Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear inequalities with randomness confined to the right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A random right-hand-side chance constraint has a deterministic linear operator \(A\) and a random threshold vector \(b(\xi)\). Its joint form is
\[
\mathbb{P}(Ax\le b(\xi))\ge1-\varepsilon,
\]
where the vector inequality is componentwise. For fixed \(x\), satisfaction is the upper-orthant event \(\{\xi\in\Xi:b(\xi)\ge Ax\}\). For a scalar row \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\), an individual form is \(\mathbb{P}(b_i(\xi)\ge a_i^{\mathsf T}x)\ge1-\varepsilon_i\), where \(\varepsilon_i\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only the constraint thresholds are random; feasibility requires the random right-hand side to dominate the deterministic linear image with sufficient probability.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is deterministic and \(b:\Xi\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The chance-feasible set is \(\{x\in X:\mathbb{P}(Ax\le b(\xi))\ge1-\varepsilon\}\), with componentwise inequality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The random-coefficient chance constraint is \(\mathbb{P}(a(\xi)^{\mathsf T}x\le b(\xi))\ge1-\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Scalar random residual at decision x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar affine inequality with randomness in its coefficients.

source_refs.locator: 1.6 Properties of Probabilistic Constraints p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A random-coefficient constraint is a scalar affine random inequality
\[
a(\xi)^{\mathsf T}x\le b(\xi),
\]
whose coefficient vector, and possibly its threshold, depend measurably on \(\xi\). At reliability \(1-\varepsilon\), it imposes \(\mathbb{P}(a(\xi)^{\mathsf T}x\le b(\xi))\ge1-\varepsilon\). Defining the random residual \(r_x(\xi)=a(\xi)^{\mathsf T}x-b(\xi)\), the same condition is \(\mathbb{P}(r_x(\xi)\le0)\ge1-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random-coefficient constraint requires a scalar affine inequality with random coefficients to hold with the prescribed probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Coefficient Constraints

source_witnesses.locator: 1.6 Properties of Probabilistic Constraints p. 46

children.title: Random-Matrix Constraints
children.top_down_role: Chance constraints with uncertainty entering through matrix-valued operators.

assumptions_latex: The allowed joint violation probability is \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is \(\{x\in X:\mathbb{P}(A(\xi)x\le b(\xi))\ge1-\varepsilon\}\).

notation.meaning: Random matrix defining the linear operator
Allowed probability that at least one row fails

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint linear chance constraint with a random matrix operator.

source_refs.locator: 1.6 Properties of Probabilistic Constraints p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A random-matrix chance constraint applies the random linear operator \(A(\xi)\) to a deterministic decision \(x\) and requires
\[
\mathbb{P}(A(\xi)x\le b(\xi))\ge1-\varepsilon,
\]
with componentwise inequality. Writing \(a_i(\xi)^{\mathsf T}\) for row \(i\), its satisfaction event is \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{a_i(\xi)^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i(\xi)\}\). Hence arbitrary dependence among matrix rows and right-hand-side entries is retained by the joint probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random matrix maps the decision into several random linear inequalities whose simultaneous satisfaction probability must meet the reliability target.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Matrix Constraints

source_witnesses.locator: 1.6 Properties of Probabilistic Constraints p. 46

children.title: Correlated Entry Structure
children.top_down_role: Dependence patterns among uncertain coefficients or matrix entries.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Cov}(A(\xi)x)=(I_m\otimes x^{\mathsf T})\Sigma(I_m\otimes x)\), so cross-entry covariance affects joint row residuals.

notation.meaning: Covariance matrix of all random entries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covariance representation for dependent entries of a random constraint matrix.

source_refs.locator: 6.7 The Probability of a Rectangle in Case of a Multivariate Normal Distribution p. 208

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Correlated entry structure is encoded by the covariance matrix \(\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(\operatorname{vec}(A(\xi)))\), whose off-diagonal terms record dependence at second order between matrix entries. For fixed \(x\),
\[
A(\xi)x=(I_m\otimes x^{\mathsf T})\operatorname{vec}(A(\xi)),
\]
and therefore
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(A(\xi)x)=(I_m\otimes x^{\mathsf T})\Sigma(I_m\otimes x).
\]
Thus correlated entries generally induce correlated row residuals and preclude factorization of their joint satisfaction probability without stronger independence assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vectorizing a random matrix exposes entrywise covariance, which propagates linearly to covariance among the constraint rows evaluated at a fixed decision.
knowledge_statements.title: Correlated Entry Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 6.7 The Probability of a Rectangle in Case of a Multivariate Normal Distribution p. 208

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the standard column-stacking convention, the identity is A(ξ)x=(x^T⊗I_m)vec(A(ξ)), not the displayed expression; the latter requires an explicitly defined row-stacking convention. The cited section on multivariate-normal rectangle probabilities does not clearly support this covariance-propagation formula, so an authoritative matching source and convention are required.

children.title: Rank-Structured Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Low-rank, factorized, or otherwise rank-constrained random-matrix regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(r\ll mn\) expresses a low-dimensional uncertainty parameterization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(\eta)=A_0+\sum_{k=1}^r\eta_kA_k\) lies almost surely in the affine subspace \(A_0+\operatorname{span}\{A_1,\ldots,A_r\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine low-dimensional factor representation of random matrix uncertainty.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Stochastic optimization problems p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A random matrix has rank-structured uncertainty when it admits the finite-factor representation
\[
A(\eta)=A_0+\sum_{k=1}^r\eta_kA_k,
\]
where the deterministic matrices \(A_k\) span the admissible perturbation directions and \(r\) is small relative to the ambient number of entries. Consequently, \(A(\eta)\) lies almost surely in \(A_0+\operatorname{span}\{A_1,\ldots,A_r\}\), and the random constraint \(A(\eta)x\le b(\eta)\) depends on matrix uncertainty only through \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random matrix is represented by a nominal matrix plus a small number of deterministic matrix directions weighted by random factors.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Structured Uncertainty

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Stochastic optimization problems p. 3

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A low-dimensional affine factor parameterization does not imply that the random matrix or its perturbation has low rank; the direction matrices may all be full rank. The generic stochastic-optimization locator does not establish the intended meaning of rank-structured uncertainty. A source and a precise rank condition or factorization are required.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The chance-feasible set is \(\{x\in X:\mathbb{P}(g(x,\xi)\le0)\ge1-\varepsilon\}\), with componentwise inequality.

notation.meaning: Vector of nonlinear uncertain constraint functions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General measurable chance constraints without affine dependence on decisions and uncertainty.

source_refs.locator: 1.6 Properties of Probabilistic Constraints p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonlinear uncertain chance constraint is specified by a measurable vector mapping \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\) and requires
\[
\mathbb{P}(g(x,\xi)\le0)\ge1-\varepsilon,
\]
where the inequality is componentwise. The mapping may be nonlinear in \(x\), in \(\xi\), or in both. Its feasible set is determined by the probability of the preimage \(\{\xi:g_i(x,\xi)\le0\text{ for all }i\}\); no linear-operator or random-threshold representation is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general measurable nonlinear constraint must hold componentwise with the required probability, without assuming affine dependence on the decision or uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Uncertain Constraints

knowledge_statements.title: Fully Specified Distribution Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chance constraints evaluated under one completely known probability distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the fully specified distribution regime, the uncertainty state space \((\Xi,\mathcal{F})\) and a single probability law \(P_\xi\) on it are known and used directly. For measurable satisfaction sets \(E(x)\in\mathcal{F}\), the chance-feasible set is
\[
F=\left\{x\in X:\int_{\Xi}\mathbf{1}_{E(x)}(u)\,P_\xi(du)\ge1-\varepsilon\right\}.
\]
Thus reliability is evaluated under the stated law itself, rather than under an empirical distribution, an ambiguity set of laws, or a bound inferred only from partial distributional information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complete probability law of the uncertainty is known, and each decision's reliability is evaluated directly under that single law.
assumptions_latex: \((\Xi,\mathcal{F})\) is the measurable uncertainty state space and the law \(P_\xi\) is completely specified.
\(X\) is the decision set, and \(E(x)\in\mathcal{F}\) is specified for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is evaluated under the single known law: \(x\in F\iff\int_{\Xi}\mathbf{1}_{E(x)}(u)\,P_\xi(du)\ge1-\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Known probability law of the uncertainty

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Discrete Distribution Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scenario-sum representation for a known finite-support distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(\xi\) has the finite distribution \(P_\xi(\{\xi^s\})=p_s\) for \(s=1,\ldots,N\). Then every satisfaction event \(E(x)\) has probability
\[
P_\xi(E(x))=\sum_{s=1}^N p_s\mathbf{1}_{E(x)}(\xi^s).
\]
Accordingly, the chance constraint \(P_\xi(E(x))\ge1-\varepsilon\) is exactly the weighted scenario condition \(\sum_{s=1}^N p_s\mathbf{1}_{E(x)}(\xi^s)\ge1-\varepsilon\). No sampling approximation is involved when all support points and their probabilities are specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a known finite distribution, reliability is exactly the total probability weight of the support scenarios in which the decision satisfies the event.
assumptions_latex: \(\sum_{s=1}^N p_s=1\), and \(E(x)\) is defined for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A decision \(x\in X\) is chance-feasible exactly when \(\sum_{s=1}^N p_s\mathbf{1}_{E(x)}(\xi^s)\ge1-\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Indicator of satisfaction at decision x

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Only Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical replacement of an unknown probability law by observed scenarios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given samples \(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^N\in\Xi\), a decision set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a measurable constraint function \(g:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\in[0,1)\), the sample-only chance-constrained program is
\[
\inf_{x\in X} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \widehat P_N\{g(x,\xi)\le 0\}:=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf 1_{\{g(x,\xi^i)\le0\}}\ge 1-\varepsilon.
\]
Equivalently, at most \(\lfloor N\varepsilon\rfloor\) sampled constraints may be violated. This empirical condition alone makes no out-of-sample reliability guarantee unless additional sampling assumptions and a statistical validation bound are supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unknown chance constraint is replaced by requiring satisfaction on all but an allowed fraction of the observed scenarios.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb N\) and \(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^N\) are the available observations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is empirically feasible exactly when \(\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf 1_{\{g(x,\xi^i)>0\}}\le\lfloor N\varepsilon\rfloor\).

notation.meaning: Empirical probability measure of the observed scenarios.

review_flags: A source specifically supporting the empirical chance-constraint formulation and its lack of automatic out-of-sample guarantees is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The empirical formulation, integer violation-count equivalence, and warning about absent automatic out-of-sample guarantees are mathematically sound, but no source is supplied for these nontrivial claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Limited Distributional Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributionally robust chance constraints under an ambiguity set of probability laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty family of probability measures on \((\Xi,\mathcal F)\), specified through partial information such as moments, support, or statistical distance from a nominal law. For \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), measurable \(g:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\), and \(\varepsilon\in[0,1)\), the limited-information chance-constrained model is
\[
\inf_{x\in X} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \inf_{P\in\mathcal P}P\{\xi:g(x,\xi)\le0\}\ge1-\varepsilon.
\]
Thus a feasible decision meets the reliability requirement simultaneously for every distribution consistent with the stated information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility requires the chance constraint to hold under every probability distribution consistent with the available partial information.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\neq\varnothing\) consists of probability measures on a common measurable space \((\Xi,\mathcal F)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible if and only if \(P\{g(x,\xi)\le0\}\ge1-\varepsilon\) for every \(P\in\mathcal P\).

notation.meaning: Ambiguity set of distributions consistent with limited information.
A candidate probability law in the ambiguity set.

review_flags: A distributionally robust chance-constraint source with an exact ambiguity-set formulation is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ambiguity-set formulation is a standard distributionally robust chance constraint and fits the container, but it has no supporting citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Chance-Constrained Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chance-constrained optimization with continuously valued decision variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(\xi\) have probability law \(P\) on \((\Xi,\mathcal F)\), and let \(g_j:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) be measurable in \(\xi\). A continuous chance-constrained program has the form
\[
\inf_{x\in X} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad P\{g_j(x,\xi)\le0\}\ge1-\varepsilon_j,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,m,
\]
where every component of \(x\) is real-valued and \(\varepsilon_j\in[0,1)\). Joint chance constraints arise by replacing the separate conditions with \(P\{g_j(x,\xi)\le0\text{ for all }j\}\ge1-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous chance-constrained program optimizes over real-valued decisions subject to individual or joint probabilistic reliability requirements.
assumptions_latex: \(g_j(x,\cdot)\) is measurable for every \(x\in X\) and \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set consists of continuous decisions satisfying the specified probability thresholds.

notation.meaning: Allowed violation probability for constraint j.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Chance-Constrained Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chance-constrained models combining continuous and integer decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb Z^q\), let \(\xi\) have law \(P\), and let \(g_j:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) be measurable in \(\xi\). A mixed-integer chance-constrained program is
\[
\inf_{(y,z)\in X} f(y,z)\quad\text{subject to}\quad P\{g_j(y,z,\xi)\le0\}\ge1-\varepsilon_j,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,m,
\]
where \(y\in\mathbb R^p\), \(z\in\mathbb Z^q\), and \(\varepsilon_j\in[0,1)\). Binary variables are included through restrictions \(z_k\in\{0,1\}\). The probabilistic constraints and integrality restrictions jointly determine feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model combines real and integer decisions, all of which must satisfy the prescribed probabilistic reliability constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible solution lies in \(\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb Z^q\) and satisfies each stated chance constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: Semi-Infinite Probabilistic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional decisions subject to an infinite indexed family of chance constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(T\) be an infinite index set, and let \(\xi\) have law \(P\) on \((\Xi,\mathcal F)\). A semi-infinite probabilistic program has the form
\[
\inf_{x\in X} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad P\{g_t(x,\xi)\le0\}\ge1-\varepsilon_t
\quad\text{for every }t\in T,
\]
where \(g_t(x,\cdot)\) is measurable and \(\varepsilon_t\in[0,1)\). The decision vector is finite-dimensional, whereas the probabilistic constraint system has infinitely many members. A uniform version uses \(\inf_{t\in T}P\{g_t(x,\xi)\le0\}\ge1-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional decision must satisfy an infinite indexed collection of probabilistic constraints, possibly under one uniform reliability threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) with finite \(n\), while \(T\) is infinite.
\(g_t(x,\cdot)\) is measurable for every \(x\in X\) and \(t\in T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires the probability inequality to hold for every index \(t\in T\).
review_flags: A source explicitly defining the semi-infinite probabilistic formulation is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly describes a finite-dimensional decision problem with infinitely many probabilistic constraints, but no source supports this terminology and formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Higher-order stochastic dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines kth-order dominance through kth integrated distribution functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\in\mathcal L_{k-1}(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\). Then \(X\) dominates \(Y\) in the \(k\)th order, written \(X\succcurlyeq_{(k)}Y\), if and only if \[F_X^{(k)}(\eta)\le F_Y^{(k)}(\eta)\qquad\forall\eta\in\mathbb R.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For random variables in the stated integrability class, X kth-order stochastically dominates Y exactly when its kth integrated distribution function is no greater than that of Y at every real threshold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Jump Utility Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-constant representation of a utility function satisfying the necessary optimality conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the assumptions of the necessary optimality theorem, there exists a piecewise-constant utility function \(w\in\mathcal U\) satisfying
\[
-\nabla_xL(\widehat x,w)\in\mathcal N_{\mathcal X}(\widehat x),\qquad
\mathbb E[w(g(\widehat x,Z))]=\mathbb E[w(Y)].
\]
Moreover, there exist \(\eta_i\in[a,b]\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\), with \(0\leq k\leq n+2\), such that \(w\) is constant on \(( -\infty,\eta_1]\), \((\eta_1,\eta_2],\ldots,(\eta_k,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the necessary-condition theorem's assumptions, the utility function can be chosen piecewise constant while satisfying both optimality conditions, with at most n+2 jump points in [a,b].

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity condition for the referenced semi-infinite probabilistic problem.

Problem \((4.9)\) satisfies the differential uniform dominance condition at \(\widehat x\in\mathcal X\) if there exists \(x^0\in\mathcal X\) such that

\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficiency of the Utility-Based Optimality Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient optimality result for the referenced semi-infinite probabilistic problem under convexity, concavity, and distributional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widehat x\) be feasible for problem \((4.9)\). Suppose that there exists \(\widehat u\in\mathcal U\), \(\widehat u\neq0\), such that
\[
-\nabla_xL(\widehat x,\widehat u)\in\mathcal N_{\mathcal X}(\widehat x),
\qquad
\mathbb E[\widehat u(g(\widehat x,Z))]=\mathbb E[\widehat u(Y)].
\]
If \(c\) is convex, \(g\) satisfies the stated concavity assumptions, and \(Z\) has an \(\alpha\)-concave probability distribution, then \(\widehat x\) is an optimal solution of problem \((4.9)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Logconcave Probability Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logconcavity of a probability measure under Minkowski interpolation of compact sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d\in\mathbb N\). A Borel probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^d\) is logconcave if, for all nonempty compact sets \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and every \(\lambda\in(0,1)\),
\[
\mu\bigl(\lambda A+(1-\lambda)B\bigr)\ge \mu(A)^\lambda\mu(B)^{1-\lambda},
\]
where \(\lambda A+(1-\lambda)B=\{\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}\), and the right-hand side is zero if either set has zero measure. An absolutely continuous probability measure with a logconcave density is a standard instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Borel probability measure is logconcave when the probability of every Minkowski interpolation of nonempty compact sets dominates the corresponding geometric interpolation of their probabilities.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb N\) and \(\mu\) is a Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R^d\).
\(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) are nonempty compact sets and \(0<\lambda<1\).

source_refs.locator: 4.2 The Basic Theorems of Logconcave Measures p. 89

review_flags: Definition restricted to compact test sets to ensure the Minkowski interpolation is Borel measurable.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave Uncertain-Constraint Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint concavity condition supporting convex chance-constrained feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and \(g:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\). The uncertain-constraint mapping is jointly concave when, for all \((x_1,\xi_1),(x_2,\xi_2)\in X\times\Xi\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),
\[
g\bigl(\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2,\lambda\xi_1+(1-\lambda)\xi_2\bigr)
\ge\lambda g(x_1,\xi_1)+(1-\lambda)g(x_2,\xi_2).
\]
Consequently, the joint satisfaction set \(C=\{(x,\xi):g(x,\xi)\ge0\}\) is convex. This orientation is appropriate when chance feasibility is written as \(P\{g(x,\xi)\ge0\}\ge1-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint concavity of the constraint mapping makes its joint superlevel satisfaction set convex.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(\Xi\) are convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Random Linear-Constraint Specializations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prékopa specialization for affine decision and uncertainty dependence without bilinear cross-terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\xi\in\mathbb R^d\) have a logconcave probability law, and fix matrices \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) and vector \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). Define
\[
p(x)=P\{Ax+B\xi\le b\},
\]
with componentwise inequalities. Then \(p\) is logconcave on \(\mathbb R^n\). Hence, for every \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), the chance-constrained feasible region
\[
F_\alpha=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:p(x)\ge\alpha\}
\]
is convex. The conclusion applies because \(\{(x,\xi):Ax+B\xi\le b\}\) is a convex joint satisfaction set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For affine joint constraints and logconcave uncertainty, the satisfaction probability is logconcave and every positive reliability superlevel set is convex.
assumptions_latex: The probability law of \(\xi\) is logconcave on \(\mathbb R^d\).
\(A\), \(B\), and \(b\) are deterministic and dimensionally compatible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is logconcave, and \(F_\alpha\) is convex for every \(\alpha\in(0,1]\).

notation.meaning: Probability that all affine random constraints are satisfied.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlogconcave Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A discrete nonlogconcave law can produce a disconnected chance-feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\xi\) take values \(-1\) and \(1\), each with probability \(1/2\), and choose \(r\in(0,1)\). For the satisfaction event \(|x-\xi|\le r\), define \(p(x)=P\{|x-\xi|\le r\}\). Then
\[
\{x:p(x)\ge1/2\}=[-1-r,-1+r]\cup[1-r,1+r].
\]
The two intervals are disjoint, so this reliability superlevel set is nonconvex and disconnected. Thus, after removal of logconcavity of the probability law, convexity of chance-constrained feasible regions is not guaranteed even though each realized constraint \(|x-\xi|\le r\) defines a convex set in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-point distribution yields two disjoint feasible intervals, showing that convex scenario sets alone do not ensure convex chance feasibility.

notation.meaning: Radius of each realized feasible interval.

review_flags: The explicit construction is directly checkable, but an external source for the nonlogconcave failure boundary is still required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit two-point construction and disconnected feasible set are correct and fit the failure-boundary container, but the record supplies no external source.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Concave Measure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-mean generalization of logconcavity for probability measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(s\in\mathbb R\), \(a,b\ge0\), and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), define
\[
M_s(a,b;\lambda)=\bigl(\lambda a^s+(1-\lambda)b^s\bigr)^{1/s}
\]
when \(s\ne0\), with the continuous extension \(M_0(a,b;\lambda)=a^\lambda b^{1-\lambda}\); endpoint conventions apply when a value is zero. A probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^d\) is \(s\)-concave if
\[
\mu(\lambda A+(1-\lambda)B)\ge M_s(\mu(A),\mu(B);\lambda)
\]
for all Borel sets \(A,B\) of positive measure. The case \(s=0\) is logconcavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An s-concave measure bounds probabilities of interpolated sets below by the corresponding weighted power mean; logconcavity is the zero-order case.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a probability measure on the Borel subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\).
\(A,B\) are Borel sets with positive \(\mu\)-measure and \(0<\lambda<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu\) is \(s\)-concave exactly when the displayed power-mean inequality holds for every admissible \(A,B,\lambda\).

notation.meaning: Weighted power mean of order s.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alpha-concave probability measures and distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized concavity of a probability measure under Minkowski combinations of measurable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a probability measure on the Lebesgue-measurable subsets of a convex set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^s\). It is \(\alpha\)-concave if, for every Borel-measurable \(A,B\subset\Omega\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[P(\lambda A+(1-\lambda)B)\ge m_\alpha(P(A),P(B),\lambda),\] where \(\lambda A+(1-\lambda)B=\{\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y:x\in A,\ y\in B\}\). A random vector \(Z\) has an \(\alpha\)-concave distribution when its induced probability measure \(P_Z\) is \(\alpha\)-concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability measure is alpha-concave when the probability of every Minkowski convex combination of two Borel sets is at least the generalized alpha-mean of their probabilities. A random vector has an alpha-concave distribution when its induced measure has this property.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is a probability measure on the Lebesgue-measurable subsets of }\Omega

knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconcave Probability Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability mappings characterized by convex reliability superlevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(p:X\to[0,1]\) be a satisfaction-probability function, such as \(p(x)=P\{g(x,\xi)\le0\}\). The function \(p\) is quasiconcave if, for all \(x,y\in X\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),
\[
p(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\ge\min\{p(x),p(y)\}.
\]
Equivalently, every superlevel set \(F_\alpha=\{x\in X:p(x)\ge\alpha\}\), \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), is convex. Therefore a chance constraint \(p(x)\ge1-\varepsilon\) has a convex feasible region whenever its probability function is quasiconcave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability function is quasiconcave exactly when every reliability superlevel set, and hence every associated chance-feasible region, is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is quasiconcave if and only if \(F_\alpha\) is convex for every \(\alpha\in[0,1]\).

notation.meaning: Probability superlevel set at reliability α.

knowledge_statements.title: Connected Nonconvex Feasible Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectedness of a chance-feasible region does not imply convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\ge2\), \(U\) be uniform on \([0,1]\), and define \(p(x)=\exp(-(\lVert x\rVert_2-1)^2)\). Represent this probability as \(p(x)=P\{U\le p(x)\}\). For any \(\delta\in(0,1)\), the reliability threshold \(\alpha=e^{-\delta^2}\) produces
\[
F_\alpha=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:p(x)\ge\alpha\}
=\{x:1-\delta\le\lVert x\rVert_2\le1+\delta\}.
\]
This annulus is path-connected when \(n\ge2\), but it is not convex because it excludes the origin while containing opposite points of norm one. Hence connected chance-feasible regions need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability constraint can generate a path-connected annulus, demonstrating that connectedness is strictly weaker than convexity.

notation.meaning: Reliability superlevel set, here an annulus.

review_flags: The explicit construction is directly checkable, but a scholarly source for this connectivity-versus-convexity boundary is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constructed probability function has the stated annular superlevel set, which is path-connected for dimension at least two and nonconvex. It fits the counterexample container but lacks a scholarly source.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuity of Probability Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity, relative to a finite-dimensional decision set, under almost-sure constraint continuity and zero boundary mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(\xi:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m\) be a random vector, and let \(g:X\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be such that \(g(x,\xi)\) is measurable for every \(x\in X\). Define \(p(x)=\mathbb P\{g(x,\xi)\leq0\}\), and fix \(\bar x\in X\). Suppose that for \(\mathbb P\)-almost every \(\omega\in\Omega\), the map \(x\mapsto g(x,\xi(\omega))\) is continuous at \(\bar x\) relative to \(X\), and suppose \(\mathbb P\{g(\bar x,\xi)=0\}=0\). Then, for every sequence \((x_k)\subseteq X\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(\mathbf 1_{\{g(x_k,\xi)\leq0\}}\to\mathbf 1_{\{g(\bar x,\xi)\leq0\}}\) almost surely. Consequently, \(p(x_k)\to p(\bar x)\), so \(p\) is continuous at \(\bar x\) relative to \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to the decision set, a chance probability is continuous when the random constraint is almost surely continuous and the limiting boundary has zero probability.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space, \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and \(\xi:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m\) is a random vector.
For almost every \(\omega\), \(x\mapsto g(x,\xi(\omega))\) is continuous at \(\bar x\) relative to \(X\).

notation.meaning: probability that the random inequality is satisfied

children.title: Probability-Function Differentiability

knowledge_statements.title: Probability-Function Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiability through a regular moving boundary for an absolutely continuous random vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p(x)=\int_{\{z:g(x,z)\leq0\}}f(z)\,dz\) near \( ar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Assume \(g\) is continuously differentiable in \((x,z)\), \(f\) is continuous near the boundary, and \(
abla_z g( ar x,z)
eq0\) whenever \(g( ar x,z)=0\). If the boundary integrals are finite and locally dominated, then \(p\) is differentiable at \( ar x\), with
\[

abla p( ar x)=-\int_{\{z:g( ar x,z)=0\}} rac{
abla_x g( ar x,z)}{\|
abla_z g( ar x,z)\|}f(z)\,d\mathcal H^{m-1}(z).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under smoothness, nonvanishing boundary normals, and integrability, the probability gradient equals a density-weighted integral over the active random boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(g\in C^1\) near \(\{(\bar x,z):g(\bar x,z)=0\}\), and \(f\) is locally continuous.
\(\nabla_z g(\bar x,z)\neq0\) on the active boundary.
The displayed surface integrand admits a locally integrable dominating function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\) with the displayed boundary-integral gradient.

notation.meaning: Lebesgue density of the random vector

children.title: Chance-Boundary Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Variation of active probability boundaries under model or parameter perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Chance-Boundary Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional sensitivity represented as probability flux across a smoothly moving chance boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A(x)=\{z:g(x,z)\leq0\}\) and \(p(x)=\int_{A(x)}f(z)\,dz\), fix a direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Under the regularity and domination conditions for a smooth moving boundary, the normal velocity of \(\partial A(x)\) at \(\bar x\) is \(-\nabla_xg(\bar x,z)^{\mathsf T}d/\|\nabla_zg(\bar x,z)\|\). Hence
\[
p'(\bar x;d)=-\int_{\{g(\bar x,z)=0\}}\frac{\nabla_xg(\bar x,z)^{\mathsf T}d}{\|\nabla_zg(\bar x,z)\|}f(z)\,d\mathcal H^{m-1}(z).
\]
Thus only probability mass transported through the active boundary contributes to first-order sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional probability sensitivity is the density-weighted flux generated by normal motion of the active random boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is continuously differentiable and \(\nabla_zg\neq0\) on the active boundary.
The random vector has density \(f\), and the surface integral is finite.
Boundary differentiation is valid under local domination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The directional derivative \(p'(\bar x;d)\) equals the displayed boundary-flux integral.

children.title: Nonsmooth Boundary Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric or distributional settings where boundary sensitivity becomes discontinuous or set-valued.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Boundary Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of classical boundary differentiation at singular, intersecting, or positive-mass active boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The smooth boundary formula need not apply at \(\bar x\) if \(\nabla_zg(\bar x,z)=0\) on an active set, if several active surfaces intersect with nonnegligible contribution, or if \(\mathbb{P}\{g(\bar x,\xi)=0\}>0\). In these regimes the normal velocity may be undefined or nonintegrable, and \(p(x)=\mathbb{P}\{g(x,\xi)\leq0\}\) may have only one-sided directional derivatives, may be locally Lipschitz but nondifferentiable, or may be discontinuous. Therefore the classical surface-gradient expression is not a valid derivative certificate without additional stratification, generalized differentiation, or an explicit treatment of boundary atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singular normals, intersecting surfaces, or boundary atoms can destroy the classical probability gradient and may even cause discontinuity.
assumptions_latex: At least one smooth-boundary hypothesis fails at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Classical differentiability and the regular surface-gradient formula cannot be inferred at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: decision point at which regularity fails

children.title: Distributional Atoms
children.top_down_role: Discrete probability mass affecting chance-constraint probability functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atoms of a probability distribution and their boundary-mass interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on a measurable space \((S,\mathcal S)\). A measurable set \(A\in\mathcal S\) is an atom of \(\mu\) if \(\mu(A)>0\) and every measurable \(B\subseteq A\) satisfies either \(\mu(B)=0\) or \(\mu(B)=\mu(A)\). For a random vector \(\xi\) on \(\mathbb{R}^m\), a point atom is a point \(a\) with \(\mathbb{P}\{\xi=a\}>0\). If an active chance boundary contains such an atom, then its boundary probability is positive and zero-boundary-mass continuity conditions fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atom is an indivisible positive-probability set; a point atom on an active boundary creates positive boundary mass.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a probability measure on \((S,\mathcal S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is an atom exactly when \(\mu(A)>0\) and no measurable proper part has intermediate mass.

children.title: Probability Jumps
children.top_down_role: Discontinuities in satisfaction probabilities induced by discrete mass or threshold crossings.

knowledge_statements.title: Probability Jumps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jump size of a scalar distribution function at a point atom and its effect on a continuous decision-dependent threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\xi\) be a real-valued random variable and define \(F(t)=\mathbb P\{\xi\leq t\}\). For every \(a\in\mathbb R\), \(F(a-)=\mathbb P\{\xi<a\}\), and hence
\[
F(a)-F(a-)=\mathbb P\{\xi=a\}.
\]
Thus \(F\) is discontinuous at \(a\) exactly when \(\mathbb P\{\xi=a\}>0\), and its jump has that magnitude. Moreover, let \(h\) be continuous at \(x_0\), with \(h(x_0)=a\), and suppose there is a sequence \(x_k\to x_0\) satisfying \(h(x_k)<a\). If \(p(x)=F(h(x))\) and \(\mathbb P\{\xi=a\}>0\), then \(p(x_k)\to F(a-)\neq F(a)=p(x_0)\), so \(p\) is discontinuous at \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distribution function jumps exactly at point atoms, with jump size equal to the atomic mass; a continuous threshold approaching such an atom from below transfers that jump to the chance probability.
assumptions_latex: \(\xi\) is a real-valued random variable and \(F(t)=\mathbb P\{\xi\leq t\}\).
For the composition claim, \(h\) is continuous at \(x_0\), \(h(x_0)=a\), and some sequence \(x_k\to x_0\) satisfies \(h(x_k)<a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(a)-F(a-)=\mathbb P\{\xi=a\}\); under the stated threshold condition, positive mass at \(a\) makes \(F\circ h\) discontinuous at \(x_0\).

notation.meaning: cumulative distribution function of the random variable
left limit of the distribution function at a

children.title: Atom-Induced Feasible-Set Discontinuity

knowledge_statements.title: Atom-Induced Feasible-Set Discontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-point distribution causing discontinuity of the chance-feasible-set mapping in the reliability level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q\in(0,1)\), let \(\mathbb{P}\{\xi=0\}=q\) and \(\mathbb{P}\{\xi=1\}=1-q\), and define
\[
C(\alpha)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:\mathbb{P}(\xi\leq x)\geq\alpha\},\qquad \alpha\in(0,1].
\]
Then \(C(\alpha)=[0,\infty)\) for \(0<\alpha\leq q\), whereas \(C(\alpha)=[1,\infty)\) for \(q<\alpha\leq1\). Hence the lower endpoint of the feasible set jumps from \(0\) to \(1\) as \(\alpha\) crosses the atomic mass \(q\); in particular, \(C(\cdot)\) is not lower semicontinuous at \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Bernoulli distribution, crossing an atom’s cumulative mass shifts the chance-feasible set endpoint discontinuously from zero to one.
assumptions_latex: \(q\in(0,1)\) and \(\xi\) has mass \(q\) at \(0\) and mass \(1-q\) at \(1\).

notation.meaning: chance-feasible set at reliability level alpha

knowledge_statements.title: Probability-Efficient Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-minimal threshold vectors attaining a prescribed joint probability level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m)\) be a random vector, let \(F_Y(z)=\mathbb{P}\{Y_i\leq z_i\text{ for all }i\}\), and fix \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Define the upper probability set \(Z_\alpha=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^m:F_Y(z)\geq\alpha\}\). A point \(z\in Z_\alpha\) is probability-efficient at level \(\alpha\) if no distinct \(w\in Z_\alpha\) satisfies \(w\leq z\) componentwise. Equivalently, every componentwise decrease that produces a distinct threshold vector destroys feasibility or must be offset by an increase in another component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability-efficient threshold is a componentwise minimal vector whose joint satisfaction probability reaches the required reliability level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\) is probability-efficient exactly when \(z\in Z_\alpha\) and no \(w\in Z_\alpha\setminus\{z\}\) satisfies \(w\leq z\).

knowledge_statements.title: Probability-Efficient Frontiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto frontier of the upper set of threshold vectors satisfying a joint chance requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Z_\alpha=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^m:F_Y(z)\geq\alpha\}\), its probability-efficient frontier is
\[
\mathcal E_\alpha=\operatorname{Min}_{\leq}Z_\alpha
=\{z\in Z_\alpha:(z-\mathbb{R}_+^m)\cap Z_\alpha=\{z\}\}.
\]
Because \(F_Y\) is componentwise nondecreasing, \(Z_\alpha\) is an upper set: \(z\in Z_\alpha\) and \(u\geq z\) imply \(u\in Z_\alpha\). If every point of \(Z_\alpha\) dominates some minimal point, then
\[
Z_\alpha=\mathcal E_\alpha+\mathbb{R}_+^m.
\]
Thus the frontier generates the entire probability-feasible threshold region by upward closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The probability-efficient frontier contains all minimal feasible thresholds and, when minimal points exist below every feasible point, generates the full upper set.
assumptions_latex: \(F_Y\) is the joint lower-orthant distribution function of an \(\mathbb{R}^m\)-valued random vector.
Every \(z\in Z_\alpha\) dominates at least one order-minimal point of \(Z_\alpha\) for the final equality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E_\alpha=\operatorname{Min}_{\leq}Z_\alpha\), and under the stated attainment condition \(Z_\alpha=\mathcal E_\alpha+\mathbb{R}_+^m\).
