knowledge_statements.title: Empirical Probability Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-average approximation of a scalar chance constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^N\) be independent samples from the distribution of \(\xi\), let \(X\) be a decision set, and let \(g:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) be measurable in its second argument. The empirical satisfaction probability and empirical violation probability at \(x\in X\) are
\[\widehat p_N(x)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf 1\{g(x,\xi^i)\le 0\},\qquad \widehat V_N(x)=1-\widehat p_N(x).\]
Thus the empirical approximation of \(\mathbb P\{g(x,\xi)\le0\}\ge1-\alpha\) is \(\widehat p_N(x)\ge1-\alpha\), equivalently \(\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf 1\{g(x,\xi^i)>0\}\le\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace the unknown satisfaction probability by the fraction of sampled constraints satisfied, allowing at most floor(alpha times the sample size) observed violations.
assumptions_latex: \(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^N\) are independent and identically distributed as \(\xi\).
review_flags: Exact source locator for empirical chance-constraint approximation is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and counting equivalence are mathematically correct and fit the leaf, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports the empirical chance-constraint formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical Quantile Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-statistic representation of an empirical chance constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in X\), set \(L_i(x)=g(x,\xi^i)\) and define the empirical distribution \(\widehat F_{N,x}(t)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf 1\{L_i(x)\le t\}\). Its lower empirical \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile is
\[\widehat q_{1-\alpha,N}(x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:\widehat F_{N,x}(t)\ge1-\alpha\}.\]
If \(L_{(1)}(x)\le\cdots\le L_{(N)}(x)\) are the ordered losses and \(k=\lceil(1-\alpha)N\rceil\), then \(\widehat q_{1-\alpha,N}(x)=L_{(k)}(x)\). Consequently, the empirical chance constraint is equivalent to \(\widehat q_{1-\alpha,N}(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The empirical chance constraint holds exactly when the designated upper order statistic of sampled constraint losses is nonpositive.
review_flags: Exact source locator for the order-statistic representation is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower empirical quantile and order-statistic equivalence are correct for N>=1 and alpha in [0,1), and representation is the appropriate kind. No source supports the stated quantile convention or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Empirical Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact big-M formulation of empirical violation counting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and suppose finite constants \(M_i\) satisfy \(g(x,\xi^i)\le M_i\) for every \(x\in X\). For \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\), the empirical chance constraint has the mixed-integer representation
\[g(x,\xi^i)\le M_i z_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,N),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^N z_i\le\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor.\]
A feasible \(x\) admits such a binary vector exactly when no more than \(\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor\) sampled inequalities are violated. Hence any objective \(c(x)\) may be optimized over this system to obtain an exact big-M formulation of the empirical problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary variables mark sampled violations; valid big-M bounds make the resulting mixed-integer system exactly equivalent to the empirical chance constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists z:\ g(x,\xi^i)\le M_i z_i,\ \sum_i z_i\le\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor\iff\sum_i\mathbf1\{g(x,\xi^i)>0\}\le\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor\).

notation.meaning: binary indicator permitting violation of sample i

review_flags: Exact source locator for the big-M equivalence is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The existential big-M representation is correct under the stated finite valid upper bounds and fits the leaf as a representation. It lacks a source and specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Scenario Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite sampled approximation of a convex uncertain program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex; let \(c:X\to\mathbb R\) be convex; and let \(f(\cdot,\delta):X\to\mathbb R\) be convex for every uncertainty realization \(\delta\in\Delta\). Given independent samples \(\delta^1,\ldots,\delta^N\), the convex scenario program is
\[\min_{x\in X} c(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f(x,\delta^i)\le0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.\]
Whenever the feasible set is nonempty and the minimum is attained, a fixed deterministic tie-breaking rule defines its scenario solution \(x_N\). Its out-of-sample violation probability is \(V(x_N)=\mathbb P\{\delta:f(x_N,\delta)>0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex scenario program enforces a convex uncertain constraint only at finitely many independent uncertainty samples and evaluates the optimizer by its out-of-sample violation probability.
assumptions_latex: The sampled problem is feasible, attains its minimum, and uses deterministic tie-breaking.
review_flags: Authoritative scenario-approach definition locator is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a suitable definition of a convex scenario program, with attainment and deterministic selection stated. The authoritative scenario-approach citation required for this nontrivial definition is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Constraint Scenario Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario approximation with several uncertain constraint families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(c:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(f_j:X\times\Delta_j\to\mathbb R\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). For each family \(j\), draw samples \(\delta_j^1,\ldots,\delta_j^{N_j}\) from its prescribed uncertainty law. The multiple-constraint scenario program is
\[\min_{x\in X}c(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_j(x,\delta_j^i)\le0,\qquad j=1,\ldots,m,\quad i=1,\ldots,N_j.\]
If \(X\), \(c\), and every sampled constraint are convex in \(x\), this is a convex program. Each family has violation probability \(V_j(x)=\mathbb P_j\{f_j(x,\delta_j)>0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate sample collections enforce multiple uncertain constraint families, each retaining its own out-of-sample violation probability.
assumptions_latex: Samples within each family are independent with law \(\mathbb P_j\).
All sampled feasible sets and the objective are convex when convexity is claimed.

notation.meaning: sample size for constraint family j

review_flags: Exact source and sampling convention for multiple-constraint scenario programs are missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed multi-family program fits the leaf, but the conclusion introduces an optimizer without assuming attainment or deterministic selection. A source is also needed to determine the intended dependence or independence convention across constraint families.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Programs with Discarding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint optimization over a decision and a bounded discarded-sample set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given samples \(\delta^1,,\ldots,,\delta^N\), an integer \(r\in\{0,,\ldots,,N-1\}\), a decision set \(X\), objective \(c\), and constraint function \(f\), solve
\[\min_{x\in X,\ I\subseteq\{1,,\ldots,,N\}} c(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad |I|\le r,\qquad f(x,,\delta^i)\le0\ \text{for every }i\notin I.\]
Initialize with all samples available; choose \(I\) either jointly or by a specified removal rule; re-solve after removals; and output the final optimizer \(x_{N,r}\), the discarded index set \(I\), and the retained sampled constraints. Ties in both \(x\) and \(I\) are resolved deterministically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method optimizes after discarding at most a prescribed number of sampled constraints and returns both the optimizer and discarded indices.
assumptions_latex: Every retained-sample subproblem considered by the procedure attains a minimum.
A deterministic rule resolves optimizer and discard-set ties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_{N,r},I)\) satisfies \(|I|\le r\) and \(f(x_{N,r},\delta^i)\le0\) for every \(i\notin I\).
review_flags: Exact source locator and intended discard rule are missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record blends joint optimization over discarded indices with an unspecified iterative removal rule, which are distinct variants. The intended algorithm cannot be determined without a source; repeated double commas in the mathematical text must also be repaired.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Scenario Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative scenario optimization with independent validation batches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a maximum iteration \(K\), design sizes \(N_k\), validation sizes \(M_k\), and thresholds \(\tau_k\in[0,1]\). At iteration \(k\), draw or augment to \(N_k\) design samples, solve the corresponding scenario program to obtain \(x_k\), and draw an independent validation batch \(\widetilde\delta_k^1,\ldots,\widetilde\delta_k^{M_k}\). Compute
\[\widehat V_k=\frac1{M_k}\sum_{i=1}^{M_k}\mathbf1\{f(x_k,\widetilde\delta_k^i)>0\}.\]
Stop and return \(x_k\) when \(\widehat V_k\le\tau_k\); otherwise increase \(k\). If no earlier test accepts, return the prescribed terminal output at \(k=K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve enlarging scenario programs and accept the first candidate whose independent validation batch has sufficiently few violations.
assumptions_latex: Each validation batch is independent of the design data used to compute \(x_k\).
Each scenario subproblem has a deterministically selected solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\) is accepted at the first \(k\le K\) satisfying \(M_k^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf1\{f(x_k,\widetilde\delta_k^i)>0\}\le\tau_k\).
review_flags: Several sequential scenario algorithms exist; the intended confidence-calibrated schedule lacks a source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is only a generic validation-loop template. Sequential scenario algorithms require sourced schedules and acceptance thresholds to support their confidence properties, and the terminal output at K is left unspecified.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Scenario Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of dimension-based support bounds without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convex dimension-based support bounds need not survive nonconvexity. For any \(N\ge1\), take the scalar decision set \(X=\{0,1,,\ldots,,N\}\), objective \(c(x)=x\), samples \(\delta^i=i-1\), and sampled constraints \(x\ne\delta^i\) for \(i=1,,\ldots,,N\). The full scenario program has the unique optimizer \(x_N=N\). If sample \(i\) is removed, the unique optimizer becomes \(x=i-1\), so every one of the \(N\) sampled constraints is a support constraint. Thus a one-dimensional nonconvex scenario program can have arbitrarily many support constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convexity, even a scalar scenario program can have arbitrarily many support constraints, invalidating bounds based only on decision dimension.
assumptions_latex: Support means that removing the sampled constraint strictly improves the optimal objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(X)=1\) in the ambient scalar sense, while the number of support constraints equals \(N\), which is unbounded.
review_flags: The explicit counterexample is self-contained but lacks an external source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly shows that ambient scalar dimension alone does not bound support-set size in this nonconvex construction, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. It nevertheless lacks evidence, and repeated double commas should be corrected.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampled constraints essential to a scenario optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a feasible scenario program with attained optimal value \(J_N\) and a deterministically selected optimizer. For a sampled constraint indexed by \(i\), let \(J_N^{(-i)}\) denote the optimal value after removing only that constraint. Constraint \(i\) is a support constraint if
\[J_N^{(-i)}<J_N\]
for a minimization problem. Equivalently, its removal changes the optimal objective value; under uniqueness, it necessarily changes the optimizer. The support set is \(S_N=\{i:J_N^{(-i)}<J_N\}\). This definition concerns objective-essential sampled constraints and is stronger than merely being active at the selected optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sampled constraint is supporting when deleting it strictly improves the scenario program’s optimal value; activity alone is insufficient.
assumptions_latex: The full and leave-one-out scenario programs are feasible and attain finite minima.
A deterministic selection rule is fixed when optimizer comparisons are used.

notation.meaning: optimal value after removing sample i

review_flags: Authoritative locator for the chosen objective-value definition of support is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The objective-value definition is internally coherent for attained minimization problems and correctly distinguishes support from activity. An authoritative locator is required because scenario literature uses convention-sensitive formulations involving value or solution changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Helly Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform essential bound on scenario support-set size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a class of scenario programs and every sample size \(N\), let \(S_N(\boldsymbol\delta)\) be the support set produced by sample tuple \(\boldsymbol\delta=(\delta^1,,\ldots,,\delta^N)\). The Helly dimension \(h\) is the smallest integer such that
\[\mathbb P^N\bigl\{\boldsymbol\delta:|S_N(\boldsymbol\delta)|\le h\bigr\}=1\qquad\text{for every }N\ge1.\]
Equivalently, \(h=\sup_{N\ge1}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\boldsymbol\delta\sim\mathbb P^N}|S_N(\boldsymbol\delta)|\), when this supremum is finite. The definition depends on the program class, probability law, and deterministic solution rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Helly dimension is the smallest uniform almost-sure upper bound on the number of support constraints over all sample sizes.
assumptions_latex: Support sets are measurable under \(\mathbb P^N\).
A deterministic scenario-solution rule is fixed.
The displayed essential supremum is finite when \(h<\infty\) is asserted.

notation.meaning: support set for a sample tuple

review_flags: Scenario-specific Helly-dimension convention requires an authoritative source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed almost-sure support-cardinality bound is plausible, but the scenario-specific Helly-dimension convention needs a source and should explicitly address the unbounded value h=infinity. Repeated double commas also require correction.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective dimension on which an uncertain constraint depends.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the decision space be \(\mathbb R^n\), and let \(f(x,,\delta)\le0\) be one uncertain constraint family. An unconstrained subspace is a linear subspace \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) such that
\[f(x+v,,\delta)=f(x,,\delta)\]
for every \(v\in L\), every \(x\) for which both \(x\) and \(x+v\) lie in the decision domain, and every \(\delta\). If \(L_{\max}\) is an unconstrained subspace of greatest dimension, the support rank of the family is \(\rho=n-\dim(L_{\max})\). It counts the decision directions potentially restricted by that uncertain family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support rank is the ambient decision dimension minus the largest subspace along which the uncertain constraint is invariant.
assumptions_latex: The decision variables lie in a finite-dimensional space \(\mathbb R^n\).
A maximum-dimensional invariant linear subspace exists.
Constraint invariance holds for every uncertainty realization.
review_flags: Exact support-rank definition and domain convention require a scenario-theory source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The effective-dimension formula is plausible, but support-rank definitions depend on the precise maximal unconstrained-subspace and decision-domain convention. That convention needs authoritative support; repeated double commas should also be repaired.

children.title: Compression Sets
children.top_down_role: Subsets that retain the essential information of a scenario program.

knowledge_statements.title: Compression Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subsamples that reconstruct and certify the full-sample solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be a deterministic scenario solver mapping each finite indexed sample set \(T\) to a decision \(A(T)\). For a full sample index set \(I_N=\{1,,\ldots,,N\}\), a subset \(C\subseteq I_N\) is a compression set if
\[A(C)=A(I_N)\quad\text{and}\quad f(A(C),,\delta^i)\le0\ \text{for every }i\in I_N.\]
Thus the decisions reconstructed from \(C\) and from all samples coincide, and the reconstructed decision satisfies every sampled constraint. The compression size is \(|C|\); a minimal compression set has minimum cardinality among all subsets satisfying these two conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compression set is a subsample that reconstructs the full-sample decision and whose reconstructed decision remains feasible for every original sample.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is deterministic on every finite subsample under consideration.
The full sampled problem has a selected feasible solution.
Sample indices are retained, including when uncertainty values repeat.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\subseteq I_N\) is compressing exactly when \(A(C)=A(I_N)\) and \(f(A(C),\delta^i)\le0\) for all \(i\in I_N\).

notation.meaning: decision reconstructed from indexed sample set T

review_flags: Compression-set conventions vary; an authoritative source for the intended reconstruction and consistency conditions is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Compression conventions vary: some require reconstruction consistency, while this record additionally requires equality with the full-sample solver output. Under its own feasibility assumptions that equality makes the separate full-sample feasibility condition redundant. A source is needed to establish the intended definition, and repeated double commas require correction.

children.title: Support Subsamples
children.top_down_role: Scenario subsamples identified through their influence on the optimizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Subsamples
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Irreducible subsamples that reproduce a scenario algorithm’s full-sample decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) map every finite indexed scenario sample \(S_I=(\xi_i)_{i\in I}\) to a decision \(A(S_I)\). For a full sample \(S_{[N]}\), a subset \(I\subseteq[N]\) is a support subsample if \(A(S_I)=A(S_{[N]})\) and every retained index is essential within that subsample: \(A(S_{I\setminus\{i\}})\ne A(S_I)\) for every \(i\in I\). Thus the subsample reproduces the full-sample decision and is inclusion-minimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support subsample reproduces the full scenario decision, while deleting any one of its retained scenarios changes that decision.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but no citation supports this specific use of “support subsample.” Moreover, deleting the sole member of a singleton subsample invokes A on the empty sample, although the assumption only defines A for nonempty subsamples.

children.title: Minimal Compression Size
children.top_down_role: Cardinality measures governing the smallest informative scenario subset.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Compression Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smallest subsample cardinality sufficient to reconstruct the full-sample decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a deterministic scenario-solution map \(A\) and sample \(S_{[N]}\), define the compression family by \(\mathcal C(S_{[N]})=\{I\subseteq[N]:A(S_I)=A(S_{[N]})\}\). When this family is nonempty, its minimal compression size is \[k_*(S_{[N]})=\min_{I\in\mathcal C(S_{[N]})}|I|.\] Any minimizing index set is a minimal compression set; minimality here concerns cardinality, not merely inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal compression size is the fewest sampled scenarios needed to reproduce the decision obtained from all scenarios.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, but the record has no source establishing that decision equality alone is the intended compression and reconstruction convention.

children.title: Compression–Support Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationships between compression sets and support-based representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Compression–Support Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nondegenerate convex scenario programs with a unique optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a convex scenario program with unique optimizer \(x_N\). Let \(J\subseteq[N]\) contain exactly the support constraints, meaning that deleting any \(j\in J\) changes the optimizer. If the program is nondegenerate in the sense that the constraints indexed by \(J\) alone yield \(x_N\), then \(J\) is an inclusion-minimal compression set. If, additionally, every compression set contains \(J\), then \(J\) is the unique minimum-cardinality compression set and \(k_*(S_{[N]})=|J|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under uniqueness and nondegeneracy, support constraints reconstruct the optimizer; with containment of supports, they form the unique smallest compression set.
assumptions_latex: The scenario program is convex and has a unique optimizer \(x_N\).
Every decision-reproducing compression set contains all support indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J\) is the unique minimum-cardinality compression set and \(k_*(S_{[N]})=|J|\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the correspondence leaf, but its conclusions depend on specialized definitions of support, compression, and nondegeneracy. No source is supplied to verify that these hypotheses imply the stated inclusion and uniqueness claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Dimension Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical convex scenario bound using ambient decision dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) independent scenarios define a feasible convex scenario program in \(\mathbb R^d\), and let \(x_N\) be its measurable, almost surely unique and nondegenerate optimizer. For violation probability \(V(x)=\mathbb P\{\xi:f(x,\xi)>0\}\) and \(0<\epsilon<1\), \[\mathbb P^N\{V(x_N)>\epsilon\}\le \sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\binom Ni\epsilon^i(1-\epsilon)^{N-i}.\] Consequently, any \(N\) making the displayed binomial tail at most \(\beta\) certifies confidence at least \(1-\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nondegenerate convex program in dimension d, a binomial tail through d−1 bounds the probability that the scenario solution exceeds violation level ε.
assumptions_latex: The sampled constraints are convex in \(x\in\mathbb R^d\).
The optimizer is measurable, almost surely unique, and nondegenerate.
The \(N\) scenarios are independent and identically distributed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role and classical binomial form fit the leaf, but no cited theorem or locator verifies the precise feasibility, measurability, uniqueness, nondegeneracy, and dimension hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Helly-Dimension Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario bound parameterized by a uniform support-cardinality bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a measurable scenario algorithm is consistent with all \(N\) independent samples and has Helly dimension \(\zeta\), meaning that its number of support constraints is almost surely at most \(\zeta\). Under uniqueness and nondegeneracy, for \(0<\epsilon<1\), \[\mathbb P^N\{V(x_N)>\epsilon\}\le \sum_{i=0}^{\zeta-1}\binom Ni\epsilon^i(1-\epsilon)^{N-i}.\] Hence it suffices to choose \(N\) so that this tail does not exceed the desired failure probability \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing ambient dimension by a valid Helly-dimension bound yields a binomial scenario certificate governed by at most ζ support constraints.
assumptions_latex: The scenario solution is consistent with every sampled constraint.
The support cardinality is almost surely at most \(\zeta\).
The solution is measurable, unique, and nondegenerate.

notation.meaning: Violation probability of the scenario solution.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind fits, but Helly dimension has convention-dependent definitions. A source is required to verify that the stated support-cardinality convention yields a tail ending at ζ−1 under exactly these assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Rank Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-specific scenario bound using effective rather than ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider one convex uncertain constraint family whose dependence on the decision is confined to an effective subspace of support rank \(\rho\). If the associated scenario solution \(x_N\) is measurable, consistent, unique, and nondegenerate, and the family admits at most \(\rho\) support constraints almost surely, then \[\mathbb P^N\{V(x_N)>\epsilon\}\le \sum_{i=0}^{\rho-1}\binom Ni\epsilon^i(1-\epsilon)^{N-i}.\] Thus \(\rho\), rather than the full decision dimension, controls the required sample size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an uncertain constraint acts only through support rank ρ, its scenario sample bound uses ρ instead of the full decision dimension.
assumptions_latex: The uncertain constraint is convex and has support rank \(\rho\).
Its scenario solution is measurable, consistent, unique, and nondegenerate.
Samples are independent and identically distributed.

notation.meaning: Support rank of the uncertain constraint family.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record belongs in the support-rank bound leaf, but no source verifies the definition of support rank or that the family-specific violation probability of the joint scenario solution obeys this direct binomial bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Constraint Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Familywise scenario certification via allocated violation and confidence budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\) convex uncertain constraint families have violation probabilities \(V_j(x_N)\), sample counts \(N_j\), and valid support bounds \(\zeta_j\). Assume the samples used for each family satisfy the hypotheses of its scenario bound. If numbers \(\epsilon_j,\beta_j\in(0,1)\) satisfy \[\sum_{i=0}^{\zeta_j-1}\binom{N_j}{i}\epsilon_j^i(1-\epsilon_j)^{N_j-i}\le\beta_j\quad(j=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \sum_{j=1}^m\beta_j\le\beta,\] then the union bound gives \(\mathbb P\{\exists j:V_j(x_N)>\epsilon_j\}\le\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate violation and confidence budgets across constraint families; summing their individual scenario failure bounds controls the probability that any family fails.
assumptions_latex: Each family satisfies a scenario bound with support parameter \(\zeta_j\).

notation.meaning: Violation probability for constraint family j.
Allocated failure budget for family j.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The union-bound step is standard, but the substantive individual bounds for the jointly determined optimizer are only assumed and have no cited theorem. A source must establish the sampling and support conditions for each family.

children.title: Scenario Discard Bounds
children.top_down_role: Sample-complexity guarantees permitting selected scenario removals.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Discard Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex scenario programs allowing removal of a prescribed number of samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a convex scenario program in \(\mathbb R^d\) use \(N\) independent samples, discard exactly \(r\) constraints, and return a measurable, unique, nondegenerate optimizer \(x_{N,r}\). Assume every discarded constraint is violated by \(x_{N,r}\). A standard removal bound is \[\mathbb P^N\{V(x_{N,r})>\epsilon\}\le \binom{r+d-1}{r}\sum_{i=0}^{r+d-1}\binom Ni\epsilon^i(1-\epsilon)^{N-i}.\] Therefore any \(N\) making the right-hand side at most \(\beta\) provides confidence at least \(1-\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discarding r scenarios enlarges the support order and adds a combinatorial penalty; the resulting binomial expression bounds excess violation probability.
assumptions_latex: The sampled program is convex with a measurable, unique, nondegenerate optimizer.
Exactly \(r\) sampled constraints are discarded and each is violated by the returned optimizer.
The \(N\) scenarios are independent and identically distributed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits, but the combinatorial prefactor and tail order depend on the exact scenario-removal theorem and discard rule. No source verifies them, and admissible ranges for ε, N, r, and d are not fully stated.

children.title: Compression-Based Bounds
children.top_down_role: Sample-complexity guarantees parameterized by compression structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Compression-Based Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-free union bound for consistent sample-compression reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) scenarios be independent and identically distributed. Suppose an output hypothesis is reconstructed from some indexed subsample of exactly \(k\) scenarios and violates at most \(r\) of the remaining \(N-k\) observations. For any \(0<\epsilon<1\), a union bound over compression subsets gives \[\mathbb P^N\{V>\epsilon\}\le \binom Nk\sum_{j=0}^{r}\binom{N-k}{j}\epsilon^j(1-\epsilon)^{N-k-j}.\] The right-hand side, capped at \(1\), is a valid confidence bound whenever reconstruction depends only on the selected compression subsample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unioning over all k-point compression sets yields a distribution-free violation bound, including a binomial allowance for up to r observed errors.
assumptions_latex: The observations are independent and identically distributed.
Reconstruction depends only on the selected \(k\)-element subsample.
The reconstructed hypothesis violates at most \(r\) remaining observations.

notation.meaning: Allowed errors outside the compression set.
True violation probability of the reconstruction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed union bound is plausible and fits the leaf, but its validity depends on the precise sample-compression reconstruction model and treatment of residual errors. No authoritative theorem or locator is supplied.

children.title: Discard Budget Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes distinguished by the permitted number or proportion of discarded scenarios.

knowledge_statements.title: Discard Budget Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic behavior of scenario-removal bounds under different discard growth rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(d\), \(0<\epsilon<1\), and use the scenario-discard bound \(B_{N,r}\) displayed in the removal theorem. If \(r\) is fixed while \(N\to\infty\), then \(B_{N,r}\to0\) exponentially up to a polynomial factor. If \(r/N\to\alpha<\epsilon\), the binomial lower-tail term still decays exponentially, while the fixed-dimensional prefactor grows only polynomially. If \(r/N\to\alpha>\epsilon\), that lower-tail probability tends to one, so this bound cannot certify a vanishing failure probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed or subcritical discard budgets permit asymptotic certification, whereas discarding a fraction above the target violation level destroys this binomial-tail guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The decision dimension \(d\) and violation level \(\epsilon\) are fixed.
The scenario-removal bound applies for every \(N\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the regimes leaf, but the asymptotic conclusions inherit an unverified removal formula. The critical regime α=ε is also intentionally unresolved and requires a sourced, more precise treatment.

children.title: Compression Cardinality Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes distinguished by the size of an informative compression set.

knowledge_statements.title: Compression Cardinality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic regimes for the elementary consistent-compression bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For consistent reconstruction from \(k_N\) samples, define \(B_N=\min\{1,\binom{N}{k_N}(1-\epsilon)^{N-k_N}\}\). If \(k_N\) is fixed, then \(B_N\) decays exponentially up to a polynomial factor. More generally, if \(k_N=o(N)\) and \(k_N\log(N/k_N)=o(N)\), then \(N^{-1}\log B_N\to\log(1-\epsilon)<0\). If \(k_N/N\to\kappa\in(0,1)\), its exponential-rate upper estimate is \(H(\kappa)+(1-\kappa)\log(1-\epsilon)\), so decay is certified only when this quantity is negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small compression sets give exponential confidence improvement; proportional compression sizes require a negative entropy-adjusted exponent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_N\to0\) in the stated fixed and sublinear regimes, and in the proportional regime when \(H(\kappa)+(1-\kappa)\log(1-\epsilon)<0\).

notation.meaning: Compression cardinality at sample size N.
Binary entropy, equal to minus κ log κ minus (1−κ) log(1−κ).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asymptotic calculations are plausible and the property role fits, but they rely on an uncited compression bound and supply no authoritative source for the entropy-rate characterization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-Sure Uniqueness and Constant Minimal Compression Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nondegeneracy condition requiring the minimal informative scenario set to be uniquely determined and to have an eventually fixed cardinality almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists $\mathfrak n\in\mathbb N$ such that, for every $N\geq\mathfrak n$, the minimal set $\mathcal J(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^N)$ is uniquely defined almost surely and has cardinality $\mathfrak n$ almost surely; in particular, $P^N\{|\mathcal J|=\mathfrak n\}=1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There is a fixed integer such that, for every sufficiently large sample size, the minimal informative scenario set is almost surely unique and almost surely has that fixed size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall N\geq\mathfrak n,\quad \mathcal J(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^N)\text{ is uniquely defined a.s. and }P^N\{|\mathcal J|=\mathfrak n\}=1

source_evidence.locator: Statistical Inference / 5.7. Chance Constrained Problems / Assumption F2

source_refs.locator: Statistical Inference / 5.7. Chance Constrained Problems / Assumption F2

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Sure Uniqueness and Constant Minimal Compression Cardinality

source_witnesses.locator: Statistical Inference / 5.7. Chance Constrained Problems / Assumption F2

children.title: Discard–Compression Bound Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relative tightness and applicability of discard-based versus compression-based guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Discard–Compression Bound Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural comparison of removal-specific and generic compression confidence bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For common parameters \((N,\epsilon)\), scenario-discard and compression bounds are compared by their complete right-hand sides, not by identifying discard count with compression size. A removal theorem uses support order \(d+r\), a binomial tail, and assumptions on convexity, nondegeneracy, and the discard rule. A generic compression theorem instead unions over \(k\)-element reconstruction sets and permits \(r\) residual sample errors. Thus either certificate is admissible when its own bound is at most \(\beta\); no ordering follows solely from \(d\), \(r\), and \(k\) without matching their hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discard and compression bounds use different combinatorics and assumptions, so compare their full numerical bounds only after matching the reconstruction and removal models.
assumptions_latex: Both candidate bounds are evaluated at the same \(N\) and \(\epsilon\).
Each theorem’s distinct structural hypotheses are satisfied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{disc}}\le\beta\) or \(B_{\mathrm{comp}}\le\beta\) supplies its corresponding certificate; no universal ordering is asserted.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cautious comparison and property role fit the leaf, but both bound versions and their structural assumptions remain uncited. Sources are needed before the claimed distinction and absence of a universal ordering can be retained as knowledge.

assumptions_latex: The sampled problem is convex and feasible, and its optimizer \(x_N\) is selected measurably and uniquely by a fixed tie-breaking rule.
The \(N\) scenarios are independent and identically distributed, and the scenario solution has support dimension at most \(d\).

notation.meaning: Number of sampled scenarios and support-dimension bound.
Violation probability of a decision under a fresh scenario.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional convex scenario bound using a support-dimension upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_N\) solve the convex scenario program obtained by imposing \(g(x,\xi_i)\leq 0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,N\). If its support dimension is at most \(d\), then for every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \[\mathbb{P}^N\{V(x_N)>\varepsilon\}\leq \sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\binom{N}{i}\varepsilon^i(1-\varepsilon)^{N-i}.\] Consequently, any \(N\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\binom{N}{i}\varepsilon^i(1-\varepsilon)^{N-i}\leq\beta\) gives confidence at least \(1-\beta\) that \(V(x_N)\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the binomial scenario tail is at most beta, the scenario optimizer violates a fresh constraint with probability at most epsilon, except on a sampling event of probability beta.
knowledge_statements.title: A Priori Scenario Guarantees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem and content kind fit the a priori guarantee container, but no citation supports the exact support-dimension tail bound or its regularity hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: A Posteriori Support Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic support-indexed posterior certificate whose calibration must be supplied by a valid scenario theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Before sampling, choose thresholds \(\varepsilon_0,\ldots,\varepsilon_N\in[0,1]\) satisfying a support-sensitive theorem that guarantees \[\mathbb{P}^N\!\left\{V(x_N)>\varepsilon_{s_N}\right\}\leq\beta.\] After solving the scenario program, identify a support subsample and let \(s_N\) be its cardinality. The resulting a posteriori certificate reports \(V(x_N)\leq\varepsilon_{s_N}\) and records \(x_N\), the support subsample, its size, the calibration table, and the fixed optimization rule. Substitution of \(s_N\) into an a priori bound is valid only when the cited calibration theorem permits it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid support-sensitive theorem pre-calibrates thresholds indexed by the observed support count; the realized count, support subsample, and fixed solver rule form the posterior certificate.
assumptions_latex: The scenario program has a measurably selected optimizer \(x_N\) under a fixed optimization and tie-breaking rule.
A cited support-sensitive theorem validates the preselected thresholds \((\varepsilon_k)_{k=0}^{N}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(x_N)\leq\varepsilon_{s_N}\) is reported with confidence at least \(1-\beta\).

notation.meaning: Observed cardinality of the identified support subsample.
Violation probability under a fresh scenario.

children.title: Deferred Certificate Assessment
children.top_down_role: Certification settings in which reliability is assessed after solving the scenario program.

knowledge_statements.title: Deferred Certificate Assessment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precommitted error allocation permitting support-indexed certificate selection after optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Before sampling, select nonnegative budgets \((\beta_k)_{k=0}^{N}\) and thresholds \((\varepsilon_k)_{k=0}^{N}\) such that \(\sum_{k=0}^{N}\beta_k\leq\beta\) and \[\mathbb{P}^N\!\left\{s_N=k,\ V(x_N)>\varepsilon_k\right\}\leq\beta_k\qquad(k=0,\ldots,N).\] After observing \(s_N\), the deferred certificate reports \(V(x_N)\leq\varepsilon_{s_N}\), with joint failure probability at most \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precommitted thresholds and error budgets for every possible support count allow the observed count to select a certificate while keeping total failure probability at most beta.
assumptions_latex: The tables \((\varepsilon_k)_{k=0}^{N}\) and \((\beta_k)_{k=0}^{N}\) are fixed before sampling.
For every \(k\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\), a cited theorem gives \(\mathbb{P}^N\{s_N=k,\ V(x_N)>\varepsilon_k\}\leq\beta_k\).

notation.meaning: Violation probability of the scenario decision.

children.title: Observed-Support Judgment
children.top_down_role: Reliability assessment based on the realized support structure.

assumptions_latex: A support scenario is defined relative to a fixed sampled optimization problem and a fixed deterministic tie-breaking rule.
The sampled program is feasible and has finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_N=|I_N|\), where \(I_N\) is determined by leave-one-out objective changes.

notation.meaning: Optimal value of the full scenario program.
Optimal value after removing scenario i.
Support index set and observed support count.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-value definition of support scenarios for a minimization-form scenario program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization scenario program with optimal value \(J_N\), let \(J_{N,-i}\) be the optimal value after deleting sampled constraint \(i\) and applying the same tie-breaking rule. The observed support set and support count are \[I_N:=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}:J_{N,-i}<J_N\},\qquad s_N:=|I_N|.\] Thus scenario \(i\) is judged supporting exactly when its removal strictly improves the optimal value. The judgment is made on the realized sample and is distinct from an a priori upper bound on support dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sampled constraint is supporting when removing it strictly improves the minimization optimum; the observed support count is the number of such constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Observed-Support Judgment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The objective-value definition and definition content kind fit observed-support judgment, but no source establishes that this is the support notion used by the surrounding posterior theorem.

children.title: A Posteriori Violation Certificates
children.top_down_role: Post-solution certificates for violation probability based on observed scenario information.

knowledge_statements.title: A Posteriori Violation Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Violation upper bound selected from a precommitted family using the realized support count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\varepsilon_k,eta_k)_{k=0}^{N}\) be fixed before sampling, with \(\sum_{k=0}^{N}\beta_k\leq\beta\), and suppose a cited support-sensitive theorem gives \[\mathbb{P}^N\!\left\{s_N=k,\ V(x_N)>\varepsilon_k\right\}\leq\beta_k\qquad(k=0,\ldots,N).\] After computing \(x_N\) and identifying its support set of size \(s_N\), issue the certificate \(V(x_N)\leq\varepsilon_{s_N}\). Its joint failure probability is at most \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A precommitted calibration table converts the realized support count into a violation upper bound whose overall false-certificate probability is at most beta.
assumptions_latex: The thresholds \((\varepsilon_k)_{k=0}^{N}\) and budgets \((\beta_k)_{k=0}^{N}\) are fixed before sampling.
For each \(k\), a cited theorem gives \(\mathbb{P}^N\{s_N=k,\ V(x_N)>\varepsilon_k\}\leq\beta_k\).

notation.meaning: Violation probability of the scenario decision.
Precommitted violation thresholds and failure allocations.

children.title: Support-Sensitive Confidence Levels
children.top_down_role: Confidence calibration indexed by realized support information.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Sensitive Confidence Levels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inversion of valid support-stratified joint failure bounds using precommitted error allocations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(k\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\), let \(B_{N,k}(\varepsilon)\) be a valid nonincreasing upper bound satisfying \[\mathbb{P}^N\!\left\{s_N=k,\ V(x_N)>\varepsilon\right\}\leq B_{N,k}(\varepsilon).\] Given precommitted allocations \(\beta_k\geq0\) with \(\sum_{k=0}^{N}\beta_k\leq\beta\), define \[\varepsilon_k:=\inf\{\varepsilon\in[0,1]:B_{N,k}(\varepsilon)\leq\beta_k\},\] using \(\varepsilon_k:=1\) if the set is empty. The observed count \(s_N\) selects \(\varepsilon_{s_N}\), and the familywise certificate has confidence at least \(1-\beta\). The quantity \(1-\beta_k\) is an allocated joint confidence contribution, not generally a confidence level conditional on \(s_N=k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invert each valid support-stratified joint failure bound at a preallocated error level; the observed support count selects the threshold, while the overall certificate has familywise confidence at least one minus beta.
assumptions_latex: For every \(k\), \(B_{N,k}(\varepsilon)\) is nonincreasing in \(\varepsilon\) and bounds \(\mathbb{P}^N\{s_N=k,\ V(x_N)>\varepsilon\}\).

notation.meaning: Upper bound on the joint failure event in support-count stratum k.
Allocated and total joint failure levels.

children.title: Certificate Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting the validity or usefulness of post-solution certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions outside which a support-based posterior scenario guarantee is not established.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nominal guarantee \(\mathbb{P}^N\{V(x_N)>\varepsilon_{s_N}\}\leq\beta\) is not established by the stated support-certificate theorem if an observed support count is substituted into a nonadaptive a priori formula, thresholds are tuned after sampling without simultaneous error control, the sampling law violates the theorem's independence or distribution assumptions, or the recorded set does not satisfy the theorem's definition of support. Such departures do not imply that every realized certificate is false, but they remove the advertised guarantee and can produce false-certificate probabilities greater than \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncontrolled post-selection, invalid support identification, dependence, or distribution shift removes the theorem's confidence guarantee and can increase false-certificate probability beyond beta.
assumptions_latex: The nominal certificate theorem requires independent sampling from its stated deployment distribution.
Support identification, optimization, and threshold selection follow the theorem's predeclared measurable procedure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outside the stated assumptions, \(\mathbb{P}^N\{V(x_N)>\varepsilon_{s_N}\}\leq\beta\) is not guaranteed.

assumptions_latex: The candidate decision \(\widehat{x}\) is independent of the validation sample \(\xi'_1,\ldots,\xi'_M\).
The validation scenarios are independent and identically distributed from the deployment distribution.

notation.meaning: Candidate decision and its true violation probability.
Validation sample size and observed violation count.
Acceptance count and target violation level.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-decision validation by an independent identically distributed holdout sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathbf{1}\{g(\widehat{x},\xi'_i)>0\}\). Conditional on \(\widehat{x}\), the count \(K\) has distribution \(\operatorname{Bin}(M,V(\widehat{x}))\). Hence, for every \(r\in\{0,\ldots,M\}\) and \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \[\mathbb{P}\{K\leq r,\ V(\widehat{x})>\varepsilon\}\leq\sum_{j=0}^{r}\binom{M}{j}\varepsilon^j(1-\varepsilon)^{M-j}.\] If the displayed tail is at most \(\beta\), acceptance on \(K\leq r\) falsely certifies a decision with violation exceeding \(\varepsilon\) with probability at most \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent validation count is binomial, so its lower tail bounds the probability that a truly over-risky decision nevertheless passes validation.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Validation Guarantees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-decision binomial theorem is mathematically standard and fits independent validation guarantees, but the record supplies no inspectable citation.

assumptions_latex: The candidate decision \(\widehat{x}\) is fixed independently of \(M\) validation scenarios.
The validation scenarios are independent and identically distributed from the target distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepting when \(K\leq r\) has false-acceptance probability at most \(\beta\) whenever the binomial tail at \(\varepsilon\) is at most \(\beta\).

notation.meaning: Validation sample size and permitted violations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-shot holdout test with a preselected acceptance threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(\widehat{x}\), \(M\), \(r\), \(\varepsilon\), and \(\beta\). Draw an independent validation sample and compute \[K:=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathbf{1}\{g(\widehat{x},\xi'_i)>0\}.\] Accept and report \(V(\widehat{x})\leq\varepsilon\) only if \(K\leq r\) and \[\sum_{j=0}^{r}\binom{M}{j}\varepsilon^j(1-\varepsilon)^{M-j}\leq\beta.\] Otherwise return no certificate. The decision, sample size, threshold, and confidence level must be fixed without using the holdout outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Count violations on untouched data and certify only when the count is below a preselected threshold whose binomial tail meets the desired confidence.
knowledge_statements.title: Holdout Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and one-shot holdout rule fit the container, but no source with a specific locator supports the binomial false-acceptance calibration.

assumptions_latex: Conditional on the independently selected decision \(\widehat{x}\), validation indicators are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter \(p=V(\widehat{x})\).

notation.meaning: Observed failures among M validation trials.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-sided binomial inversion for independent validation data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0\leq K<M\), define \(U(K,M;\beta)\) as the unique \(u\in(0,1)\) satisfying \[\sum_{j=0}^{K}\binom{M}{j}u^j(1-u)^{M-j}=\beta,\] and set \(U(M,M;\beta):=1\). Then \(U(K,M;\beta)\) is an exact conservative upper confidence bound: \[\mathbb{P}_{p}\{p\leq U(K,M;\beta)\}\geq1-\beta\qquad\text{for every }p\in[0,1].\] Thus \((K,M,U)\) certifies \(V(\widehat{x})\leq U\) without asymptotic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invert the exact binomial lower tail at beta to obtain a conservative upper confidence bound on the candidate decision's violation probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Binomial Confidence Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact one-sided binomial inversion is appropriate as a certificate and is stated consistently, but it has no inspectable authoritative citation.

assumptions_latex: The candidate decision is independent of the sequential validation stream.
For each time \(t\), the reported confidence sequence \(C_t\) satisfies \(\mathbb{P}_p\{p\in C_t\ \text{for all }t\geq1\}\geq1-\beta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At any stopping time \(\tau\), reporting \(p\leq U_\tau\) has coverage at least \(1-\beta\).

notation.meaning: Anytime-valid confidence interval and its upper endpoint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anytime-valid validation using a Bernoulli confidence sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Observe validation indicators \(Y_t:=\mathbf{1}\{g(\widehat{x},\xi'_t)>0\}\) sequentially. After each observation, update an anytime-valid Bernoulli confidence sequence \(C_t=[L_t,U_t]\). Stop at the first prescribed time \(\tau\) for which \(U_\tau\leq\varepsilon\), \(L_\tau>\varepsilon\), or a fixed resource limit is reached. Certify \(p\leq\varepsilon\) only in the first case. Since \(\mathbb{P}_p\{p\in C_t\text{ for every }t\}\geq1-\beta\), optional stopping does not increase the probability of a false certificate beyond \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Update an anytime-valid Bernoulli confidence sequence and stop when its upper endpoint crosses the risk target; simultaneous coverage protects the data-dependent stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits sequential validation and its optional-stopping conclusion follows from the assumed simultaneous coverage, but no concrete confidence-sequence construction or authoritative source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Multiple-Constraint Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bonferroni simultaneous certification from valid marginal validation bounds; constraintwise counts may be dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\geq1\) and let the fixed candidate \(\widehat{x}\) be independent of the common validation sample. For every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\), construct an upper bound \(U_j\) satisfying \[\mathbb{P}\{V_j(\widehat{x})>U_j\}\leq\beta_j.\] If \(\beta_j\geq0\) and \(\sum_{j=1}^{q}\beta_j\leq\beta\), then \[\mathbb{P}\!\left\{V_j(\widehat{x})\leq U_j\text{ for every }j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\right\}\geq1-\beta.\] Independence among the constraintwise validation counts is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate the failure budget across constraints and use valid marginal upper bounds; all constraintwise bounds then hold simultaneously with confidence at least one minus beta, even when their counts are dependent.
assumptions_latex: The candidate \(\widehat{x}\) is independent of the validation sample.

notation.meaning: Marginal upper confidence bound for constraint j.

children.title: Risk-Measure Chance-Constraint Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondences and conservative approximation routes connecting tail-risk control with probabilistic feasibility.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Shapiro, Dentcheva, and Ruszczynski, Lectures on Stochastic Programming
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Section 6.3.4: relation of coherent risk measures to ambiguous chance constraints
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Shapiro, Dentcheva, and Ruszczynski, Lectures on Stochastic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Violation-Loss Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-quantile encoding for a scalar chance constraint with violation defined by strict positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in X\), let \(\xi\) be a random element, and let \(Z_x=g(x,\xi)\) be real-valued. For \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), define the lower quantile by \(\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\varepsilon}(Z_x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:\mathbb P(Z_x\le t)\ge 1-\varepsilon\}\). Then
\[
\mathbb P\bigl(g(x,\xi)>0\bigr)\le\varepsilon
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathbb P(Z_x\le0)\ge1-\varepsilon
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\varepsilon}(Z_x)\le0.
\]
Thus the scalar chance constraint is exactly a value-at-risk constraint under this quantile and strict-violation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar chance constraint is exactly a nonpositive lower value-at-risk constraint when violation means that the loss is strictly positive.
assumptions_latex: \(g(x,\xi)\) is a measurable real-valued random variable for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: scalar violation loss at decision x

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary lower-quantile characterization of a chance constraint

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically precise and fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation supports the lower-quantile convention and equivalence.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint-Event Maximum-Loss Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-loss reduction of finitely many simultaneous random inequalities to one scalar chance constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For measurable losses \(g_i(x,\xi)\), indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,m\), define \(Z_x^{\max}=\max_{1\le i\le m}g_i(x,\xi)\). Because
\[
\{Z_x^{\max}\le0\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\{g_i(x,\xi)\le0\},
\]
the joint chance constraint satisfies
\[
\mathbb P\bigl(g_i(x,\xi)\le0\ \text{for all }i\bigr)\ge1-\varepsilon
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\varepsilon}(Z_x^{\max})\le0,
\]
where \(\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\varepsilon}(Z)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:\mathbb P(Z\le t)\ge1-\varepsilon\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of finitely many constraint losses is nonpositive exactly when every constraint holds, converting their joint chance constraint into one VaR constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\) is finite and each \(g_i(x,\xi)\) is measurable.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite intersection equals the nonpositive sublevel event of the maximum

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite maximum-loss encoding and content kind fit the container, but the record has no citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Quantile Discontinuity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary failure caused by atoms at zero and inconsistent strict-event or quantile conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The equivalence with \(\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\varepsilon}(Z)\le0\) applies to \(\mathbb P(Z>0)\le\varepsilon\), not generally to \(\mathbb P(Z\ge0)\le\varepsilon\). Indeed, let \(Z=0\) almost surely and let \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Under the lower-quantile convention
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\varepsilon}(Z)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:\mathbb P(Z\le t)\ge1-\varepsilon\}=0,
\]
whereas \(\mathbb P(Z\ge0)=1>\varepsilon\). Thus an atom at the feasibility boundary separates strict and non-strict violation events; changing either convention without a no-atom condition can invalidate the claimed correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atom at zero makes strict and non-strict violation probabilities differ, so a VaR reformulation can fail if event or quantile conventions are changed.
assumptions_latex: \(Z=0\) almost surely in the displayed counterexample.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: boundary atom counterexample follows directly from the lower-quantile definition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct and failure_boundary is appropriate, but no inspectable source supports the convention-sensitive boundary claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Individual-Constraint Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: AVaR safe approximations applied separately, with risk allocation for joint reliability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For losses \(Z_{i,x}=g_i(x,\xi)\) and budgets \(\varepsilon_i\in(0,1)\), define
\[
\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon_i}(Z_{i,x})=
\inf_{t\in\mathbb R}\left\{t+\varepsilon_i^{-1}\mathbb E[(Z_{i,x}-t)_+]\right\}.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\varepsilon_i}(Z_{i,x})\le\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon_i}(Z_{i,x})\), imposing \(\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon_i}(Z_{i,x})\le0\) implies \(\mathbb P(Z_{i,x}>0)\le\varepsilon_i\). If this holds for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_i\le\varepsilon\), then the union bound yields \(\mathbb P(\max_i Z_{i,x}>0)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonpositive AVaR constraints safely enforce individual chance constraints; allocating individual probability budgets whose sum is at most ε also guarantees joint reliability.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint-Constraint Maximum-Loss Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct AVaR safe approximation of a joint chance constraint through maximum loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z_x^{\max}=\max_{1\le i\le m}g_i(x,\xi)\) be integrable and let \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Define
\[
\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_x^{\max})=
\inf_{t\in\mathbb R}\left\{t+\varepsilon^{-1}\mathbb E[(Z_x^{\max}-t)_+]\right\}.
\]
The dominance \(\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\varepsilon}(Z_x^{\max})\le\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_x^{\max})\) gives
\[
\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_x^{\max})\le0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb P\bigl(g_i(x,\xi)\le0\ \text{for every }i\bigr)\ge1-\varepsilon.
\]
Hence the AVaR inequality is a sufficient, generally non-equivalent surrogate for joint chance feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying AVaR to the maximum constraint loss gives a sufficient, generally conservative condition for satisfying every constraint jointly with the required probability.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) is finite and \(\max_i g_i(x,\xi)\) is integrable.

notation.meaning: average value-at-risk over the upper ε-tail

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: AVaR dominates the corresponding upper-tail quantile

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The direct maximum-loss AVaR surrogate is correctly stated and principle fits the container, but the AVaR dominance and safe-approximation claim lack an inspectable citation.

children.title: Surrogate Scaling Choices
children.top_down_role: Scaling conventions used to calibrate safe risk-measure surrogates.

knowledge_statements.title: Surrogate Scaling Choices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive component scalings preserve the joint violation event while changing its AVaR surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a scaling vector \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\), define the scaled maximum loss
\[
Z_{a,x}=\max_{1\le i\le m}a_i g_i(x,\xi).
\]
Because every \(a_i\) is positive,
\[
\{Z_{a,x}>0\}=\bigcup_{i=1}^m\{g_i(x,\xi)>0\},
\]
so all positive scalings encode the same joint chance constraint. The sufficient condition \(\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_{a,x})\le0\), however, depends on the relative components of \(a\). Common-scale redundancy may be removed by a normalization such as \(\sum_i a_i=1\) or \(\max_i a_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive relative scalings leave the joint violation event unchanged but alter the AVaR approximation; normalization removes irrelevant common scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\max_i a_i g_i(x,\xi)>0\}=\bigcup_i\{g_i(x,\xi)>0\}\), while \(\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(\max_i a_i g_i(x,\xi))\) may vary with \(a\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: positive scaling preserves component signs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Positive scaling preserves the violation event and representation fits the leaf. A source is still needed, particularly for the assertion that relative scaling changes the AVaR surrogate and for the normalization discussion.

children.title: Sources of Conservatism
children.top_down_role: Structural sources of excess restriction in surrogate feasibility conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sources of Conservatism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation between chance feasibility and its AVaR safe approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(0<\varepsilon<1\) and \(M>0\). Let the scalar loss \(Z\) equal \(1\) with probability \(\varepsilon\) and equal \(-M\) with probability \(1-\varepsilon\). Then
\[
\mathbb P(Z>0)=\varepsilon,
\]
so the chance constraint is feasible at equality. Nevertheless, the upper \(\varepsilon\)-tail consists entirely of the outcome \(Z=1\), and therefore
\[
\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z)=1>0.
\]
Thus replacing a tail-probability bound by nonpositive AVaR can be conservative because AVaR controls the average magnitude of upper-tail losses, whereas chance feasibility controls only their probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A loss positive with probability exactly ε can satisfy the chance constraint while failing AVaR because AVaR also penalizes the magnitude of tail outcomes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit two-point distribution permits direct AVaR evaluation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-point counterexample is correct and counterexample is an appropriate content kind, but it has no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Scaling–Tightness Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: How surrogate calibration affects approximation tightness.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling–Tightness Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common scaling is immaterial, whereas relative scaling changes surrogate tightness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z_{a,x}=\max_i a_i g_i(x,\xi)\) for \(a\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\). Positive homogeneity of average value-at-risk gives, for every \(c>0\),
\[
\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_{ca,x})
=
\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(cZ_{a,x})
=
c\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_{a,x}).
\]
Consequently, the feasibility sign of the surrogate is invariant under common scaling. Relative scaling can change which component dominates the upper tail and hence can enlarge or shrink the AVaR-feasible decision set. Comparing scaling choices therefore requires a normalization, such as \(\sum_i a_i=1\), and no componentwise ordering of tightness follows solely from positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying all weights by one positive constant does not change surrogate feasibility, but changing relative weights can tighten some regions and loosen others.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_{ca,x})\le0\iff\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_{a,x})\le0\), but relative rescaling need not preserve feasibility.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Common-scale invariance follows correctly from positive homogeneity, and property fits the leaf. The homogeneity and broader relative-scaling tightness claims require cited support.

children.title: Exactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem classes where surrogate scaling preserves the target feasibility boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A probability-gap condition under which the AVaR surrogate and chance constraint coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\{Z_x:x\in X\}\) be integrable losses and fix \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\). Suppose the family has the probability-gap property
\[
\text{for every }x\in X,
\qquad
\mathbb P(Z_x>0)=0
\quad\text{or}\quad
\mathbb P(Z_x>0)>\varepsilon.
\]
Then chance feasibility implies \(Z_x\le0\) almost surely and hence \(\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_x)\le0\). The reverse implication follows from \(\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\varepsilon}(Z_x)\le\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_x)\). Therefore, throughout this family,
\[
\mathbb P(Z_x>0)\le\varepsilon
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_x)\le0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AVaR is exact when every decision either has no positive loss or violates with probability strictly exceeding the allowed budget.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: probability gap reduces feasible losses to almost-sure nonpositivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The probability-gap condition is a valid sufficient exactness regime and condition fits the container, but no citation supports this particular regime or the AVaR–VaR dominance it uses.

children.title: Degenerate Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scaling choices that yield vacuous, unstable, or excessively restrictive surrogates.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Scaling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero or negative weights destroy the event-preserving maximum-loss construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Strict positivity of maximum-loss scaling is essential. If zero weights are permitted, choosing \(a=0\) gives
\[
Z_{a,x}=\max_i a_i g_i(x,\xi)=0
\]
for every decision and outcome, so \(\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z_{a,x})=0\) even when the original joint chance constraint is violated. More generally, setting \(a_j=0\) suppresses violations occurring only in component \(j\). If \(a_j<0\), the sign of the corresponding loss is reversed. Hence
\[
a\notin\mathbb R_{++}^m
\]
need not preserve \(\{\max_i a_i g_i>0\}=\bigcup_i\{g_i>0\}\), and optimization over scaling vectors must exclude such degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero weights can hide constraints, and negative weights reverse violations; therefore event-preserving maximum-loss scaling requires every weight to be strictly positive.
assumptions_latex: Scaling coefficients are allowed outside \(\mathbb R_{++}^m\) in the failure construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\notin\mathbb R_{++}^m\) can make the scaled surrogate feasible while the original joint chance constraint is infeasible.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: zero-vector and sign-reversal counterexamples are algebraic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero- and negative-weight failure mechanisms are correct and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Tail-Probability Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributionally robust chance feasibility expressed through worst-case tail probability and pointwise quantiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty ambiguity set of probability measures under which the loss \(Z_x\) is measurable. For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), distributionally robust chance feasibility is
\[
\sup_{Q\in\mathcal P}Q(Z_x>0)\le\varepsilon.
\]
Equivalently, every \(Q\in\mathcal P\) satisfies \(Q(Z_x\le0)\ge1-\varepsilon\). With
\[
\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\varepsilon}^{Q}(Z_x)=
\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:Q(Z_x\le t)\ge1-\varepsilon\},
\]
this becomes
\[
\sup_{Q\in\mathcal P}\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\varepsilon}^{Q}(Z_x)\le0.
\]
The equivalence uses the same strict-violation and lower-quantile conventions for every distribution in the ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case chance feasibility requires every distribution in the ambiguity set to assign at most ε probability to positive loss, equivalently requiring all corresponding lower quantiles to be nonpositive.

notation.meaning: a probability law in the ambiguity set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise ambiguity-set equivalence is consistent with the stated strict-event and lower-quantile conventions, and representation fits the leaf. No inspectable source supports the distributionally robust interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Coherent Risk-Envelope Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual risk-envelope representation linking coherent tail risk to robust expected loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be a reference probability measure, let \(Z\in L^1(P)\), and let \(0<\varepsilon<1\). The upper-tail average value-at-risk has the coherent risk-envelope representation
\[
\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z)
=
\sup_{q\in\mathcal Q_{\varepsilon}}
\mathbb E_P[qZ],
\qquad
\mathcal Q_{\varepsilon}=
\left\{q\in L^{\infty}(P):0\le q\le\varepsilon^{-1}\ \ P\text{-a.s.},\ \mathbb E_P[q]=1\right\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{AVaR}_{\varepsilon}(Z)\le 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathbb E_Q[Z]\le 0
\ \text{for every }Q\ll P\text{ with }\frac{dQ}{dP}\in\mathcal Q_{\varepsilon}.
\]
Thus an AVaR safe approximation is equivalently a robust expected-loss constraint over its coherent risk envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AVaR equals the worst expected loss over probability densities bounded by 1/ε, so its nonpositivity is a robust expectation constraint over that envelope.

notation.meaning: Radon–Nikodym density defining an envelope measure

knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Based Ambiguity Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-covariance ambiguity interface for distributionally robust chance feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a decision set, let \(\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be Borel, let \(\mu\in\mathbb R^d\), and let \(\Sigma\in\mathbb S_+^d\). Define \(\mathcal P(\mu,\Sigma)\) as the set of Borel probability measures \(P\) on \(\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(P(\Xi)=1\), \(\mathbb E_P[\xi]=\mu\), and \(\mathbb E_P[(\xi-\mu)(\xi-\mu)^{\mathsf T}]=\Sigma\). For \(x\in X\), a function \(g:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) with measurable section \(g(x,\cdot)\), and \(\varepsilon\in[0,1)\), \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal P(\mu,\Sigma)}P\bigl(g(x,\xi)\le0\bigr)\ge1-\varepsilon\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(\mu,\Sigma)}P\bigl(g(x,\xi)>0\bigr)\le\varepsilon.\] Thus prescribed moments and support define an ambiguity-set interface for worst-case chance feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributions with the prescribed support, mean, and covariance form an ambiguity set; robust chance feasibility is equivalent to requiring that the largest failure probability over this set not exceed the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(g(x,\cdot)\) is Borel measurable for each \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Borel probability measures with the prescribed support, mean, and covariance.
Random constraint function whose positive values represent failure.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: complement identity for a mean-covariance ambiguity set
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Failure Budgets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Individual risk allocations for a finite family of random constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Xi,\mathcal A,P)\) be a probability space, let \(X\) be a decision set, and let \(g_i:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), have measurable sections \(g_i(x,\cdot)\). A vector \(\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)\in[0,1]^m\) is a componentwise failure budget at \(x\in X\) when \[P\bigl(g_i(x,\xi)>0\bigr)\le\varepsilon_i\quad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m.\] Its componentwise-feasible set is \[F(\varepsilon)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in X:P(g_i(x,\xi)>0)\le\varepsilon_i\}.\] These marginal bounds do not determine the joint failure probability without information about dependence among the failure events.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each random constraint receives its own maximum failure probability; satisfying all marginal budgets does not determine the exact system failure probability.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i(x,\cdot)\) is measurable for every \(x\in X\) and \(i\).

notation.meaning: Failure budget assigned to component constraint i.
Set satisfying all componentwise chance constraints.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: System-Level Reliability Budgets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Union-bound conversion from component risks to a system reliability guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) be a probability space, let \(A_i(x)\in\mathcal F\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be component-failure events at a fixed decision \(x\), and define \(A_{\mathrm{sys}}(x)=\bigcup_{i=1}^mA_i(x)\). If \(P(A_i(x))\le\varepsilon_i\) with \(\varepsilon_i\in[0,1]\), then \[P(A_{\mathrm{sys}}(x))\le\sum_{i=1}^mP(A_i(x))\le\sum_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_i.\] Consequently, if \(\sum_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_i\le\bar\varepsilon\) for \(\bar\varepsilon\in[0,1]\), then \[P\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^mA_i(x)^c\right)\ge1-\bar\varepsilon,\] without an independence assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the component failure budgets sum to at most the system budget, the union bound guarantees the requested system reliability regardless of dependence.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) is a probability space and \(A_i(x)\in\mathcal F\).

notation.meaning: Event that at least one component fails.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite union bound applied to component failure events
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Budget Reallocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redistribution of component risk allowances while preserving a union-bound system guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) be a probability space, fix \(x\), and let \(A_i(x)\in\mathcal F\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be component-failure events. Suppose \(\bar\varepsilon\in[0,1]\), \(\varepsilon_i\ge0\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_i\le\bar\varepsilon\). Define reallocated budgets by \(\varepsilon_i'=\varepsilon_i+\Delta_i\). If \[\varepsilon_i'\ge0\quad\text{for all }i,\qquad\sum_{i=1}^m\Delta_i\le0,\] then \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i'\le\bar\varepsilon\). If also \(P(A_i(x))\le\varepsilon_i'\) for every \(i\), then \[P\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^mA_i(x)\right)\le\bar\varepsilon.\] Reallocation can change componentwise feasibility while preserving this aggregate guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component budgets may be changed without weakening the union-bound system guarantee when every revised budget is nonnegative and their total does not increase.

notation.meaning: Change in the failure budget of component i.
