children.title: Nonconvex Feasible Regions
children.top_down_role: Feasible sets whose global geometry is not convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Feasible Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar chance constraint whose feasible set is a disconnected union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\) take values \(-1\) and \(1\), each with probability \(1/2\), and fix \(0<r<1\). The scalar chance constraint \[P(|x-\xi|\le r)\ge\tfrac12\] has feasible set \[F_r=[-1-r,-1+r]\cup[1-r,1+r].\] Both intervals are nonempty and disjoint. Hence \(F_r\) is nonconvex: its feasible points \(-1\) and \(1\) have midpoint \(0\notin F_r\). Thus even a one-dimensional chance constraint can destroy convexity when the distribution is discrete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-point distribution yields two disjoint feasible intervals, showing that chance-constrained feasible regions need not be convex even in one dimension.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit finite-distribution counterexample verified directly from the chance constraint

children.title: Disconnected Feasible Components
children.top_down_role: Feasible sets separated into multiple isolated components.

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected Feasible Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of chance-feasible decisions into distinct path components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological space, let \((\Xi,\mathcal A,P)\) be a probability space, let \(g:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) have measurable sections, and let \(\varepsilon\in[0,1)\). Define \[F=\{x\in X:P(g(x,\xi)\le0)\ge1-\varepsilon\}.\] A path component of \(F\) is a maximal path-connected subset of \(F\). If \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) are distinct path components, then no continuous map \(\gamma:[0,1]\to F\) can satisfy \(\gamma(0)\in F_1\) and \(\gamma(1)\in F_2\). Thus feasible motion constrained to continuous paths cannot transfer a decision between distinct path components. Having multiple path components establishes failure of path-connectedness, though it does not by itself imply topological disconnectedness in an arbitrary topological space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct path components cannot be joined by a continuous feasible path, so path-constrained local motion cannot move between them; this is specifically a failure of path-connectedness.

notation.meaning: Distinct path components of the feasible set.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition and invariance of path components
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Local Geometry Traps
children.top_down_role: Local geometric features that obscure globally relevant feasible regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Geometry Traps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A component-local optimum that is not globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]\) and minimize \(f(x)=(x-3/2)^2\) over \(F\). The point \(x=-1\) is a strict local minimizer relative to \(F\), because all sufficiently close feasible points lie in \([-2,-1]\) and have larger objective value. Nevertheless, \(x=3/2\) is feasible and satisfies \(f(3/2)=0<f(-1)=25/4\). Thus a method restricted to local feasible neighborhoods can terminate within one component while missing a better component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a disconnected feasible set, a strict local minimizer in one component can be substantially worse than the global minimizer in another.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[-1\text{ is a strict local minimizer on }F,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)=\{3/2\}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit elementary counterexample to global validity of local optimality

children.title: Componentwise Search Limitations
children.top_down_role: Limitations of numerical searches confined to a single feasible component.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Search Limitations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reachability limitation of continuous feasible-path search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological space, let \(F\subseteq X\), and let \(F_0\) be the path component of \(F\) containing an initial iterate \(x_0\). Suppose that, for every \(k\ge0\), there is a continuous path in \(F\) joining \(x_k\) to \(x_{k+1}\). Then \[x_k\in F_0\quad\text{for every }k\ge0.\] Consequently, the search cannot reach a different path component without an infeasible transition, a move not representable by a continuous feasible path, or an independent restart. Convergence within \(F_0\) supplies no objective comparison with unvisited components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A search whose consecutive iterates are joined by feasible continuous paths remains in its initial path component and cannot certify objective quality over unvisited components.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \(F\subseteq X\).
\(F\) has at least two path components.
Each consecutive pair \(x_k,x_{k+1}\) is joined by a continuous path in \(F\).

notation.meaning: Path component containing the initial decision.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: path-component invariance under concatenated feasible paths

children.title: Connectivity Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Parameter ranges where feasible-set connectivity changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical tolerance at which two chance-feasible components merge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(\xi=-1)=P(\xi=1)=1/2\), and for \(r\ge0\) define \(F_r=\{x\in\mathbb R:P(|x-\xi|\le r)\ge1/2\}\). Then \[F_r=[-1-r,-1+r]\cup[1-r,1+r].\] For \(0\le r<1\), the two intervals are disjoint and \(F_r\) has two connected components. At \(r=1\) they meet at \(0\), and for \(r>1\) they overlap. Hence \(r_c=1\) is the boundary between disconnected and connected feasibility regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a two-point distribution, increasing the tolerance to one merges the two feasible intervals; the critical tolerance is the connectivity boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_r\text{ is disconnected for }0\le r<1\quad\text{and connected for }r\ge1.\]

notation.meaning: Feasible set at tolerance radius r.
Critical tolerance at which the components merge.

knowledge_statements.title: Nondifferentiable Probability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An atomic distribution producing a discontinuous chance-feasibility function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\) take values \(-1\) and \(1\), each with probability \(1/2\), and set \(p(x)=P(\xi\le x)\). Then \[p(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<-1,\\1/2,&-1\le x<1,\\1,&x\ge1.\end{cases}\] Thus \(p\) is discontinuous, and hence nondifferentiable, at \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\). For the chance constraint \(p(x)\ge1/2\), the feasible set is \([-1,\infty)\), whose boundary point \(-1\) coincides with a probability jump. Gradient-based boundary regularity therefore fails under atomic uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With atomic uncertainty, the satisfaction probability is a step function, so a chance-feasible boundary can occur exactly where no probability gradient exists.

notation.meaning: Probability that the uncertain value does not exceed x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit atomic-distribution calculation of a discontinuous probability function

children.title: Empty-Interior Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Feasible regions lacking interior points in the ambient decision space.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Interior Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological criterion excluding ambiently interior feasible decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological decision space, let \((\Xi,\mathcal A,P)\) be a probability space, let \(g:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) have measurable sections, and let \(\varepsilon\in[0,1)\). Define \[F=\{x\in X:P(g(x,\xi)\le0)\ge1-\varepsilon\}.\] Feasibility has empty interior in \(X\) when \(\operatorname{int}_X(F)=\varnothing\). Equivalently, every open neighborhood in \(X\) of every point of \(F\) contains a point outside \(F\). Thus no feasible decision has an ambient open neighborhood consisting entirely of feasible decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chance-feasible set has empty interior when every ambient neighborhood of every feasible point also contains an infeasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{int}_X(F)=\varnothing\iff\forall x\in F\ \forall U\ni x\text{ open in }X,\ U\cap(X\setminus F)\ne\varnothing.\]

notation.meaning: Interior of F in the ambient decision space X.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard topological characterization of empty interior
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Boundary-Only Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Feasibility restricted to probability boundaries or lower-dimensional sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Only Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility attained only at the prescribed probability threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a decision set, let \((\Xi,\mathcal A,P)\) be a probability space, let \(g:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) have measurable sections, and let \(\varepsilon\in[0,1)\). Define \(p(x)=P(g(x,\xi)\le0)\) and \(F=\{x\in X:p(x)\ge1-\varepsilon\}\). Boundary-only feasibility occurs when \(F\ne\varnothing\) and \[p(x)=1-\varepsilon\quad\text{for every }x\in F.\] Equivalently, \(F\ne\varnothing\) and \(\{x\in X:p(x)>1-\varepsilon\}=\varnothing\). Every feasible decision then exhausts the failure-probability budget, so no strictly chance-feasible decision exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility is boundary-only when feasible decisions exist but all attain the probability threshold exactly, leaving no strictly chance-feasible decision.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a decision set and \((\Xi,\mathcal A,P)\) is a probability space.

notation.meaning: Feasible set at probability threshold one minus epsilon.

children.title: Constraint Qualification Failures
children.top_down_role: Loss of regularity associated with thin or boundary-supported feasible sets.

assumptions_latex: The chance-constraint function \(g(x)=1-\varepsilon-\mathbb{P}(G(x,\xi)\leq 0)\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists d\in T_X(\bar x)\) such that \(\nabla g(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}d<0\).

notation.meaning: Tangent cone of the deterministic domain at the boundary point.
Failure probability in excess of the permitted level.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative Mangasarian-Fromovitz failure for one differentiable chance constraint.

source_refs.locator: 1.4.9 Methods of feasible directions p. 41

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=\{x\in X:g(x)\leq0\}\). At an active point \(\bar x\in F\), the relative Mangasarian-Fromovitz constraint qualification fails precisely when there is no tangent direction that strictly decreases the active constraint:
\[
\nexists d\in T_X(\bar x)\quad\text{such that}\quad \nabla g(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}d<0.
\]
In this regime, first-order feasible-direction arguments requiring a strict inward direction are inapplicable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an active chance constraint, constraint qualification fails when no direction tangent to the deterministic domain strictly moves toward feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Qualification Failures

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4.9 Methods of feasible directions p. 41

children.title: Boundary Feasibility Fragility
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of boundary-feasible solutions to numerical or distributional perturbations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fragility under total-variation perturbations of the uncertainty law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a decision \(\bar x\) satisfying the nominal chance constraint exactly at equality, the total-variation ambiguity ball obeys
\[
\inf_{Q:\,d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q,P)\leq\delta}Q(A_{\bar x})=
\max\{P(A_{\bar x})-\delta,0\}=1-\varepsilon-\delta.
\]
Consequently, every positive admissible radius \(\delta\) contains a distribution under which \(\bar x\) violates the reliability requirement \(Q(A_{\bar x})\geq1-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision feasible exactly on the nominal probability boundary can become infeasible under an arbitrarily small total-variation distribution shift.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Feasibility Fragility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim is plausible under the stated nontrivial event probabilities and the usual total-variation convention, but the exact infimum and its attainability require an inspectable source establishing the convention and admissible probability-space construction.

children.title: Lower-Dimensional Feasible Faces
children.top_down_role: Feasible structures confined to faces or manifolds of reduced dimension.

assumptions_latex: There exists an affine set \(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(F\subseteq L\) and \(\dim L<n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(F)=\varnothing\) and \(\nexists x\in F,\ r>0\) with \(B(x,r)\subseteq F\).

notation.meaning: A proper affine hull containing the feasible set.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean geometry of a feasible set contained in a proper affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If the chance-constrained feasible set \(F\) is contained in an affine set \(L\) of dimension strictly below \(n\), then
\[
\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(F)=\varnothing
\quad\text{and}\quad
\nexists x\in F,\ r>0:\ B(x,r)\subseteq F.
\]
Thus feasibility can possess relative interior in \(L\) while having no full-dimensional interior or positive Euclidean feasibility margin in the ambient decision space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible face contained in a proper affine subspace has no full-dimensional interior, even when it has relative interior within that face.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Feasible Faces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ambient-interior conclusion is elementary and correct, and the property kind fits the container, but no inspectable source is supplied. The assumptions also establish containment in a lower-dimensional affine set rather than that F is formally a face.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown Dependence Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fréchet bounds demonstrate nonidentification from marginal probabilities alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Knowing only the marginal probabilities does not determine joint reliability. For events \(E_1,\ldots,E_m\) with common marginal probability \(q\), the sharp Fréchet bounds are
\[
\max\{0,mq-(m-1)\}
\leq P\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^mE_i\right)
\leq q.
\]
Both endpoints are attainable by dependence structures having the same marginals. Hence a joint chance constraint can be certified from those marginals alone only when its required reliability is at most the lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed marginal safety probabilities permit widely different joint reliabilities; without dependence information, joint reliability is guaranteed only up to the sharp Fréchet lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{0,mq-(m-1)\}\leq P(\bigcap_{i=1}^mE_i)\leq q\), with both endpoints attainable.

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Combined Use of Inclusion-Exclusion and Simulation to Estimate the Probability of a Composite Event p. 191

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Combined Use of Inclusion-Exclusion and Simulation to Estimate the Probability of a Composite Event p. 191

assumptions_latex: All intersection probabilities required by inclusion-exclusion are available exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact inclusion-exclusion uses \(2^m-1\) nonempty intersection terms.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Term complexity of exact joint-event evaluation by inclusion-exclusion.

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Combined Use of Inclusion-Exclusion and Simulation to Estimate the Probability of a Composite Event p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Exact evaluation of the probability of at least one component failure by inclusion-exclusion is
\[
P\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^mF_i\right)
=
\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}}
(-1)^{|S|+1}P\!\left(\bigcap_{i\in S}F_i\right).
\]
The sum contains exactly \(2^m-1\) nonempty-subset terms. Therefore direct exact evaluation has exponential term complexity in \(m\), even before accounting for the cost of computing each multivariate intersection probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact inclusion-exclusion for a joint failure probability requires exponentially many intersection probabilities: 2^m minus one terms.
knowledge_statements.title: High-Dimensional Joint-Probability Evaluation

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Combined Use of Inclusion-Exclusion and Simulation to Estimate the Probability of a Composite Event p. 191

assumptions_latex: \(F_i\) is the failure event of component \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(\bigcup_{i=1}^mF_i)\leq\varepsilon\), but the bound can exceed the exact union probability by a factor \(m\).

notation.meaning: Allocated risk budget for component i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservatism of Boole-based decomposition of a joint chance constraint.

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Combined Use of Inclusion-Exclusion and Simulation to Estimate the Probability of a Composite Event p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Boole risk allocation gives the sufficient implication
\[
P(F_i)\leq\varepsilon_i\ \text{for all }i,
\quad \sum_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_i\leq\varepsilon
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
P\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^mF_i\right)\leq\varepsilon.
\]
It need not be necessary. If \(F_1=\cdots=F_m=F\) and \(P(F)=p>0\), then the exact union probability is \(p\), whereas the sum of marginal probabilities is \(mp\). Thus allocation can overstate joint risk by factor \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boole risk allocation guarantees joint reliability but can overstate failure probability by a factor equal to the number of identical component events.
knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Allocation Overconservatism

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Combined Use of Inclusion-Exclusion and Simulation to Estimate the Probability of a Composite Event p. 191

assumptions_latex: \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_N\) are independent Bernoulli failure indicators with \(P(Y_i=1)=p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{RRMSE}(\widehat p_N)=\sqrt{(1-p)/(Np)}\), so \(N\geq(1-p)/(pr^2)\) is necessary and sufficient for relative root-mean-square error at most \(r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crude Monte Carlo sample complexity for relative rare-event accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The crude Monte Carlo estimator satisfies
\[
\mathbb{E}[\widehat p_N]=p,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_N)=\frac{p(1-p)}{N},
\qquad
\frac{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(\widehat p_N-p)^2]}}{p}
=
\sqrt{\frac{1-p}{Np}}.
\]
Consequently, achieving relative root-mean-square error at most \(r>0\) requires
\[
N\geq\frac{1-p}{pr^2}.
\]
For fixed \(r\), the required sample size therefore grows on the order of \(p^{-1}\) as \(p\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crude Monte Carlo needs sample size proportional to the reciprocal of the rare failure probability to maintain fixed relative accuracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Rare-Event Sample Explosion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Bernoulli variance calculation and resulting order-1/p crude-Monte-Carlo requirement are mathematically precise, but the record supplies no inspectable rare-event sampling source.

assumptions_latex: The variables \(Y_{kj}\) are mutually independent Bernoulli variables with common mean \(p\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat p_{\widehat k}]<p\) for \(K>1\), and \(P(\widehat p_{\widehat k}=0)=1-[1-(1-p)^N]^K\).

notation.meaning: Estimated failure probability of candidate k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: minimum of independent unbiased estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-candidate counterexample to post-selection unbiasedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Each \(\widehat p_k\) is unbiased for the common true failure probability \(p\), but optimization changes the reported estimator into \(\widehat p_{\widehat k}=\min_k\widehat p_k\). For \(K>1\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[\widehat p_{\widehat k}]<p,
\qquad
P(\widehat p_{\widehat k}=0)
=1-\left[1-(1-p)^N\right]^K.
\]
Hence searching over more candidates increases the probability of selecting an apparently failure-free decision even though every candidate has true failure probability \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing estimated risk over many candidates biases the selected estimate downward, even when every candidate has the same true risk.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-Induced Selection Bias

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The independent finite-candidate construction does yield strict downward selection bias and the stated zero-count probability, but no source is supplied and K and N are not explicitly introduced as positive integers.

assumptions_latex: The sampled problem is \(\min_{x\in X}f(x)\) subject to \(g(x,\xi_i)\leq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,N\).
The functions \(g(\cdot,\xi_i)\) are differentiable at a feasible point \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Index set of active sampled constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-gradient degeneracy in a finite sampled constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sampled constraint system is active-gradient degenerate at \(\bar x\) when
\[
\operatorname{rank}\!\left([\nabla_xg(\bar x,\xi_i)]_{i\in I(\bar x)}\right)
<|I(\bar x)|.
\]
Equivalently, the active sampled gradients are linearly dependent. In this regime, the active scenario representation is nonunique or redundant, the linear-independence constraint qualification fails, and conclusions that require a uniquely determined full-rank support set do not apply without a separate degeneracy treatment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario solution is gradient-degenerate when its active sampled constraints are linearly dependent, invalidating arguments that require a full-rank support set.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Degeneracy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Linear dependence of active gradients correctly characterizes LICQ failure, but 'scenario degeneracy' has distinct support-constraint definitions in the scenario literature. Linear dependence alone also does not generally imply that the active scenario representation is nonunique or redundant. A precise source and corrected consequences are required.

notation.meaning: Common Bernoulli variable generating perfectly dependent observations.
Observed failure indicator for sample i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perfect dependence shows failure of independent-sample concentration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under perfect dependence, the empirical failure frequency is
\[
\widehat p_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^NY_i=Z.
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_N)=p(1-p),
\qquad
P(\widehat p_N=0)=1-p,
\]
for every \(N\). The variance does not decay as \(N^{-1}\), and the no-failure probability is not \((1-p)^N\). Thus independent identically distributed binomial calibration is invalid for these dependent observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With perfectly dependent samples, increasing sample size gives no variance reduction and the usual binomial no-failure probability is wrong.
knowledge_statements.title: Dependent or Nonidentically Distributed Samples

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The perfectly dependent Bernoulli counterexample is correct and fits the dependence portion of the container, but it does not address nonidentically distributed sampling and has no inspectable source.

assumptions_latex: For each \(k\leq K\) and \(j\leq N\), \(Y_{kj}\) are independent Bernoulli variables with mean \(p\in(0,1)\).
The same data choose \(\widehat k\in\arg\min_k\widehat p_k\) and report \(\widehat p_{\widehat k}\), where \(\widehat p_k=N^{-1}\sum_jY_{kj}\).

notation.meaning: Validation failure frequency for candidate k.
Candidate selected using the validation data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample to binomial validation after adaptive data reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any fixed candidate, the probability of observing no validation failures is \((1-p)^N\). When the same validation sample is searched to select the best of \(K\) candidates, however,
\[
P(\widehat p_{\widehat k}=0)
=1-\left[1-(1-p)^N\right]^K
>(1-p)^N
\]
whenever \(K>1\). Consequently, a confidence statement calibrated for one fixed, data-independent candidate does not retain its nominal interpretation after adaptive reuse of the validation data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reusing validation data to select among candidates makes zero observed failures more likely than fixed-candidate binomial calibration claims.
knowledge_statements.title: Data Reuse in Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed probability is correct for mutually independent candidate-specific Bernoulli arrays, but that model is not literally a common validation sample reused across candidates; evaluations on shared observations are generally dependent. K and N also lack explicit integer domains. An adaptive-validation source and an accurately specified reuse model are required.

assumptions_latex: The nominal law is \(P\), while deployment uses \(Q\) with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\leq\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(A_x)\geq1-\varepsilon-\delta\), and nominal equality does not guarantee \(Q(A_x)\geq1-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reliability degradation under total-variation distribution shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every measurable event \(A_x\), total variation gives
\[
|Q(A_x)-P(A_x)|\leq d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\leq\delta.
\]
Hence nominal feasibility implies only
\[
Q(A_x)\geq P(A_x)-\delta\geq1-\varepsilon-\delta.
\]
In particular, if \(P(A_x)=1-\varepsilon\), a shift of any positive radius may reduce deployment reliability below the original target. A nominal margin of at least \(\delta\) is therefore required for this bound alone to preserve the target under all such shifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A total-variation shift of radius delta can reduce safety probability by delta, so nominal boundary feasibility is not shift-robust.
knowledge_statements.title: Distribution Shift

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The total-variation event inequality and resulting reliability degradation are standard and fit the distribution-shift failure boundary, but no inspectable source is supplied and the total-variation convention should be documented.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tailed Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite-variance confidence surrogates under Pareto-tailed uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be a random variable satisfying \(\mathbb P(Z>t)=t^{-\alpha}\) for every \(t\ge 1\), where \(1<\alpha<2\). Then \(\mathbb E[Z]<\infty\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\infty\). For a decision \(x\) and a measurable constraint function \(g\), the chance constraint \(\mathbb P\{g(x,Z)>0\}\le\varepsilon\), with \(0<\varepsilon<1\), remains well-defined. However, a reliability certificate whose stated assumptions require \(\mathbb E[Z^2]<\infty\), including a variance-based concentration bound or the classical finite-variance \(N^{-1/2}\) standard-error approximation for a sample mean, cannot be invoked for this distribution without additional assumptions or a heavy-tail-robust analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pareto uncertainty with tail index between one and two has a finite mean but infinite variance. Chance constraints remain well-defined, but certificates requiring a finite second moment or the classical finite-variance square-root-N approximation do not apply without further assumptions or robust heavy-tail analysis.
assumptions_latex: The certificate under consideration explicitly requires a finite second moment or the classical finite-variance central limit theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\infty\), so a certificate requiring \(\mathbb E[Z^2]<\infty\) is outside its stated validity domain.

notation.meaning: sample size used by a sample-mean approximation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The Pareto moment criterion and the stated applicability restriction for finite-variance certificates are standard.

knowledge_statements.title: Misspecified Tail Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equal marginals do not determine joint tail-event probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(p\in(0,1)\). Under the fitted model, let \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) be independent Bernoulli random variables with \(\mathbb P(I_j=1)=p\). Under the true model, let \(I_1=I_2=I\), where \(I\) is Bernoulli with parameter \(p\). Both models have identical marginal exceedance probabilities, but the joint failure event \(F=\{I_1=I_2=1\}\) has fitted probability \(p^2\) and true probability \(p\). Thus a reliability calculation using independence can understate joint tail risk by the factor \(1/p\), despite correctly specified marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent and perfectly dependent models can share the same marginal tails while assigning joint failure probabilities p-squared and p, respectively.
assumptions_latex: System failure requires simultaneous component exceedances.

notation.meaning: indicator of a tail exceedance in component j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The Bernoulli construction directly exhibits non-identification of joint tails from marginals.

knowledge_statements.title: Contaminated Samples
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Target-distribution guarantees degrade under Huber contamination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)\) be a measurable space and let \(P\) and \(Q\) be probability measures on it. Suppose observations are sampled independently from \(R=(1-\eta)P+\eta Q\), where \(0\le\eta<1\). For a returned decision \(x\), let \(A_x=\{z\in\mathcal Z:g(x,z)>0\}\in\mathcal F\) be its violation event. Since \(R(A_x)=(1-\eta)P(A_x)+\eta Q(A_x)\ge(1-\eta)P(A_x)\), a valid certificate \(R(A_x)\le\varepsilon\) implies \(P(A_x)\le\varepsilon/(1-\eta)\). The unadjusted claim \(P(A_x)\le\varepsilon\) does not follow in general, and equality in the degraded bound is possible when \(Q(A_x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under eta-contaminated sampling, a certificate bounding the observed-law violation probability by epsilon implies only a target-law bound of epsilon divided by one minus eta. The unadjusted target guarantee need not hold.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal Z,\mathcal F)\) is a measurable space and \(P,Q\) are probability measures on it.
The violation set \(A_x\) is measurable, the certificate controls \(R(A_x)\), and deployment performance is measured by \(P(A_x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(A_x)\le\varepsilon\) implies \(P(A_x)\le\varepsilon/(1-\eta)\), and this implication is sharp when \(Q(A_x)=0\).

notation.meaning: target, contaminating, and observed sampling laws
constraint function defining the measurable violation event

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The degradation and its sharpness follow directly from the Huber mixture identity.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Scope of Classical Scenario Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applicability boundary of the classical convex scenario certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the scenario program minimizing a convex objective over a convex set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), subject to \(g(x,\xi_i)\le0\) for \(N\) independent samples, with \(g(\cdot,\xi)\) convex. Suppose the selected optimizer is measurable and has support dimension at most \(d\), where \(1\le d\le N\). Writing \(V(x)=\mathbb P\{g(x,\xi)>0\}\), the classical scenario certificate is \[\mathbb P^N\{V(x_N)>\varepsilon\}\le\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}{N\choose k}\varepsilon^k(1-\varepsilon)^{N-k}.\] Without convexity or another valid compression/support argument, this bound cannot be asserted merely from scenario feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical binomial scenario guarantee requires convexity and a valid support-dimension argument; sample feasibility alone does not extend it to nonconvex programs.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and the objective are convex, and \(g(\cdot,\xi)\) is convex.
The samples are independent and identically distributed.
The optimizer is measurably selected with support dimension at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed binomial bound controls \(\mathbb P^N\{V(x_N)>\varepsilon\}\) only within the stated structural scope.

notation.meaning: selected optimizer of the N-scenario program
valid upper bound on support dimension

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Dimension Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Underestimating support dimension makes a scenario certificate anti-conservative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(N\in\mathbb N\), \(0<\varepsilon<1\), and \(r\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\), define \(B(N,\varepsilon,r)=\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}{N\choose k}\varepsilon^k(1-\varepsilon)^{N-k}\). Suppose an applicable scenario theorem bounds the support dimension by an integer \(d\in\{1,ldots,N\}\), but a reported certificate uses an integer \(\widehat d\) satisfying \(1\le\widehat d<d\). Then \[B(N,\varepsilon,\widehat d)<B(N,\varepsilon,d).\] Consequently, the theorem supplies \(\mathbb P^N\{V(x_N)>\varepsilon\}\le B(N,\varepsilon,d)\), not the smaller reported bound. A confidence claim based on \(\widehat d\) is therefore unsupported unless \(\widehat d\) is proved to upper-bound the relevant support dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a valid scenario theorem uses support dimension d, substituting a smaller integer d-hat produces a strictly smaller binomial tail that the theorem does not certify.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb N\), \(0<\varepsilon<1\), and \(1\le\widehat d<d\le N\), with \(d,\widehat d\in\mathbb N\).
An applicable scenario theorem certifies the violation bound using support-dimension upper bound \(d\).

knowledge_statements.title: In-Sample Feasibility Without Generalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A rich decision class can memorize every sampled constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be uniformly distributed on \([0,1]\), and let a decision be any measurable set \(A\subseteq[0,1]\), interpreted as its violation region. Given samples \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N\), select \(A_N=[0,1]\setminus\{Z_1,\ldots,Z_N\}\). Then every sampled constraint is satisfied because \(Z_i\notin A_N\), so the empirical violation frequency is zero. Nevertheless, the sample set is finite and has Lebesgue measure zero, whence \(\mathbb P(Z\in A_N)=1\). Thus perfect in-sample feasibility alone provides no positive out-of-sample reliability guarantee for an unrestricted decision class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unrestricted rule can exclude exactly the observed samples, attaining zero empirical violations while violating with probability one on new data.
assumptions_latex: The admissible decision class contains every measurable subset of \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected decision has zero in-sample violations but \(V(A_N)=1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence Multiplicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous confidence requires accounting for every reported certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb N\), and let \(E_1,\ldots,E_M\) be certificate-failure events on a common probability space. Suppose \(0\le\beta_j\le1\) and \(\mathbb P(E_j)\le\beta_j\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,M\}\). No independence is required. The union bound gives \[\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{M}E_j\right)\le\sum_{j=1}^{M}\beta_j.\] Hence, if every certificate is reported with failure budget \(\beta\), the guaranteed simultaneous confidence from these marginal bounds is at least \(\max\{0,1-M\beta\}\). To guarantee familywise confidence at least \(1-\beta\), it suffices to choose nonnegative budgets satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^{M}\beta_j\le\beta\), including the Bonferroni allocation \(\beta_j=\beta/M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Marginal confidence guarantees do not automatically remain simultaneous. The union bound adds the certificate-failure budgets, and allocating total budget beta across all certificates controls familywise error without requiring independence.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb N\) and \(E_1,\ldots,E_M\) are events on a common probability space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\bigcup_{j=1}^{M}E_j)\le\sum_{j=1}^{M}\beta_j\); therefore \(\sum_{j=1}^{M}\beta_j\le\beta\) ensures familywise confidence at least \(1-\beta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The statement is the finite union bound and its Bonferroni allocation consequence.
